items.title: Nobody Tells You When an OAuth Refresh Token Expires
items.summary: While integrating third-party OAuth providers into the Agentic Identity Broker , three things cost me the most. Refresh tokens expired without any announcement. When they did, the provider answered with the same invalid_grant it uses for every other cause. And some providers, Databricks in my case, let an administrator change how refresh tokens rotate, with side effects on token issuing and expiry. In October, lost third-party sessions were the broker’s most visible problem . All three have the same cause. OAuth gives a provider no standard way to tell a client how long a refresh token lives or why it stopped working. So each vendor writes its limits into its documentation, returns them in a custom field it made up, or simply says nothing. Different limits and behaviours are fine with me, as long as a client can read them. An IETF draft proposes that for the token lifetime. Why providers pick their own limits # The specifications leave refresh token lifetimes open. The draft I discuss below sums up RFC 6749 like this: OAuth 2.0 “does not contain any normative language around expiration or lack thereof for refresh tokens, mentioning only that they are ’typically long-lasting’”. The security best practice (RFC 9700) says that refresh tokens “SHOULD expire if the client has been inactive for some time” and puts the expiration time “at the discretion of the authorization server”. Most providers bind the refresh token to the grant that the user gave the client and give it a lifetime of its own. Off-the-shelf identity products let the tenant’s administrator set that lifetime, usually per client application, so two integrations with the same provider can behave differently. Idle and absolute limits each have a good reason to exist. An idle limit ends refresh tokens that nobody uses any more, as RFC 9700 asks. An absolute limit ends access that is still in use, which providers want, according to the draft, when access is “too sensitive to allow indefinite access (e.g. mail or health data)”. So I don’t question that providers set these limits. The trouble starts on the integrator’s side, where I have to look up each provider’s combination and hard-code it or work around it. Refresh token lifetimes at 18 providers # The table lists what each vendor documents as of November 2026. “Renewed by refreshing” means that a successful refresh starts the clock again, and “tenant” means that whoever operates or administers the tenant sets the limit. Provider Refresh token limit Renewed by refreshing Set by In the token response Airtable 60 days yes vendor refresh_expires_in Amazon Cognito 30 days after sign-in by default, 60 minutes to 10 years no tenant no Atlassian 90 days of inactivity yes vendor no Auth0 idle 30 days by default, maximum up to 1 year or switched off idle yes, maximum no tenant no Box 60 days yes vendor no Databricks 7 days by default, 5 minutes to 90 days only with single-use tokens tenant no GitHub Apps 6 months, with expiring user tokens enabled yes vendor refresh_token_expires_in Google 6 months without use, 7 days for apps in testing yes vendor, or the user with time-based access no Intuit QuickBooks 100 days without use, 5 years in total 100 days yes, 5 years no vendor x_refresh_token_expires_in Keycloak session idle and session maximum idle yes, maximum no tenant refresh_expires_in Linear 30 days yes vendor no Microsoft Entra 90 days by default, 24 hours for single-page apps and email one-time passcodes not for single-page apps vendor no Notion MCP 180 days from authorization no vendor no Okta unlimited by default, 7 days without use idle yes tenant no Salesforce until revoked by default, or idle, or fixed depends on the policy tenant no Spotify 6 months from authorization no vendor no Xero 60 days without use yes vendor no Zoom 90 days new token per refresh, restart of the 90 days not stated vendor no A “no” in the last column means that the linked documentation shows no such field. The table rests on documentation alone and not on tests, so please read it as a snapshot of vendor claims. Where the vendor fixes the limit, it goes from 24 hours for single-page apps at Microsoft to 5 years at Intuit. Where the tenant sets it, the range is wider still: from 5 minutes at Databricks to 10 years at Cognito, and the default at Salesforce has no limit at all. The numbers also mean different things. At Linear or Box, a client that refreshes regularly keeps its connection for good. At Notion or Spotify, the same client loses it after 180 days or 6 months, however often it refreshed. At 6 of the 18, the vendor doesn’t decide the limit. Auth0, Cognito, Keycloak and Okta are identity products that other companies run, and at Databricks and Salesforce the customer’s administrator configures the policy per application. For these 6, the documentation only gives me the range of what I might meet in the wild. Rotation settings change the rules per client # Databricks is the example I ran into myself. An administrator can set a refresh token time-to-live (TTL) for each OAuth application, 10080 minutes or 7 days by default, and can turn on single-use refresh tokens, which is Databricks’ name for refresh token rotation. With rotation, the provider issues a new refresh token on every refresh and invalidates the old one. The API reference explains what that switch does to the first setting: “When single-use refresh tokens are enabled, this represents the TTL of an individual refresh token. If the refresh token is used before it expires, a new one is issued with a renewed individual TTL.” About a second setting, the absolute session lifetime, it says: “Effective only when the single-use refresh token feature is enabled.” So with rotation on, the same number becomes a sliding limit, and a separate setting defines the absolute end, which with rotation off is simply the TTL. My client sees none of this. It gets a refresh token and finds out later which combination the administrator chose. Rotation can also come with a reuse interval, also called grace period or leeway, in which the previous refresh token still works, so that a lost response doesn’t end the session. Every provider that offers this concept seems to size it differently: Okta 30 seconds by default, Atlassian 10 minutes, Linear and Xero 30 minutes, and Notion keeps the one previous token valid. Outside that interval, Notion treats a reused token as stolen and can revoke the whole grant. A client that runs more than one replica has to know these numbers, and they exist in documentation only as well. One invalid_grant for every cause # When a refresh token has ended, the client learns it through invalid_grant . RFC 6749 defines that code for a grant or refresh token that “is invalid, expired, revoked, does not match the redirection URI used in the authorization request, or was issued to another client”. The providers add their own causes behind it. Atlassian returns it after the user changed their password. Microsoft documents a matrix of which password event revokes which kind of refresh token. items.summary_html:
While integrating third-party OAuth providers into the Agentic Identity Broker, three things cost me the most. Refresh tokens expired without any announcement. When they did, the provider answered with the same invalid_grant it uses for every other cause. And some providers, Databricks in my case, let an administrator change how refresh tokens rotate, with side effects on token issuing and expiry. In October, lost third-party sessions were the broker’s most visible problem.

All three have the same cause. OAuth gives a provider no standard way to tell a client how long a refresh token lives or why it stopped working. So each vendor writes its limits into its documentation, returns them in a custom field it made up, or simply says nothing. Different limits and behaviours are fine with me, as long as a client can read them. An IETF draft proposes that for the token lifetime.

Why providers pick their own limits #

The specifications leave refresh token lifetimes open. The draft I discuss below sums up RFC 6749 like this: OAuth 2.0 “does not contain any normative language around expiration or lack thereof for refresh tokens, mentioning only that they are ’typically long-lasting’”. The security best practice (RFC 9700) says that refresh tokens “SHOULD expire if the client has been inactive for some time” and puts the expiration time “at the discretion of the authorization server”.

Most providers bind the refresh token to the grant that the user gave the client and give it a lifetime of its own. Off-the-shelf identity products let the tenant’s administrator set that lifetime, usually per client application, so two integrations with the same provider can behave differently.

Idle and absolute limits each have a good reason to exist. An idle limit ends refresh tokens that nobody uses any more, as RFC 9700 asks. An absolute limit ends access that is still in use, which providers want, according to the draft, when access is “too sensitive to allow indefinite access (e.g. mail or health data)”. So I don’t question that providers set these limits. The trouble starts on the integrator’s side, where I have to look up each provider’s combination and hard-code it or work around it.

Refresh token lifetimes at 18 providers #

The table lists what each vendor documents as of November 2026. “Renewed by refreshing” means that a successful refresh starts the clock again, and “tenant” means that whoever operates or administers the tenant sets the limit.

ProviderRefresh token limitRenewed by refreshingSet byIn the token response Airtable60 daysyesvendorrefresh_expires_inAmazon Cognito30 days after sign-in by default, 60 minutes to 10 yearsnotenantnoAtlassian90 days of inactivityyesvendornoAuth0idle 30 days by default, maximum up to 1 year or switched offidle yes, maximum notenantnoBox60 daysyesvendornoDatabricks7 days by default, 5 minutes to 90 daysonly with single-use tokenstenantnoGitHub Apps6 months, with expiring user tokens enabledyesvendorrefresh_token_expires_inGoogle6 months without use, 7 days for apps in testingyesvendor, or the user with time-based accessnoIntuit QuickBooks100 days without use, 5 years in total100 days yes, 5 years novendorx_refresh_token_expires_inKeycloaksession idle and session maximumidle yes, maximum notenantrefresh_expires_inLinear30 daysyesvendornoMicrosoft Entra90 days by default, 24 hours for single-page apps and email one-time passcodesnot for single-page appsvendornoNotion MCP180 days from authorizationnovendornoOktaunlimited by default, 7 days without useidle yestenantnoSalesforceuntil revoked by default, or idle, or fixeddepends on the policytenantnoSpotify6 months from authorizationnovendornoXero60 days without useyesvendornoZoom90 daysnew token per refresh, restart of the 90 days not statedvendorno

A “no” in the last column means that the linked documentation shows no such field. The table rests on documentation alone and not on tests, so please read it as a snapshot of vendor claims.

Where the vendor fixes the limit, it goes from 24 hours for single-page apps at Microsoft to 5 years at Intuit. Where the tenant sets it, the range is wider still: from 5 minutes at Databricks to 10 years at Cognito, and the default at Salesforce has no limit at all. The numbers also mean different things. At Linear or Box, a client that refreshes regularly keeps its connection for good. At Notion or Spotify, the same client loses it after 180 days or 6 months, however often it refreshed. At 6 of the 18, the vendor doesn’t decide the limit. Auth0, Cognito, Keycloak and Okta are identity products that other companies run, and at Databricks and Salesforce the customer’s administrator configures the policy per application. For these 6, the documentation only gives me the range of what I might meet in the wild.

Rotation settings change the rules per client #

Databricks is the example I ran into myself. An administrator can set a refresh token time-to-live (TTL) for each OAuth application, 10080 minutes or 7 days by default, and can turn on single-use refresh tokens, which is Databricks’ name for refresh token rotation. With rotation, the provider issues a new refresh token on every refresh and invalidates the old one. The API reference explains what that switch does to the first setting: “When single-use refresh tokens are enabled, this represents the TTL of an individual refresh token. If the refresh token is used before it expires, a new one is issued with a renewed individual TTL.” About a second setting, the absolute session lifetime, it says: “Effective only when the single-use refresh token feature is enabled.”

So with rotation on, the same number becomes a sliding limit, and a separate setting defines the absolute end, which with rotation off is simply the TTL. My client sees none of this. It gets a refresh token and finds out later which combination the administrator chose.

Rotation can also come with a reuse interval, also called grace period or leeway, in which the previous refresh token still works, so that a lost response doesn’t end the session. Every provider that offers this concept seems to size it differently: Okta 30 seconds by default, Atlassian 10 minutes, Linear and Xero 30 minutes, and Notion keeps the one previous token valid. Outside that interval, Notion treats a reused token as stolen and can revoke the whole grant. A client that runs more than one replica has to know these numbers, and they exist in documentation only as well.

One invalid_grant for every cause #

When a refresh token has ended, the client learns it through invalid_grant. RFC 6749 defines that code for a grant or refresh token that “is invalid, expired, revoked, does not match the redirection URI used in the authorization request, or was issued to another client”. The providers add their own causes behind it. Atlassian returns it after the user changed their password. Microsoft documents a matrix of which password event revokes which kind of refresh token. Google invalidates the oldest token “without warning” once an account holds more than 100 for the same client.

I can’t tell these causes apart in the client, so I can’t tell my own user either. “Your access expired after 90 days” and “someone revoked this app” call for different messages, and my client only knows that the person has to log in again. Google is an exception for one case: when an administrator’s session policy ends the access, it adds an error_subtype to the response. In case you want to read more about the revocation side, see my field guide entry on consent and revocation.

Four vendors report the lifetime in their own fields #

Four vendors already return the remaining lifetime in the token response, and (of course) they use three different names for it:

VendorField in the token responseMeaning GitHubrefresh_token_expires_inseconds until the refresh token expires, always 6 monthsAirtablerefresh_expires_inseconds until the refresh token expires, 60 days expectedKeycloakrefresh_expires_inseconds until the refresh token expires, per its token response classIntuitx_refresh_token_expires_inseconds left of the rolling 100 daysIntuitx_refresh_token_hard_expires_inseconds left of the 5 years, only with a request header

A known date lets my client plan ahead. I can ask users to reauthorize the next time they are around, or contact them out of band, well before the connection ends and a business process breaks. I can also refresh idle connections just before the provider would end them, instead of running a generic cron job. Planning ahead currently still needs a code path per provider.

What the IETF draft adds #

OAuth 2.0 Refresh Token and Authorization Expiration by Nick Watson of Google started as an individual draft in June 2025. The OAuth working group adopted it in December 2025, and revision 03 is from 6 July 2026. It defines two parameters for the token response:

  • refresh_token_timeout is the “time in seconds that the refresh token may be held by the client without exchanging”, which is the idle limit.
  • authorization_expires_in is the “lifetime in seconds of the user’s authorization for the scopes contained in the issued or presented refresh token”, which is the absolute limit.

A provider with a 7-day idle limit and a user who granted access for 10 days would answer like this:

File: token-response.json
{
 "access_token": "...",
 "token_type": "Bearer",
 "expires_in": 3600,
 "refresh_token": "...",
 "refresh_token_timeout": 604800,
 "authorization_expires_in": 864000
}

The two parameters match the two clocks from the table above. Linear could send only the first, Spotify only the second and Intuit both. An authorization server can announce its support in its metadata with refresh_token_expiration_types_supported, and the draft extends token introspection so that a client can ask about a refresh token it already holds. For rotating tokens, the draft says that the duration can now “be communicated as part of the API rather than relying on documentation”.

What I still miss in the draft #

I consider the draft a good start, but it leaves three things open.

The error stays as it is. According to the draft, the “existing invalid_grant error code already explicitly covers token expiration and should be sufficient”. For a planned expiry I agree, because the client knew the date. For every other cause, the client is where it was. I’d like to see a machine-readable reason next to invalid_grant, along the lines of Google’s error_subtype, that separates expired, revoked and rotated-out tokens.

Rotation settings are missing too. Whether refresh tokens rotate and how long the previous one stays valid could be two more fields in the authorization server metadata. For a client with several replicas, they matter as much as the lifetime.

My biggest doubt is about adoption. The draft currently targets Informational as the intended status, and it’s marked as optional. Without that field, a missing parameter can mean that the token has no limit or that the provider doesn’t support the draft, and the draft tells clients to handle both in the same way. GitHub, Airtable, Keycloak and Intuit already ship field names that their clients might depend on, and I see little that would make them add a second set. What could help is a profile that requires the parameters, such as the MCP Authorization specification.

What an integrator can do today #

Until providers report their limits, the limits have to live in the client. This is what I’d do in an integration today, and the vendor documentation backs most of it:

  • Treat invalid_grant as final, discard the refresh token and start a new authorization instead of retrying.
  • Allow only one refresh per grant at a time, across all replicas, and store the new refresh token together with the new access token before using either.
  • Read the vendor’s own expiry field where one exists, and read it from every response, because the value can change from one refresh to the next.
  • Refresh connections that nobody uses before a known idle limit ends them.
  • Keep the limits in configuration per provider, per tenant and per client application. With admin-set policies, two customers of the same vendor, or two applications of the same customer, can behave differently.
  • Tell the user the date where there is one, so they can reconnect before a job fails.

For MCP servers, I started to collect what vendors state about refresh token rotation in the MCP auth atlas of Letsauth Lab, which I maintain and introduced in Measuring How MCP Servers Authorize Agents. If you know how a provider expires or rotates its refresh tokens and the table above has it wrong, I’d like to hear about it. And if you miss the same things in the draft as I do, its issue tracker is the place to say so.

items.title: DDoS Support for NATGWv2 IP - Public Preview
items.summary: Introduction Azure DDoS Protection now covers the public IP addresses used by Azure NAT Gateway StandardV2, in public preview. Customers can protect the StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IPs that carry their outbound internet traffic from network-layer DDoS attacks, using the same DDoS Network Protection and IP Protection they already use. There's no new API, feature registration or appliance to manage, and DDoS protection doesn't open the gateway to unsolicited inbound connections. Why it matters NAT Gateway doesn't accept inbound connections, but its public IPs are still reachable from the internet, and they're the identity of everything behind them. Your outbound IPs are known to others. Every external service your workloads call sees these IPs. Partners, SaaS providers and banks often keep them on allow-lists. Anyone who learns them can aim traffic at them. One IP set serves many workloads. Every VM in the associated subnets shares the gateway's public IPs. A flood that saturates these IPs can disrupt outbound connectivity for all of them at once. That includes calls to external APIs, partner integrations, package and update downloads, and telemetry. Outbound failures hurt production. An attack on the NAT IPs doesn't have to reach your workloads to cause an outage. It only has to break their path to the internet. Same protection as your inbound endpoints. Until now, customers could protect inbound public IPs but not the IPs behind NAT Gateway StandardV2. With this preview, outbound IPs get automatic network-layer mitigation, plus the DDoS metrics, diagnostics and alerts they already use. Easier compliance. Security policies and posture checks that require DDoS protection on all public IPs no longer have an exception for NAT Gateway IPs. Figure 1: Outbound workloads use a StandardV2 NAT Gateway and a DDoS-protected public IP to reach the internet. Conceptual diagram, not an Azure portal screenshot. Protect the public IPs behind your outbound connectivity A NAT gateway uses its associated public IP addresses when workloads initiate connections to the internet. With this preview, eligible StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IP addresses can receive Azure DDoS Protection while associated with a StandardV2 NAT Gateway. Figure 2: The Outbound IP blade of a StandardV2 NAT Gateway lists an individual public IP address and a public IP prefix. Resource names, subscription details, and IP addresses in this and the following screenshots are generic examples. You use the familiar Azure DDoS Protection model. There is no separate DDoS setting on the NAT Gateway resource: DDoS Network Protection: Protect eligible NAT Gateway public IPs through the virtual network's protection configuration when the gateway is associated with a subnet in that virtual network. DDoS IP Protection: Enable protection on an eligible individual public IP address associated with StandardV2 NAT Gateway. This brings network-layer DDoS protection to a public IP that plays an important role in your outbound architecture, without changing how NAT Gateway establishes outbound connections. It does not make NAT Gateway an inbound endpoint: unsolicited inbound connections remain blocked. See it in the Azure portal The Configure DDoS Protection pane on the public IP resource shows the protection status and lets you choose the protection type. Network Protection, inherited from the virtual network. The public IP shows Protected: IP is DDoS protected, with the Network type selected. This type inherits DDoS protection from the virtual network. Figure 3: The public IP shows protected status with Network Protection inherited from the virtual network. IP Protection, specific to the public IP. Selecting the IP type applies protection to this IP address only. The pane lets you add the IP to an existing DDoS protection plan and pick that plan from a list. Figure 4: The same public IP shows protected status with IP Protection selected and an existing DDoS protection plan. Disabled. Selecting Disable shows the public IP as unprotected, even when protection is configured on the virtual network. The pane warns that the IP will not receive any protection while this option is selected. Figure 5: Selecting Disable shows the public IP as unprotected, even when protection is configured on the virtual network. Get started in the Azure portal Create or use a StandardV2 NAT Gateway, associate it with your workload subnet, and configure an eligible native StandardV2 public IP address. Choose your protection model. For Network Protection, configure Azure DDoS Protection on the virtual network. For IP Protection, open the individual Public IP address resource and configure DDoS protection there. Return to the public IP resource to check its protection status. Use its monitoring experience to review applicable DDoS metrics and alerts. The portal experience follows the existing public IP workflow. Depending on your configuration, the public IP can show protection inherited from the virtual network or IP-specific protection. Preview scope and considerations This preview supports eligible native StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IP addresses used with StandardV2 NAT Gateway. Some scenarios are not part of it: It does not extend DDoS protection to the Standard NAT Gateway SKU. DDoS custom policies for NAT Gateway public IPs are not part of the initial preview. Public IP prefixes are supported only through DDoS Network Protection. When a virtual network uses Network Protection, the protection is inherited and applies automatically to the entire IP prefix. DDoS IP Protection does not support public IP prefixes. Figure 6: The StandardV2 public IP prefix resource overview. This screenshot does not establish IP-level protection eligibility for a prefix. Figure 7: The prefix Metrics blade lists DDoS-related metrics. Metric availability alone does not establish the final preview support boundary. Azure DDoS Protection addresses network-layer attacks. It is not a substitute for application-layer protection where your architecture requires it. Ready to explore? Start with a StandardV2 NAT Gateway and an eligible native StandardV2 public IP, then choose the virtual-network or individual-public-IP protection model that fits your deployment.
items.summary_html:
Introduction

Azure DDoS Protection now covers the public IP addresses used by Azure NAT Gateway StandardV2, in public preview. Customers can protect the StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IPs that carry their outbound internet traffic from network-layer DDoS attacks, using the same DDoS Network Protection and IP Protection they already use. There's no new API, feature registration or appliance to manage, and DDoS protection doesn't open the gateway to unsolicited inbound connections.

Why it matters

NAT Gateway doesn't accept inbound connections, but its public IPs are still reachable from the internet, and they're the identity of everything behind them.

  • Your outbound IPs are known to others. Every external service your workloads call sees these IPs. Partners, SaaS providers and banks often keep them on allow-lists. Anyone who learns them can aim traffic at them.
  • One IP set serves many workloads. Every VM in the associated subnets shares the gateway's public IPs. A flood that saturates these IPs can disrupt outbound connectivity for all of them at once. That includes calls to external APIs, partner integrations, package and update downloads, and telemetry.
  • Outbound failures hurt production. An attack on the NAT IPs doesn't have to reach your workloads to cause an outage. It only has to break their path to the internet.
  • Same protection as your inbound endpoints. Until now, customers could protect inbound public IPs but not the IPs behind NAT Gateway StandardV2. With this preview, outbound IPs get automatic network-layer mitigation, plus the DDoS metrics, diagnostics and alerts they already use.
  • Easier compliance. Security policies and posture checks that require DDoS protection on all public IPs no longer have an exception for NAT Gateway IPs.

 

 

Figure 1: Outbound workloads use a StandardV2 NAT Gateway and a DDoS-protected public IP to reach the internet. Conceptual diagram, not an Azure portal screenshot.

Protect the public IPs behind your outbound connectivity

A NAT gateway uses its associated public IP addresses when workloads initiate connections to the internet. With this preview, eligible StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IP addresses can receive Azure DDoS Protection while associated with a StandardV2 NAT Gateway.

 

 

Figure 2: The Outbound IP blade of a StandardV2 NAT Gateway lists an individual public IP address and a public IP prefix. Resource names, subscription details, and IP addresses in this and the following screenshots are generic examples.

You use the familiar Azure DDoS Protection model. There is no separate DDoS setting on the NAT Gateway resource:

  • DDoS Network Protection: Protect eligible NAT Gateway public IPs through the virtual network's protection configuration when the gateway is associated with a subnet in that virtual network.
  • DDoS IP Protection: Enable protection on an eligible individual public IP address associated with StandardV2 NAT Gateway.

This brings network-layer DDoS protection to a public IP that plays an important role in your outbound architecture, without changing how NAT Gateway establishes outbound connections. It does not make NAT Gateway an inbound endpoint: unsolicited inbound connections remain blocked.

See it in the Azure portal

The Configure DDoS Protection pane on the public IP resource shows the protection status and lets you choose the protection type.

Network Protection, inherited from the virtual network. The public IP shows Protected: IP is DDoS protected, with the Network type selected. This type inherits DDoS protection from the virtual network.

 

 

Figure 3: The public IP shows protected status with Network Protection inherited from the virtual network.

IP Protection, specific to the public IP. Selecting the IP type applies protection to this IP address only. The pane lets you add the IP to an existing DDoS protection plan and pick that plan from a list.

 

 

Figure 4: The same public IP shows protected status with IP Protection selected and an existing DDoS protection plan.

Disabled. Selecting Disable shows the public IP as unprotected, even when protection is configured on the virtual network. The pane warns that the IP will not receive any protection while this option is selected.

 

 

Figure 5: Selecting Disable shows the public IP as unprotected, even when protection is configured on the virtual network.

Get started in the Azure portal
  1. Create or use a StandardV2 NAT Gateway, associate it with your workload subnet, and configure an eligible native StandardV2 public IP address.
  2. Choose your protection model. For Network Protection, configure Azure DDoS Protection on the virtual network. For IP Protection, open the individual Public IP address resource and configure DDoS protection there.
  3. Return to the public IP resource to check its protection status. Use its monitoring experience to review applicable DDoS metrics and alerts.

The portal experience follows the existing public IP workflow. Depending on your configuration, the public IP can show protection inherited from the virtual network or IP-specific protection.

Preview scope and considerations

This preview supports eligible native StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IP addresses used with StandardV2 NAT Gateway. Some scenarios are not part of it:

  • It does not extend DDoS protection to the Standard NAT Gateway SKU.
  • DDoS custom policies for NAT Gateway public IPs are not part of the initial preview.

 

Public IP prefixes are supported only through DDoS Network Protection. When a virtual network uses Network Protection, the protection is inherited and applies automatically to the entire IP prefix. DDoS IP Protection does not support public IP prefixes.

 

 

 

Figure 6: The StandardV2 public IP prefix resource overview. This screenshot does not establish IP-level protection eligibility for a prefix.

 

 

Figure 7: The prefix Metrics blade lists DDoS-related metrics. Metric availability alone does not establish the final preview support boundary.

Azure DDoS Protection addresses network-layer attacks. It is not a substitute for application-layer protection where your architecture requires it.

Ready to explore?

Start with a StandardV2 NAT Gateway and an eligible native StandardV2 public IP, then choose the virtual-network or individual-public-IP protection model that fits your deployment.

items.title: Azure DDoS Custom Policy GA
items.summary: More control, broader coverage with Azure DDoS Protection custom policy Fine-tune protocol-specific DDoS detection for internet-facing workloads while keeping Azure’s adaptive protection as the default. Organizations depend on Azure DDoS Protection to monitor traffic continuously and mitigate network-layer attacks at cloud scale. Most workloads benefit from a hands-off, adaptive experience. But applications with planned traffic surges, unusual packet-rate patterns, strict latency requirements, or distinct environments sometimes need more control over when mitigation begins. Azure DDoS Protection custom policy adds that optional control. It lets you define fixed inbound detection thresholds for TCP, UDP, and TCP SYN traffic and apply them to supported public endpoints. The result is a protection model that remains automatic by default while giving application and network teams a precise override when their workload calls for it. In one sentence: Custom policy extends Azure DDoS Protection’s adaptive baseline with optional, protocol-specific controls; it does not replace the turnkey default. Azure DDoS Protection custom policy is now generally available, letting customers replace machine-learning auto-tuning with fixed protocol-specific detection thresholds per protected resource across Azure resource types with public IPs. Available on Network Protection and IP Protection SKUs, it already covers 929 policies and about 1,970 attachments pre-GA, led by OpenAI. Why customers asked for more control Adaptive auto-tuning works well for most workloads because Azure learns the normal traffic profile of each protected endpoint and adjusts mitigation thresholds as that profile changes. A fixed, application-specific threshold can be useful when traffic is predictable in a way that the service cannot infer ahead of time. A gaming launch, ticket sale, live stream, or seasonal event is expected to create a sudden but legitimate increase in packet rate. A high-throughput service regularly operates near a threshold and needs an explicitly controlled trigger. A latency-sensitive workload benefits from a tighter mitigation threshold for one protocol. Development, test, and production environments need separate policies and change controls. Security teams want repeatable, infrastructure-as-code deployment and verifiable associations to protected endpoints. Automatic by default; explicit where you choose A custom threshold changes behavior only for the protocol you configure on the associated resource. Azure uses the fixed value for that protocol, while protocols without a custom rule continue to use adaptive auto-tuning. Detaching the custom policy returns the endpoint to the default adaptive behavior. Design principle: Start with the default adaptive service. Add a custom rule only when you have a measured workload requirement and a monitoring plan. What is new in the expanded experience The launch experience is designed around the Azure resource and its public endpoint, rather than asking customers to reason about an internal “frontend IP” abstraction. The underlying association still depends on the resource and management interface, but the customer journey begins with the workload that needs protection. Broader resource reach. items.summary_html:
More control, broader coverage with Azure DDoS Protection custom policy

Fine-tune protocol-specific DDoS detection for internet-facing workloads while keeping Azure’s adaptive protection as the default.

Organizations depend on Azure DDoS Protection to monitor traffic continuously and mitigate network-layer attacks at cloud scale. Most workloads benefit from a hands-off, adaptive experience. But applications with planned traffic surges, unusual packet-rate patterns, strict latency requirements, or distinct environments sometimes need more control over when mitigation begins.

Azure DDoS Protection custom policy adds that optional control. It lets you define fixed inbound detection thresholds for TCP, UDP, and TCP SYN traffic and apply them to supported public endpoints. The result is a protection model that remains automatic by default while giving application and network teams a precise override when their workload calls for it.

In one sentence: Custom policy extends Azure DDoS Protection’s adaptive baseline with optional, protocol-specific controls; it does not replace the turnkey default.

Azure DDoS Protection custom policy is now generally available, letting customers replace machine-learning auto-tuning with fixed protocol-specific detection thresholds per protected resource across Azure resource types with public IPs. Available on Network Protection and IP Protection SKUs, it already covers 929 policies and about 1,970 attachments pre-GA, led by OpenAI. 

Why customers asked for more control

Adaptive auto-tuning works well for most workloads because Azure learns the normal traffic profile of each protected endpoint and adjusts mitigation thresholds as that profile changes. A fixed, application-specific threshold can be useful when traffic is predictable in a way that the service cannot infer ahead of time.

A gaming launch, ticket sale, live stream, or seasonal event is expected to create a sudden but legitimate increase in packet rate.

A high-throughput service regularly operates near a threshold and needs an explicitly controlled trigger.

A latency-sensitive workload benefits from a tighter mitigation threshold for one protocol.

Development, test, and production environments need separate policies and change controls.

Security teams want repeatable, infrastructure-as-code deployment and verifiable associations to protected endpoints.

Automatic by default; explicit where you choose

A custom threshold changes behavior only for the protocol you configure on the associated resource. Azure uses the fixed value for that protocol, while protocols without a custom rule continue to use adaptive auto-tuning. Detaching the custom policy returns the endpoint to the default adaptive behavior.

Design principle: Start with the default adaptive service. Add a custom rule only when you have a measured workload requirement and a monitoring plan.

 

What is new in the expanded experience

The launch experience is designed around the Azure resource and its public endpoint, rather than asking customers to reason about an internal “frontend IP” abstraction. The underlying association still depends on the resource and management interface, but the customer journey begins with the workload that needs protection.

Broader resource reach. Apply a custom policy to supported public endpoints across virtual machines, virtual machine scale sets, Azure Kubernetes Service, Standard Load Balancer, Application Gateway, Azure Firewall, and Azure Bastion.

A public IP-centric portal flow. Choose eligible public IP addresses from one picker, regardless of the supported resource behind them.

Consistent management options. Create and manage policies through the Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, and ARM/REST, subject to management-surface rollout.

Clear protocol controls. Set independent inbound detection thresholds for TCP, UDP, and TCP SYN traffic.

Existing observability. Continue using Azure Monitor metrics, diagnostic logs, alerts, and DDoS Protection telemetry to validate behavior and investigate mitigation activity.

Resource-oriented association model

Resource

Customer-facing scope

Underlying association

Azure Virtual Machines

VM public endpoint

Instance-level public IP

Virtual Machine Scale Sets

VMSS public endpoint

Individual public IP, subject to ownership and lifecycle

Azure Kubernetes Service

AKS public endpoint

Public IP or Standard Load Balancer frontend

Standard Load Balancer

Public frontend

Public IP or frontend IP configuration, depending on management surface

Application Gateway

Application public endpoint

Associated public IP configuration

Azure Firewall

Firewall public endpoint

Associated public IP configuration

Azure Bastion

Bastion public endpoint

Associated public IP configuration

 

How detection threshold rules work

Each rule names a traffic type and the inbound packet-per-second (PPS) value that triggers mitigation. The currently validated ranges are:

Traffic type

Valid range

Example use

TCP

50,000–2,000,000 PPS

Control general inbound TCP trigger

UDP

20,000–200,000 PPS

Tune for packet-intensive UDP services

TCP SYN

1,000–100,000 PPS

Tune connection-establishment trigger

Treat the range as a validation boundary, not a recommendation. Select a value from measured normal traffic, expected peak traffic, application capacity, and your risk tolerance.

Create a policy in the Azure portal

The portal workflow brings policy creation, public IP selection, rules, tags, and review into a single guided experience.

In the Azure portal, search for DDoS custom policies and select Create.

Choose the subscription, resource group, policy name, and region. Select the eligible public IP addresses that should use the policy.

 

 

Figure 1. Create the policy and select public IP addresses. Demo values are sanitized.

Use the public IP picker to select supported endpoints. The portal resolves the associated resource type and shows existing custom-policy associations.

 

 

 

 

Figure 2. Choose eligible public IP addresses across supported resources. Resource values are redacted.

On Custom rules, add the protocol-specific thresholds your workload requires. You do not have to define all protocols.

 

 

Figure 3. Configure independent inbound TCP, UDP, and TCP SYN thresholds.

Review the selected endpoints and rule count, then create the policy.

 

 

Figure 4. Review the policy configuration before deployment. Demo values are sanitized.

Automate with Azure CLI

The following example creates a custom policy with an inbound TCP threshold of 1,000,000 PPS and then returns the provisioning state and detection rules.

Create one detection rule

az network ddos-custom-policy create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyCustomPolicy \
  --location eastus \
  --detection-rule-name tcp-threshold \
  --detection-mode TrafficThreshold \
  --traffic-type Tcp \
  --packets-per-second 1000000

 

Verify the policy

az network ddos-custom-policy show \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyCustomPolicy \
  --query '{name:name, state:provisioningState, rules:detectionRules[].trafficDetectionRule}'

 

Association commands differ by resource and management surface. In the validated launch guidance, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are two management paths to the same capability: CLI can associate the policy through the eligible public IP, while PowerShell can use the resource-specific frontend configuration for Load Balancer. Follow the current Learn procedure for the resource you are configuring.

Automate with Azure PowerShell

Azure PowerShell can create several protocol rules in one policy.

Create a policy with TCP, UDP, and TCP SYN rules

$tcpRule = New-AzDdosCustomPolicyDetectionRule `
  -Name 'tcpRule1' -TrafficType Tcp -PacketsPerSecond 1000000
$udpRule = New-AzDdosCustomPolicyDetectionRule `
  -Name 'udpRule1' -TrafficType Udp -PacketsPerSecond 100000
$tcpSynRule = New-AzDdosCustomPolicyDetectionRule `
  -Name 'tcpSynRule1' -TrafficType TcpSyn -PacketsPerSecond 50000

$policy = New-AzDdosCustomPolicy `
  -ResourceGroupName 'MyResourceGroup' `
  -Name 'MyCustomPolicy' `
  -Location 'eastus' `
  -DetectionRule @($tcpRule, $udpRule, $tcpSynRule)

 

 

Operational guidance

Measure before you set. Use normal and peak traffic data, not a generic threshold copied from another application.

Leave headroom. Account for organic growth, failover, scale-out, and known events.

Change one protocol at a time. This makes results easier to observe and rollback.

Test outside production first. Validate policy creation, association, monitoring, and detachment in a lower environment.

Monitor after every change. Watch DDoS metrics, mitigation notifications, flow logs, and application health.

Document ownership. Treat threshold and mitigation-rule changes as production security changes with RBAC, review, and change history.

Know the rollback. Detach the policy or remove a protocol rule to return that traffic to adaptive auto-tuning, following the current product procedure.

Get started

Start with the overview, choose the management surface that fits your workflow, deploy a test policy, and validate telemetry before production rollout.

Azure DDoS Protection custom policy overview

Create and manage a custom policy in the Azure portal

Create a custom policy using Azure CLI

Azure CLI command reference: az network ddos-custom-policy

Azure PowerShell command reference: New-AzDdosCustomPolicy

Monitor Azure DDoS Protection

Azure DDoS Protection remains designed to be automatic and adaptive at scale. Custom policy adds targeted control for the workloads that need it—without turning every protected application into a manually tuned system.

items.title: Frida 17.26.4 Released
items.summary: Barebone again. Its agents are now tested in live guests on every change, from Windows 95 to Windows 10 on arm64, which shook out a long list of bugs, and Windows XP works again. The XNU agent learned to talk over a UART and to run on an iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk. Outside of Barebone, @kkuehl fixed a deadlock and a race in the module registry on Windows, @Cassian433 fixed hexdump() offsets, @tubibibo brought back tsconfig.json path aliases in the compiler, and a broken app icon on Android no longer takes the whole enumeration down with it. Barebone Live guests Until now the agents were only built by CI. They are now also run, in eight QEMU guests: Windows 95, Windows XP, Windows XP x64, Windows 10 on arm64, and Linux on x86, x86_64, Arm and arm64. Each guest is booted once until it reports ready and snapshotted, and every test then resumes a fresh QEMU from that snapshot. Most of what follows fell out of getting those green. XNU is next, more on that below. Windows Windows XP works again, on x86 and x64. Later work on the NT agent had come to rely on APIs that arrived with Vista, so each of those now has a fallback. On Windows 9x, injection hung intermittently: VMM reuses the handle of an expired time-out, so cancelling one that had already fired could cancel another waiter’s. The changelog has the rest for both. Two fixes apply to every NT version. Gum changes the protection of what it allocates a page at a time, but the pool shares a page between allocations, so a CModule made its neighbors read-only; Gum now gets whole pages. And a kernel thread without a user-mode part now reports where it waits, from the stack pointer saved in its thread object. On arm64: Kernel code is patched while the other processors wait in an IPI, so none runs a half-written instruction. ACPI only gives a line’s vector to the driver it started, so the agent takes a vector of its own and routes the line there. Windows 10 1709 has neither the vector array nor ExAllocatePool2() that the agent relied on. Threads are watched through BaseThreadInitThunk() , as newer 64-bit Windows lacks BaseThreadStart() , and spawns are held with a branch to self. Lost wakeups The agents injected into Windows processes, on both NT and 9x, could sleep through a wake. A waiter could join a slot just as its last sleeper let go, and sleep where no wake would look. Each slot is now guarded, every slot a token holds is woken, and wakes are counted with a semaphore so that none coalesce. The main loop also armed its wakeup after checking it, missing a signal that landed in between. And on Arm, retaking a held recursive mutex used a weak compare-exchange, which may fail spuriously, leaving the owner waiting on itself. Linux Kernels without BTF were the theme here. On Alpine’s x86 kernel the agent panicked on its first read of the current task, and elsewhere a spawn never learned its pid, and reading another thread’s registers failed. The agent now falls back to fixed offsets for the leading pcpu_hot members, and discovers the task layout on its own. On arm64 kernels built with patchable function entries, the prologue of fixup_exception() starts with what ftrace patches, so our fault hook was never installed, and a faulting read in the agent took the kernel down. On 32-bit Arm, removing that hook restored the address before the jump, so a fault taken in between recursed until the kernel stack overflowed. Also on 32-bit Arm, per-CPU symbol detection put swapper_pg_dir out of reach, so writes to executable memory faulted, and kernel_write() was called with a junk position, so the agent in a process was never woken. XNU The XNU agent can now use a UART that the guest kernel leaves alone, such as UART1 on t8030, as its transport: it receives on the UART’s interrupt, and waits for room to transmit on its threshold interrupt. Interrupt controllers are found by phandle, and a line can be hooked without enabling it, so a driver can mask and unmask it. It also runs on an iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk under Inferno , ChefKiss’ QEMU derivative with Apple ARM device guest support, which is what our example config for XNU now targets. That took a few changes. iOS 26.1 inlines thread_set_state() everywhere, so we fall back to thread_set_state_internal() . A restore ramdisk has no shared cache, so the agent injected into a process looks libraries up in dyld’s image list. Its code is mapped executable up front, as under a code-signing monitor, anonymous memory that only later becomes executable is taken to be a debugger patching code, and loses execute unless the process is being debugged. And it can spawn threads from the bare thread the kernel starts it on, through pthread_create_from_mach_thread() , shuts GLib down when it stops, and no longer leaks a pthread per thread. This is the groundwork for running the XNU agent live on CI too, alongside the guests above. The tests already run against the ramdisk locally, and hooking them up is what we are about to do next. Windows @kkuehl ran Gum from several threads on Windows and found two bugs in the module registry. Looking up a global export enumerated the modules with the registry’s lock held, asking the loader about each. The loader makes such a query wait while a module is being loaded, and it notifies the registry of the module it is loading, which takes the registry’s lock. A lookup on one thread and a load on another could thus wait for each other forever. The modules are now collected first, and the loader asked with the registry unlocked. The heap API lookup had the same pattern and got the same fix. The other was a race: the registry was made available to other threads before the thread that created it had activated it, so a thread obtaining it in between found no modules. With 32 threads racing to be first, that happened in 87 of 400 processes. Thanks for the thorough work! On the USB side, a device that re-enumerates under the same instance ID, such as an iPhone switching USB configuration, was seen as unchanged by our libusb’s hotplug scan, so no events were emitted and the stale device remained, with outdated descriptors and interface paths. GumJS @Cassian433 fixed hexdump() when given an offset, closing an issue @chrisdmc opened back in 2021. The row loop counted from zero while the bytes were read from the offset, so an offset left empty rows at the end, and one past the length made the loop run off the end of the buffer. The length now counts from the offset, as documented. Thanks! Compiler @marsrcm reported that path aliases in tsconfig.json stopped resolving. The parsed config is handed to esbuild as JSON, and its paths option is a type that only knows how to serialize itself through Go’s newer JSON package, so our toolchain emitted it as an empty object. @tubibibo tracked it down and fixed it. Thanks, both! Android Enumerating applications or processes with icons failed altogether if a single icon failed to load, as @YSaxon reported. Such icons are now left out. Enjoy! Changelog barebone: Run the agents in live guests in CI. barebone: Support Windows XP again: run the worker on its own stack, read hal.dll exports, copy across processes by attaching, list threads with Toolhelp, place an agent in csrss, follow forwarded exports, and report faults. barebone: Only widen a large page’s rights on Windows. barebone: Give Gum whole pages on Windows. barebone: Tell where a Windows kernel thread waits. barebone: Size the Windows wakeup token by pointer. barebone: On Windows arm64, patch kernel code with other processors held, route interrupts by hand, find vectors without the array, skip tables the kernel can’t view, hold spawns with a branch to self, and watch threads via BaseThreadInitThunk() . barebone: On Windows 9x, cancel only pending time-outs, start the agent from a new thread, park on Wait_Semaphore , give the process agent’s TIB its stack, start it via its frame, and take module bases from PE headers. barebone: Stop losing wakes in agents injected into Windows processes, and arm the wakeup before checking it. barebone: Retake a held recursive mutex reliably. barebone: Drop the registry lock to unregister. barebone: On Linux without BTF, find pcpu_hot members, where tasks keep their stack, and task ids. barebone: Hook arm64 fixup_exception() under ftrace, and unpatch the Arm fault hook jump first. barebone: Tell Linux per-CPU symbols by section, and pass kernel_write() a null position on Arm. barebone: Add a UART transport for XNU, and find IRQ controllers by phandle. barebone: Fall back to thread_set_state_internal() on XNU. barebone: Find XNU images without a shared cache, map process agent code executable up front, spawn threads from bare threads, start them detached, and shut GLib down when the agent stops. barebone: Update the example configs, with the XNU one targeting an iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk under Inferno . windows: Fix a deadlock in global export lookup. Thanks @kkuehl ! module-registry: Fix a race in obtain() . Thanks @kkuehl ! heap-api: Fix a deadlock in CRT lookup on Windows. Thanks @kkuehl ! gumjs: Fix hexdump() offset handling. Thanks @Cassian433 and @chrisdmc ! compiler: Preserve tsconfig.json paths when serializing. Thanks @tubibibo and @marsrcm ! android: Omit icons that fail to load. Thanks @YSaxon ! libusb: Detect hotplug re-enumeration on Windows. efni: Define GLIB_2_84 from the GLib found. idun: Define GLIB_2_84 from the GLib found. vala: Avoid two warnings in generated C.
items.summary_html:
Barebone again. Its agents are now tested in live guests on every change, from Windows 95 to Windows 10 on arm64, which shook out a long list of bugs, and Windows XP works again. The XNU agent learned to talk over a UART and to run on an iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk. Outside of Barebone, @kkuehl fixed a deadlock and a race in the module registry on Windows, @Cassian433 fixed hexdump() offsets, @tubibibo brought back tsconfig.json path aliases in the compiler, and a broken app icon on Android no longer takes the whole enumeration down with it.

Barebone Live guests

Until now the agents were only built by CI. They are now also run, in eight QEMU guests: Windows 95, Windows XP, Windows XP x64, Windows 10 on arm64, and Linux on x86, x86_64, Arm and arm64. Each guest is booted once until it reports ready and snapshotted, and every test then resumes a fresh QEMU from that snapshot. Most of what follows fell out of getting those green. XNU is next, more on that below.

Windows

Windows XP works again, on x86 and x64. Later work on the NT agent had come to rely on APIs that arrived with Vista, so each of those now has a fallback. On Windows 9x, injection hung intermittently: VMM reuses the handle of an expired time-out, so cancelling one that had already fired could cancel another waiter’s. The changelog has the rest for both.

Two fixes apply to every NT version. Gum changes the protection of what it allocates a page at a time, but the pool shares a page between allocations, so a CModule made its neighbors read-only; Gum now gets whole pages. And a kernel thread without a user-mode part now reports where it waits, from the stack pointer saved in its thread object.

On arm64:

  • Kernel code is patched while the other processors wait in an IPI, so none runs a half-written instruction.
  • ACPI only gives a line’s vector to the driver it started, so the agent takes a vector of its own and routes the line there.
  • Windows 10 1709 has neither the vector array nor ExAllocatePool2() that the agent relied on.
  • Threads are watched through BaseThreadInitThunk(), as newer 64-bit Windows lacks BaseThreadStart(), and spawns are held with a branch to self.
Lost wakeups

The agents injected into Windows processes, on both NT and 9x, could sleep through a wake. A waiter could join a slot just as its last sleeper let go, and sleep where no wake would look. Each slot is now guarded, every slot a token holds is woken, and wakes are counted with a semaphore so that none coalesce. The main loop also armed its wakeup after checking it, missing a signal that landed in between. And on Arm, retaking a held recursive mutex used a weak compare-exchange, which may fail spuriously, leaving the owner waiting on itself.

Linux

Kernels without BTF were the theme here. On Alpine’s x86 kernel the agent panicked on its first read of the current task, and elsewhere a spawn never learned its pid, and reading another thread’s registers failed. The agent now falls back to fixed offsets for the leading pcpu_hot members, and discovers the task layout on its own.

On arm64 kernels built with patchable function entries, the prologue of fixup_exception() starts with what ftrace patches, so our fault hook was never installed, and a faulting read in the agent took the kernel down. On 32-bit Arm, removing that hook restored the address before the jump, so a fault taken in between recursed until the kernel stack overflowed. Also on 32-bit Arm, per-CPU symbol detection put swapper_pg_dir out of reach, so writes to executable memory faulted, and kernel_write() was called with a junk position, so the agent in a process was never woken.

XNU

The XNU agent can now use a UART that the guest kernel leaves alone, such as UART1 on t8030, as its transport: it receives on the UART’s interrupt, and waits for room to transmit on its threshold interrupt. Interrupt controllers are found by phandle, and a line can be hooked without enabling it, so a driver can mask and unmask it.

It also runs on an iOS 26.1 restore ramdisk under Inferno, ChefKiss’ QEMU derivative with Apple ARM device guest support, which is what our example config for XNU now targets. That took a few changes. iOS 26.1 inlines thread_set_state() everywhere, so we fall back to thread_set_state_internal(). A restore ramdisk has no shared cache, so the agent injected into a process looks libraries up in dyld’s image list. Its code is mapped executable up front, as under a code-signing monitor, anonymous memory that only later becomes executable is taken to be a debugger patching code, and loses execute unless the process is being debugged. And it can spawn threads from the bare thread the kernel starts it on, through pthread_create_from_mach_thread(), shuts GLib down when it stops, and no longer leaks a pthread per thread.

This is the groundwork for running the XNU agent live on CI too, alongside the guests above. The tests already run against the ramdisk locally, and hooking them up is what we are about to do next.

Windows

@kkuehl ran Gum from several threads on Windows and found two bugs in the module registry. Looking up a global export enumerated the modules with the registry’s lock held, asking the loader about each. The loader makes such a query wait while a module is being loaded, and it notifies the registry of the module it is loading, which takes the registry’s lock. A lookup on one thread and a load on another could thus wait for each other forever. The modules are now collected first, and the loader asked with the registry unlocked. The heap API lookup had the same pattern and got the same fix.

The other was a race: the registry was made available to other threads before the thread that created it had activated it, so a thread obtaining it in between found no modules. With 32 threads racing to be first, that happened in 87 of 400 processes. Thanks for the thorough work!

On the USB side, a device that re-enumerates under the same instance ID, such as an iPhone switching USB configuration, was seen as unchanged by our libusb’s hotplug scan, so no events were emitted and the stale device remained, with outdated descriptors and interface paths.

GumJS

@Cassian433 fixed hexdump() when given an offset, closing an issue @chrisdmc opened back in 2021. The row loop counted from zero while the bytes were read from the offset, so an offset left empty rows at the end, and one past the length made the loop run off the end of the buffer. The length now counts from the offset, as documented. Thanks!

Compiler

@marsrcm reported that path aliases in tsconfig.json stopped resolving. The parsed config is handed to esbuild as JSON, and its paths option is a type that only knows how to serialize itself through Go’s newer JSON package, so our toolchain emitted it as an empty object. @tubibibo tracked it down and fixed it. Thanks, both!

Android

Enumerating applications or processes with icons failed altogether if a single icon failed to load, as @YSaxon reported. Such icons are now left out.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • barebone: Run the agents in live guests in CI.
  • barebone: Support Windows XP again: run the worker on its own stack, read hal.dll exports, copy across processes by attaching, list threads with Toolhelp, place an agent in csrss, follow forwarded exports, and report faults.
  • barebone: Only widen a large page’s rights on Windows.
  • barebone: Give Gum whole pages on Windows.
  • barebone: Tell where a Windows kernel thread waits.
  • barebone: Size the Windows wakeup token by pointer.
  • barebone: On Windows arm64, patch kernel code with other processors held, route interrupts by hand, find vectors without the array, skip tables the kernel can’t view, hold spawns with a branch to self, and watch threads via BaseThreadInitThunk().
  • barebone: On Windows 9x, cancel only pending time-outs, start the agent from a new thread, park on Wait_Semaphore, give the process agent’s TIB its stack, start it via its frame, and take module bases from PE headers.
  • barebone: Stop losing wakes in agents injected into Windows processes, and arm the wakeup before checking it.
  • barebone: Retake a held recursive mutex reliably.
  • barebone: Drop the registry lock to unregister.

items.title: DOQEX Expands Identity Management Support and Removes Additional SSO Licensing Fees
items.summary: UK-based secure data exchange specialist DOQEX has expanded its Single Sign-On (SSO) and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) capabilities, allowing organisations to manage user access through a wider range of identity providers without additional licensing costs. The York-based company now supports Okta, Ping Identity (PingFederate and PingOne), OneLogin, CyberArk Identity and JumpCloud, alongside its existing integration with Microsoft Entra ID. All authentication and identity provider configuration options are included within DOQEX’s managed service package, removing the need for customers to purchase additional software modules or licences. The update is designed to help organisations manage access to sensitive information more consistently, particularly as employees increasingly rely on multiple applications to share and exchange business data. Simplifying Access and Reducing Security Risks SSO allows employees to access DOQEX using their organisation’s existing identity management system, removing the need to maintain separate passwords for the platform. This means businesses can apply their established authentication policies, including multi-factor authentication (MFA) and conditional access, while maintaining central oversight of who can access sensitive information. The expanded SCIM functionality also enables organisations to automate user account management. When employees join a business, change roles or leave, their access permissions can be created, updated or removed automatically through the connected identity provider. This reduces the administrative burden on IT teams and helps address a common security problem: accounts and permissions remaining active long after they are needed. By integrating these capabilities into existing identity management systems, organisations can apply more consistent access controls across their applications. Making Identity Security More Accessible Nick Case, Director and Co-Founder of DOQEX, said manually managing user access across multiple applications creates unnecessary security risks. “Managing user access manually simply doesn’t work at scale. Every additional application creates another set of credentials to protect, another account to administer and another potential gap when somebody changes roles or leaves the business.” He explained that centralising authentication and automating account management can help organisations reduce those risks, particularly when dealing with sensitive business information. “SSO and SCIM address those problems by allowing organisations to manage access centrally and automate the processes that are too often left to manual intervention. That matters when employees are using applications to handle sensitive business information.” Case also questioned why businesses should have to pay additional fees to use security capabilities already supported by their existing identity platforms. “We also believe these capabilities should be standard, not something customers have to pay extra to unlock. Organisations are already investing in identity management platforms and shouldn’t face additional licensing charges simply to apply their existing security controls to another service. At DOQEX our aim is that the choice of IdP is yours to determine.” Supporting Secure-by-Design Principles The announcement reflects growing industry pressure on software providers to make essential security capabilities available as standard. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has highlighted this issue through its Secure by Design Pledge, which encourages software manufacturers to support standards-based SSO within baseline product offerings without additional charges. For organisations using multiple business applications, centralised identity management can also make it easier to demonstrate appropriate access controls during security reviews, supplier assessments and compliance audits. Consistent provisioning and deprovisioning processes are particularly important for businesses handling confidential information, where outdated permissions or forgotten accounts can create opportunities for unauthorised access. DOQEX said it will provide implementation support to help customers connect the expanded capabilities to their existing identity management environments. The enhancements form part of the company’s wider focus on secure data exchange , giving organisations greater control over how sensitive information is accessed, shared and managed.

items.title: Jon Penney Delivers Testimony to the House of Commons Sub-Committee on International Human Rights
items.summary: In testimony before Canada’s House of Commons Sub-Committee on International Human Rights, senior research fellow Jon Penney argues that artificial intelligence is having a twofold effect on human rights by making abuses easier and activism more difficult. Artificial intelligence is supercharging mass surveillance while making it easier to threaten and target journalists and dissidents using methods like facial recognition and the production of deepfakes. The rise in AI-generated videos and images is making disinformation easier to produce, causing confusion in the media ecosystem. Penney calls on the Canadian government to restrict surveillance and data collection, require transparency from AI companies, limit profiling, and hold enablers accountable. Read the opening statement Watch here

items.title: AI makes connected devices easier to target as UK hacktivist threats surge
items.summary: New research shows AI can find security flaws in connected equipment in hours, as politically motivated attack claims against Britain surge 337%. From supermarket fridges to factory machinery, security experts are warning UK businesses that the threat extends beyond IT systems. Last month hackers turned up the heat in supermarket fridges across Europe, exposing how easily cyberattacks can disrupt the physical world without anyone setting foot inside a building. Now, two new studies from cybersecurity firm Forescout point to a growing threat for British businesses: AI can uncover vulnerabilities in connected equipment in a fraction of the time previously needed, while politically-motivated hackers against the UK have surged. From office air-conditioning and factory machinery to hospital equipment, the concern is that systems once overlooked by hackers are becoming easier to target. When hackers turned up the heat Last month in France, hackers reportedly exploited flaws in Danfoss and Copeland controllers to raise temperatures to 50°C, leaving food exposed to hours of heat and supermarkets facing millions of euros in losses. The attacks expose a growing blind spot. While IT departments track laptops and smartphones, equipment such as air-conditioning systems, printers and industrial controllers often escapes traditional cybersecurity oversight. Today, it’s supermarket fridges. Tomorrow, cybersecurity firm Forescout warns, it could be an air-conditioning unit in a data centre, an MRI scanner or an ATM chugging along on an outdated Windows operating system. “Hacking in Operational Technology (OT) wasn’t out there among the masses, but now it is,” says Daniel dos Santos, Forescout’s VP of Research. The security blind spot in connected equipment Attackers increasingly use search engines such as Shodan and Censys, alongside homemade AI-generated tools, to find exposed equipment. Forescout estimates that around 50 million devices are exposed to the internet in the UK alone. “The vast majority are network perimeter devices, such as routers and security appliances like firewalls, which are expected to be exposed to the internet but are often vulnerable or misconfigured,” dos Santos explains. Weak passwords and inadequate network protection compound the problem. In 2022, for instance, hacktivists targeted refrigeration systems at 16 Russian and 40 Israeli supermarkets, Danfoss later reported in its newsletter that these systems lacked adequate firewall or VPN protection Following the recent French attacks, researchers also identified a predictable daily code in some Danfoss controllers that could bypass administrator passwords. In another example from 2023, attackers breached a Pennsylvania water utility through an industrial controller protected by the default password “1111”. But as Christina Hoefer, Forescout’s VP of OT/IoT Verticals & Strategy, warns, the danger extends beyond the compromised device. Hoefer recalls risk assessing a bank that had prioritised its online services while overlooking the air conditioning in its data centres. “If you bring down their air conditioning units, it would bring down all their online banking systems anyway,” she explains. In another example, Matt Poulton, Forescout’s general manager and vice president for EMEA and Asia Pacific & Japan, recalls finding an internet-connected coffee machine in a major bank’s executive meeting area. Installed to simplify supply management, it introduced another potential entry point into the bank’s network. AI uncovers 99 vulnerabilities in 90 hours There is no evidence AI was used in the refrigeration controller attacks. But new research from Forescout’s Vedere Labs suggests it could make security flaws in connected equipment dramatically faster and cheaper to discover. Using commercially available AI models, including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus, researchers uncovered 99 vulnerabilities in just 90 hours, including 66 previously unknown flaws. More than half of the new vulnerabilities were rated high or critical severity. The team examined TCP/IP stacks – software that allows devices to communicate over networks – using AI alongside conventional security tools. These stacks are reused across hundreds of products, meaning cameras, air-conditioning systems and factory controllers can share the same code – and vulnerabilities. The AI analysis took just 10 hours, with researchers spending another 80 hours validating findings and weeding out false positives. By comparison, Forescout’s 2020 Project Memoria investigation lasted 18 months, including nine months of manual code analysis. This time, the automated AI analysis cost just $935. The findings suggest that discovering vulnerabilities in connected equipment may no longer require months of specialist research. And the potential attackers are no longer limited to sophisticated criminal gangs or government-backed hackers. Forescout’s latest UK threat research points to a sharp rise in politically motivated groups targeting exposed systems. UK hacktivist attack claims surge 337% French authorities have now attributed the recent supermarket refrigeration attacks to Iranian-linked hackers, highlighting how geopolitical tensions are spilling into everyday businesses. The threat increasingly comes from hacktivists – hackers motivated by political causes rather than financial gain. Unlike state-sponsored attackers working on behalf of governments, they may operate independently, although their interests often overlap. In Britain, Forescout recorded 227 hacktivist attack claims in the first nine months of 2026 – up 337% on the whole of 2025. More than a quarter involved claims of system takeovers or disruption. Two pro-Russian groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, accounted for around 60% of those claims. Z-Pentest Alliance claimed to have manipulated air-conditioning controls at a UK manufacturing facility and accessed an industrial autoclave at another. Financially-motivated cyberattacks remain the largest category of threat actors targeting Britain, at 55%, compared with 33% state-sponsored actors and 12% hacktivists. But the boundaries between hacktivists, state-sponsored attackers and cybercriminals are blurring as groups share tools and techniques. Dos Santos says pro-Russian groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) both claimed responsibility for the French refrigeration attacks despite not being involved, illustrating how difficult attribution has become. “Gone are the days of just one person. They can share how to hack a PLC, for instance, and keep trying and learn,” says Forescout CEO Barry Mainz, referring to the industrial computers that control machinery. Cybercrime is also increasingly specialised, with different groups breaking into networks, selling access and deploying ransomware. “Specialization in cybercrime is something that we’ve been seeing for decades and it could happen next with cyber physical as well,” warns dos Santos. Why securing physical systems is harder than fixing software A second wave of supermarket attacks across Europe, just weeks after the first, illustrates how difficult securing industrial equipment can be. Many may have asked why supermarkets with Danfoss controllers didn’t take action once the French retailers were hit. Hoefer explains that older machinery often has complex dependencies. Patching can require lengthy safety testing, while shutting down systems can halt production. “How far can you go to lock things down without impacting operations?” Hoefer asks. According to Forescout, businesses need to identify their connected equipment, prioritise critical systems and use network segmentation to contain intrusions. Stronger passwords, tighter remote-access controls and continuous monitoring are equally important. Poulton adds that businesses must also rethink how they buy technology. He recalls retail customer’s camera replacement programme across its warehouses and lorries, which involved around 80,000 cameras. On closer inspection, roughly 30 turned out to be different models from those ordered because the supplier had run out of stock, potentially introducing vulnerabilities the customer hadn’t accounted for. Poulton argues that businesses need to understand not just what equipment they’re buying, but what’s inside it and how it connects to their networks. “We’ve been buying tech on the cheap for too long,” he warns. For companies, that means demanding better security assurances from suppliers – and checking that the equipment delivered is actually what they ordered.
