Now, two new studies from cybersecurity firm Forescout point to a growing threat for British businesses: AI can uncover vulnerabilities in connected equipment in a fraction of the time previously needed, while politically-motivated hackers against the UK have surged.

From office air-conditioning and factory machinery to hospital equipment, the concern is that systems once overlooked by hackers are becoming easier to target.

When hackers turned up the heat

Last month in France, hackers reportedly exploited flaws in Danfoss and Copeland controllers to raise temperatures to 50°C, leaving food exposed to hours of heat and supermarkets facing millions of euros in losses.

The attacks expose a growing blind spot. While IT departments track laptops and smartphones, equipment such as air-conditioning systems, printers and industrial controllers often escapes traditional cybersecurity oversight.

Today, it’s supermarket fridges. Tomorrow, cybersecurity firm Forescout warns, it could be an air-conditioning unit in a data centre, an MRI scanner or an ATM chugging along on an outdated Windows operating system.

“Hacking in Operational Technology (OT) wasn’t out there among the masses, but now it is,” says Daniel dos Santos, Forescout’s VP of Research.

The security blind spot in connected equipment

Attackers increasingly use search engines such as Shodan and Censys, alongside homemade AI-generated tools, to find exposed equipment.

Forescout estimates that around 50 million devices are exposed to the internet in the UK alone.

“The vast majority are network perimeter devices, such as routers and security appliances like firewalls, which are expected to be exposed to the internet but are often vulnerable or misconfigured,” dos Santos explains.

Weak passwords and inadequate network protection compound the problem.

In 2022, for instance, hacktivists targeted refrigeration systems at 16 Russian and 40 Israeli supermarkets, Danfoss later reported in its newsletter that these systems lacked adequate firewall or VPN protection

Following the recent French attacks, researchers also identified a predictable daily code in some Danfoss controllers that could bypass administrator passwords.

In another example from 2023, attackers breached a Pennsylvania water utility through an industrial controller protected by the default password “1111”.

But as Christina Hoefer, Forescout’s VP of OT/IoT Verticals & Strategy, warns, the danger extends beyond the compromised device.

Hoefer recalls risk assessing a bank that had prioritised its online services while overlooking the air conditioning in its data centres.

“If you bring down their air conditioning units, it would bring down all their online banking systems anyway,” she explains.

In another example, Matt Poulton, Forescout’s general manager and vice president for EMEA and Asia Pacific & Japan, recalls finding an internet-connected coffee machine in a major bank’s executive meeting area. 

Installed to simplify supply management, it introduced another potential entry point into the bank’s network.

AI uncovers 99 vulnerabilities in 90 hours

There is no evidence AI was used in the refrigeration controller attacks. But new research from Forescout’s Vedere Labs suggests it could make security flaws in connected equipment dramatically faster and cheaper to discover.

Using commercially available AI models, including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus, researchers uncovered 99 vulnerabilities in just 90 hours, including 66 previously unknown flaws. 

More than half of the new vulnerabilities were rated high or critical severity.

The team examined TCP/IP stacks – software that allows devices to communicate over networks – using AI alongside conventional security tools.

These stacks are reused across hundreds of products, meaning cameras, air-conditioning systems and factory controllers can share the same code – and vulnerabilities.

The AI analysis took just 10 hours, with researchers spending another 80 hours validating findings and weeding out false positives.

By comparison, Forescout’s 2020 Project Memoria investigation lasted 18 months, including nine months of manual code analysis.

This time, the automated AI analysis cost just $935.

The findings suggest that discovering vulnerabilities in connected equipment may no longer require months of specialist research.

And the potential attackers are no longer limited to sophisticated criminal gangs or government-backed hackers. 

Forescout’s latest UK threat research points to a sharp rise in politically motivated groups targeting exposed systems.

UK hacktivist attack claims surge 337%

French authorities have now attributed the recent supermarket refrigeration attacks to Iranian-linked hackers, highlighting how geopolitical tensions are spilling into everyday businesses.

The threat increasingly comes from hacktivists – hackers motivated by political causes rather than financial gain. 

Unlike state-sponsored attackers working on behalf of governments, they may operate independently, although their interests often overlap.

In Britain, Forescout recorded 227 hacktivist attack claims in the first nine months of 2026 – up 337% on the whole of 2025. More than a quarter involved claims of system takeovers or disruption.

Two pro-Russian groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, accounted for around 60% of those claims.

Z-Pentest Alliance claimed to have manipulated air-conditioning controls at a UK manufacturing facility and accessed an industrial autoclave at another.

Financially-motivated cyberattacks remain the largest category of threat actors targeting Britain, at 55%, compared with 33% state-sponsored actors and 12% hacktivists.

But the boundaries between hacktivists, state-sponsored attackers and cybercriminals are blurring as groups share tools and techniques.

Dos Santos says pro-Russian groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) both claimed responsibility for the French refrigeration attacks despite not being involved, illustrating how difficult attribution has become.

“Gone are the days of just one person. They can share how to hack a PLC, for instance, and keep trying and learn,” says Forescout CEO Barry Mainz, referring to the industrial computers that control machinery.

Cybercrime is also increasingly specialised, with different groups breaking into networks, selling access and deploying ransomware.

“Specialization in cybercrime is something that we’ve been seeing for decades and it could happen next with cyber physical as well,” warns dos Santos.

Why securing physical systems is harder than fixing software

A  second wave of supermarket attacks across Europe, just weeks after the first, illustrates how difficult securing industrial equipment can be.

Many may have asked why supermarkets with Danfoss controllers didn’t take action once the French retailers were hit. Hoefer explains that older machinery often has complex dependencies. 

Patching can require lengthy safety testing, while shutting down systems can halt production.

“How far can you go to lock things down without impacting operations?” Hoefer asks.

According to Forescout, businesses need to identify their connected equipment, prioritise critical systems and use network segmentation to contain intrusions. 

Stronger passwords, tighter remote-access controls and continuous monitoring are equally important.

Poulton adds that businesses must also rethink how they buy technology. 

He recalls retail customer’s camera replacement programme across its warehouses and lorries, which involved around 80,000 cameras. 

On closer inspection, roughly 30 turned out to be different models from those ordered because the supplier had run out of stock, potentially introducing vulnerabilities the customer hadn’t accounted for.

Poulton argues that businesses need to understand not just what equipment they’re buying, but what’s inside it and how it connects to their networks.

“We’ve been buying tech on the cheap for too long,” he warns.

For companies, that means demanding better security assurances from suppliers – and checking that the equipment delivered is actually what they ordered.

Researchers Reveal How Claude Code VS Code Extension Can Access Files Outside Trusted Workspaces
items.summary: Security researchers have found that the Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code can show a permission prompt that hides where a file really sits. A user may approve access to a path that looks safe, while the file lives outside the trusted workspace. Anthropic reviewed the report and does not treat it as a security issue. The extension has more than 29 million installs, so the problem could reach a very large number of developers. The extension is Anthropic’s official add-on that lets developers use Claude Code inside the VS Code editor. It asks for approval before the AI agent reads or writes files, and that prompt is meant to protect the user. The same type of weakness was seen before in the command-line version of the tool. A Claude Code symlink import issue reported earlier also showed how a link inside a project can quietly point to files outside it. The new finding shows the editor extension still has a similar gap. Researchers at Ultrastrike identified and described the issue in a blog post published on November 11, 2026. Carl Pearson wrote the report. He found it while reviewing several VS Code plugins for flaws. Claude Code VS Code Extension Can Access Files The problem centers on symlinks, which are shortcuts that point to another file or folder. In the test, a folder named ./helpdocs inside the workspace was a symlink to a location outside it. When the agent asked to write a file called test.txt , the prompt showed only the workspace path. It gave no sign that the file would land elsewhere. The roots of this go back to May 2026. Adversa AI published research showing that the Claude Code command-line tool had the same display flaw. A link at ./link that pointed to /etc/ would show as ./link/passwd in the prompt, not the real /etc/passwd . Anthropic reportedly called that report not a security issue, but Adversa says the company fixed it quietly a few weeks later. Plugin has over 29 million installs (Source – Ultrastrike) The command-line tool now shows the real file location. It also warns the user when a symlink leads outside a trusted folder. The VS Code extension never got the same change. Pearson says it still fails to show the link target in version 2.1.322, the latest at the time of writing. The risk grows when an agent is tricked. A rogue agent, or one fooled by a malicious instruction, could get a user to approve access that seems harmless. Attackers already target tools like this, as seen in how attackers can hijack AI coding agents with planted text. The real impact depends on which symlinks exist. A link to the home folder, for example, could expose SSH keys stored in ~/.ssh/ . Anthropic’s Trusted Workspace Argument Pearson reported the issue to Anthropic through its HackerOne program. Anthropic closed the report as informative. It said the prompt alone is enough and that the text shown in it is not part of the security control. It also said symlinks fall outside the permission threat model, although Ultrastrike says the public program guide does not list that exclusion. Anthropic’s view rests on a trust model. Once a user opens a workspace, the tool trusts everything in it, including symlinks. Pearson questions this logic. If the workspace is fully trusted, he asks, why does the tool ask for permission at all? A prompt suggests a security boundary, and that boundary only works if the user sees accurate details. He also points to two cases where the trust model can fail. First, a developer’s account in the same company may be compromised. The attacker can push a bad commit with a symlink, and it lands in every teammate’s workspace on the next sync, because Git supports symlinks. Second, depending on the permission mode, the extension can rename files without asking. A known link could be renamed, and the user would no longer spot it in the prompt. These risks matter more as teams lean on AI tools. Other recent research on AI coding agent flaws shows that weak guardrails around permissions are a repeated pattern, not a one-off bug. No patch exists yet, so Ultrastrike suggests a manual check. Before approving a request, copy the path from the prompt and run realpath in a terminal. The command prints the true location on disk. If that location is outside the workspace, the agent’s request may involve a symlink and should be denied. Developers should also review repositories for unexpected symlinks after each sync. Teams should be careful with extensions too, since a malicious Claude Code extension recently appeared in extension marketplaces and showed how much trust these tools carry. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator Type Detail Claude Code VS Code extension 2.1.322 Affected version Latest version, unpatched at publication ./helpdocs Example symlink Points outside the workspace ./link pointing to /etc/ Example symlink Prompt shows ./link/passwd , not /etc/passwd ~/.ssh/ Exposed path SSH keys reachable through a home folder symlink realpath Check command Reveals the real file location Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: Hackers Use AI-Powered Marketplace to Find Infected Computers With Corporate VPN and Cloud Access
items.summary: A new underground marketplace is making stolen computer data much easier to search. It adds a short written profile to each infected computer, so buyers can look for the exact kind of victim they want. They no longer have to dig through raw files. The service was advertised on a cybercrime forum on November 14, 2026. Buyers can type plain-language searches and narrow the results by country, operating system, and price. One example search read “citrix access to healthcare provider,” which shows how quickly a criminal could hunt for corporate VPN and cloud access. Analysts at Infostealers, the research hub run by Hudson Rock, identified several logs sold on the marketplace. They matched those logs to infection records already in their own database. The operator claims tens of millions of logs, more than one billion parsed accounts, and AI analysis of every log, with prices from $0.25. The researchers stress that these are the seller’s claims and have not been independently confirmed. Hackers Use AI-Powered Marketplace Infostealers are malware that quietly copy saved passwords, browser cookies, and other files from a computer. Criminals then sell this stolen data in bundles called logs. As we covered in how infostealer logs fuel cloud breaches , these logs are often the first step into company networks, VPN gateways, and cloud services. This marketplace adds a description to every log. A stolen machine may be shown as a clinic’s front desk, a defense contractor’s home computer, or a government worker’s family PC. Buyers can also search by domain, email, cookies, and files. The listings carry tags and scores, but the screenshots do not explain how those scores are worked out. An AI-researcher profile (Source – Infostealers) The clearest example was a $10 listing called “The Ophthalmology Clinic Front Desk Dump.” It describes a Canadian clinic computer with medical software, billing activity, and Citrix VPN credentials. The seller shows 11 password entries and 574 cookies. Those are inventory counts, not proof of working logins. Hudson Rock matched this listing to its own data using a Firefox profile name visible in the file preview. Its records showed the computer was labeled “Reception” and held saved Citrix-related login links and billing usernames. Hudson Rock’s AI agent, Enki, also judged the machine to be a front-desk workstation. Other listings followed the same pattern. A $9 listing described a defense-industry contractor’s home computer with a 100/100 score. Another $10 listing claimed a Washington, D.C. government employee’s family PC. A third claimed an AI researcher’s machine in New Delhi with “valid Anthropic Claude API session tokens.” These are the seller’s words, and the researchers could not confirm them. Why Searchable Victim Profiles Raise the Risk for Companies Descriptions save criminals time. Buyers once had to read through large logs to work out who owned a computer and what it could reach. Now a short summary does that work. Hudson Rock believes this could cut the manual effort, though the screenshots do not measure how well the system works. The idea is not entirely new. The U.S. Department of Justice said in 2023 that Genesis Market let buyers search by location and account type. Cisco Talos also described how VOLTA malware uses AI to rate what stolen data is worth. Hudson Rock found no link between VOLTA and this marketplace. Stolen cookies matter as much as passwords. A valid session cookie can let someone back into an account without a new MFA prompt, as explained in how session cookie theft leads to SaaS account takeovers. Marketplace advertisement (Source – Infostealers) Criminals can also pay little for bulk data and more for targeted access, a trend covered when stolen credentials flood criminal markets at record levels. Readers should avoid overstating the findings. The account search returned rows for uber.com and fbi.gov, but that does not show either organization was breached. A listing shows an asking price, not a completed sale. Saved passwords also do not prove a working login, and the “Saved” dates in password files are not infection dates. Hudson Rock suggests defenders follow three steps. First, map the stolen items to the affected accounts and the job the computer did. Second, clean the infected computer, reset passwords from a trusted device, and revoke active sessions and tokens. Third, review sign-in and audit logs for unfamiliar sessions or account changes. items.title: Retadup USB Worm Returns After 7 Years, Spreading CoffeeLoader Malware to Windows Systems
items.summary: The Retadup USB worm is again being used to deliver malware to Windows systems, seven years after French authorities dismantled its botnet. The latest findings connect the worm to CoffeeLoader, a malware loader that uses graphics hardware during decryption and can download and run additional payloads on infected computers. The timeline needs an important distinction: Retadup’s infrastructure began returning in 2024, rather than suddenly reappearing in 2026. Previously used command-and-control domains were registered again and used to deliver SmokeLoader before switching to CoffeeLoader in early 2025. The identity of whoever revived those servers remains unknown. Researchers from Securelist identified a new CoffeeLoader variant in August 2026 and described its connection to Retadup in a technical report published November 16. Their findings show how old USB infections can become useful delivery channels when attackers regain control of the domains those infections still contact. Retadup USB Worm Returns After 7 Years First discovered in 2017, Retadup was written using AutoIt and AutoHotkey. It copies itself onto connected USB flash drives and external drives, using hidden files and Windows shortcuts. When someone moves an infected drive to another computer and opens the malicious shortcut, the worm spreads to that system. The technique relies on user interaction, not simply inserting a drive. Similar deception appears in weaponized Windows shortcut attacks that hide genuine files and present misleading replacements, showing why familiar document names do not prove that removable storage is safe. In July 2019, French law enforcement took control of Retadup’s command servers. Infected computers received instructions to remove the worm when they checked in, leading to more than 850,000 systems being disinfected within weeks. New CoffeeLoader downloader viewed in a text editor (Source – Securelist) However, Securelist documented a 2017 variant still communicating successfully with revived infrastructure in 2026. Retadup’s command protocol is relatively simple: plaintext instructions are encoded with Base64 and then converted to hexadecimal. That simplicity leaves researchers unable to determine whether the original developer or another party restarted operations. The revived servers initially distributed SmokeLoader packed with a 32-bit Armoury version. Kaspersky blocked Retadup infection attempts on around 15,000 systems during the first three quarters of 2026, mainly in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia. These are blocked attempts, not confirmed CoffeeLoader infections. Separately, reporting on PlugX USB worm activity illustrates the continued use of removable drives for malware distribution, without establishing any connection between the campaigns. CoffeeLoader Adds GPU Decryption and a New Download Stage The observed CoffeeLoader installer drops a modified library belonging to the popular 7-Zip archiver and executes it through a legitimate Windows utility. Attackers replaced part of the library’s code with self-decrypting shellcode belonging to an updated Armoury packer. This is a maliciously altered file, not evidence of a vulnerability in 7-Zip. Armoury previously used OpenCL to decrypt its payload through the GPU. The new version switches to OpenGL, a graphics interface commonly associated with rendering applications. It also introduces an intermediate downloader that combines installation, persistence, process injection, and retrieval of CoffeeLoader’s main body. For persistence, the downloader copies its library into application-data folders and creates a registry startup entry. Folder names, library names, and registry values use eight hexadecimal characters derived from system volume information. It also changes startup-approval settings to prevent users from disabling its autorun entry through Task Manager. The downloader then injects itself into one of several Windows processes and retrieves encrypted shellcode over HTTPS. It verifies a digital signature and the decrypted payload’s checksum before executing the downloaded code in memory. CoffeeLoader retains three execution options: process injection, launching an executable, or running a downloaded DLL. The findings support checking removable drives alongside endpoint and network telemetry. Earlier coverage of CMoon worm propagation methods describes another malware family using USB shortcuts, reinforcing the value of investigating suspicious replacements rather than trusting displayed file names. The Retadup USB worm is again being used to deliver malware to Windows systems, seven years after French authorities dismantled its botnet.

The latest findings connect the worm to CoffeeLoader, a malware loader that uses graphics hardware during decryption and can download and run additional payloads on infected computers.

The timeline needs an important distinction: Retadup’s infrastructure began returning in 2024, rather than suddenly reappearing in 2026.

Previously used command-and-control domains were registered again and used to deliver SmokeLoader before switching to CoffeeLoader in early 2025. The identity of whoever revived those servers remains unknown.

Researchers from Securelist identified a new CoffeeLoader variant in August 2026 and described its connection to Retadup in a technical report published November 16.

Their findings show how old USB infections can become useful delivery channels when attackers regain control of the domains those infections still contact.

Retadup USB Worm Returns After 7 Years

First discovered in 2017, Retadup was written using AutoIt and AutoHotkey. It copies itself onto connected USB flash drives and external drives, using hidden files and Windows shortcuts.

When someone moves an infected drive to another computer and opens the malicious shortcut, the worm spreads to that system. The technique relies on user interaction, not simply inserting a drive.

Similar deception appears in weaponized Windows shortcut attacks that hide genuine files and present misleading replacements, showing why familiar document names do not prove that removable storage is safe.

In July 2019, French law enforcement took control of Retadup’s command servers. Infected computers received instructions to remove the worm when they checked in, leading to more than 850,000 systems being disinfected within weeks.

New CoffeeLoader downloader viewed in a text editor (Source – Securelist)

However, Securelist documented a 2017 variant still communicating successfully with revived infrastructure in 2026. Retadup’s command protocol is relatively simple: plaintext instructions are encoded with Base64 and then converted to hexadecimal.

That simplicity leaves researchers unable to determine whether the original developer or another party restarted operations. The revived servers initially distributed SmokeLoader packed with a 32-bit Armoury version.

Kaspersky blocked Retadup infection attempts on around 15,000 systems during the first three quarters of 2026, mainly in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

These are blocked attempts, not confirmed CoffeeLoader infections. Separately, reporting on PlugX USB worm activity illustrates the continued use of removable drives for malware distribution, without establishing any connection between the campaigns.

CoffeeLoader Adds GPU Decryption and a New Download Stage

The observed CoffeeLoader installer drops a modified library belonging to the popular 7-Zip archiver and executes it through a legitimate Windows utility.

Attackers replaced part of the library’s code with self-decrypting shellcode belonging to an updated Armoury packer. This is a maliciously altered file, not evidence of a vulnerability in 7-Zip.

Armoury previously used OpenCL to decrypt its payload through the GPU. The new version switches to OpenGL, a graphics interface commonly associated with rendering applications.

It also introduces an intermediate downloader that combines installation, persistence, process injection, and retrieval of CoffeeLoader’s main body.

For persistence, the downloader copies its library into application-data folders and creates a registry startup entry. Folder names, library names, and registry values use eight hexadecimal characters derived from system volume information.

It also changes startup-approval settings to prevent users from disabling its autorun entry through Task Manager. The downloader then injects itself into one of several Windows processes and retrieves encrypted shellcode over HTTPS.

It verifies a digital signature and the decrypted payload’s checksum before executing the downloaded code in memory. CoffeeLoader retains three execution options: process injection, launching an executable, or running a downloaded DLL.

The findings support checking removable drives alongside endpoint and network telemetry. Earlier coverage of CMoon worm propagation methods describes another malware family using USB shortcuts, reinforcing the value of investigating suspicious replacements rather than trusting displayed file names.

items.title: Apple Reveals How Secure Exclaves Prevent Hidden Camera and Microphone Access on iPhones
items.summary: Apple has detailed how Secure Exclaves protect camera and microphone data , aiming to stop attackers from secretly collecting sensitive recordings even if they compromise the main operating system. The architecture combines hardware isolation, strict data-sharing rules, and protected privacy indicators to separate background sensing from active recording. According to the supplied technical description, Apple uses these protections for sensor indicators on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The design also supports background recognition features, where devices must detect faces or wake words without exposing raw audio or video to apps. Secure Exclaves divide sensor use into ambient and active modes. In ambient mode, protected software processes camera frames or microphone input and shares only limited results, such as whether it recognized a familiar voice. Raw sensor data stays inside the protected environment and is discarded after processing. Active mode allows full sensor data to reach the operating system for tasks such as FaceTime or a Siri request . Before that transfer begins, a secure controller must confirm that the relevant privacy indicator is visible. Apple Reveals Secure Exclaves This addresses a practical problem with background sensing. A light that glowed whenever wake-word detection ran would stay on constantly, making it harder to distinguish passive processing from actual recording. The foundation is a small operating system built around an Apple microkernel. Components receive explicit permissions for memory and communication rather than broad access by default. Memory protection relies on the Secure Page Table Monitor. Apple’s platform documentation confirms that this component operates above the kernel and protects memory mappings even when attackers gain kernel write capabilities. Secure Exclaves extend that separation to keep their private memory outside the main system’s reach. Protected Neural Engine queues support demanding recognition models while keeping their workloads separate. Local storage is cleared when switching from isolated to standard queues to reduce data leakage. The Person Recognition Flow on HomeView (source: Apple) Secure IPC, written in Swift, restricts communication to approved interfaces. Only narrowly defined results should cross the boundary, not unrestricted audio buffers or camera frames. The Exclave Indicator Controller acts as the gatekeeper. It releases full sensor data only after confirming the indicator has appeared for long enough. On iPhones, a separate display exclave checks the indicator’s actual pixels, including its shape, color, brightness, and visibility. This means drawing a dot is not enough if another screen element hides it. During “Hey Siri” detection, the Always-On Processor first checks for possible wake words. Protected exclaves then clean and verify the audio. The main operating system initially receives only a wake signal. Audio is released after the indicator check, and the indicator remains visible for at least three seconds. “Hey Siri” Flow on iPhone 18 Pro (source: Apple) The approach complements Apple’s Memory Integrity Enforcement , which targets memory corruption used in advanced attacks. It also adds context to ongoing warnings about mercenary spyware affecting selected iPhone users. Apple says mathematical verification has helped uncover deep microkernel bugs, but coverage remains incomplete. Its broader formal verification work likewise stresses that proofs depend on defined assumptions. Secure Exclaves therefore raise the barrier to hidden sensor access rather than establish that an entire device cannot be compromised. items.title: Why Fragmented SOC Workflows Increase Investigation Time
items.summary: Key Takeaways In a fragmented SOC, analysts spend a big share of each case hunting down evidence and lining it up by hand. More alerts just means more of that. Most investigation delays come from the same few causes: tools that don’t share data, the same host or user showing up under different names, and one attack arriving as several unrelated alerts. Each delay gives attackers more time inside the network and makes the breach more expensive. A case handed to whoever runs the next tool usually gets re-checked from scratch. Assigning each decision to one owner prevents that. According to the SANS 2025 SOC Survey, 42% of SOCs send everything into the SIEM, often with no plan for getting it back out. Ask a SOC analyst what fills their shift. “Analyzing threats” might come up eventually. Before that, you’ll probably hear about tab-hopping, copying IPs from one console into another, rewriting a query because the next tool wants different syntax, and waiting on whoever has access to the firewall logs. Most of that work exists because of how the SOC workflow is put together. The alert fired. The evidence was sitting in some tool. Getting from one to the other took hours. That’s a long time when someone is already inside the network. So where does the time actually go? And what can a team realistically change? What a Fragmented SOC Workflow Looks Like in Practice Having a lot of tools doesn’t make a SOC fragmented. EDR, NDR , a SIEM, identity, cloud posture, email security, ticketing: seven products is a normal stack for a mature team. It turns into a problem when each one keeps its own piece of the story and no one, human or system, is putting the pieces back together. A few signs give it away: Alerts arrive from every tool separately, each with its own format and its own idea of what “high severity” means. Timestamps don’t match. One source logs in UTC and another in local time, and a third stamps the end of a session, not the start. Before anyone can build a timeline, someone has to do the math. The ticket tells one version. The evidence is scattered across five different consoles. Different people own triage, enrichment, and escalation, usually in different systems. Nobody can answer, “what else did this host or user touch?” without running new searches. Jim Skelly of Fidelis put the core issue plainly: “Looking at one piece of the picture doesn’t necessarily provide the full context of what a potential threat is for an organization.” Where Does SOC Investigation Time Actually Go? The alert itself is rarely the slow part. Time disappears afterward, while someone works out whether it matters, how far it has spread, and whose job it is to respond. Fragmentation point What the analyst ends up doing Why it adds time Siloed consoles (EDR, NDR, identity, cloud, SaaS) Jumping between tools and rerunning the same query in each Each jump is another login, query language and data model to deal with Inconsistent alert formats Fixing fields, timestamps and host names by hand One laptop can show up under three different names No shared case record Piecing the story together from tickets, chat threads and notes Earlier work gets missed or done twice Tool-based handoffs Passing the case to whoever “owns” the next data source The next person often starts over Short data retention or sparse telemetry Trying to scope an incident without enough history Analysts guess, or wait for more data to arrive Duplicate alerts for one event Triaging the same activity more than once The real incident waits in the queue behind its own copies Duplicates are easy to underestimate. Picture one phishing click setting off four alerts: email, endpoint, identity and network. In a fragmented security alert triage process those become four separate tickets. Two could be closed as benign before anybody realizes they’re all part of the same attack. One Alert, Traced Through a Fragmented Workflow Think of this as a composite. It’s pieced together from how these investigations commonly unfold, not taken from one particular SOC. 2:14 a.m. The identity tool flags a finance user signing in from a location they’ve never used. You’re on tier 1. The login went through, so you open a second tool to check MFA. Next question: what did the user do after logging in? That’s in EDR . You search by host name and get nothing, because EDR knows the machine by a different name. Off to the asset inventory to match them up. EDR shows PowerShell starting a minute or so after the login. Did anything leave the network? You can’t see that. The network team can, so you raise a ticket and wait. The reply comes back a few hours later: a list of external connections. One destination looks suspicious. The analyst checks it against threat intelligence in yet another tab. Your shift ended an hour ago. Whoever picks the ticket up reads your notes, can’t find the exact search terms you used, and runs half the queries again. Nobody did anything wrong. Still, a call that should have taken minutes stretched past a shift change, and nearly all of the waiting happened between steps 3 and 6. Handoffs: The Delay Most Dashboards Miss Tool sprawl gets most of the attention. In many SOCs, though, the handoffs between people eat more analyst time than the number of tools does. How much a handoff costs depends on what gets passed along. If the next person receives the timeline, the evidence and a note on what’s already been ruled out, they can pick up where the last one stopped. If they get a two-line ticket and a handful of IPs, they’re starting from zero. The trouble is that in a fragmented incident response workflow, cases tend to move by tool ownership. Network data belongs to the network team, cloud logs to the cloud team, so the case ends up wherever the next piece of evidence happens to live. Who ought to make the call gets decided late, or not at all. CIS Control 17 [1] , Incident Response Management, tackles this head-on. It asks organizations to name the people responsible for incident handling, define their roles, and document the process. Put simply, decide who owns which decision before the incident, not during it. Skip that, and two costs creep in: Re-investigation: The new owner can’t see why the last person concluded what they did, so they check it all again. Queue time: The case waits in someone else’s backlog, and queue time is invisible in most dashboards because nobody is “working” it. What the Data Says About Delay, and What It Does Not Start with IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 [2] . On average, organizations took 241 days to identify and contain a breach: 181 days to find it, then another 60 to contain it. That’s the best figure in nine years, and 17 days quicker than in 2024. Two details from the same report connect directly to fragmentation: Breaches involving data stored across multiple environments took 276 days to identify and contain, longer than the average. Breaches resolved in under 200 days cost an average of $3.87 million, compared with $5.01 million for those that took longer. The report also found that organizations using security AI and automation extensively shortened the breach lifecycle by 80 days and saved about $1.9 million per breach on average. A word of caution here. These are breach lifecycle figures, and they measure something wider than SOC investigation time. A 241-day lifecycle includes long stretches when nobody knew a breach existed. The numbers show that speed and cost move together. They can’t tell you how many days any single workflow change will save. The SANS 2025 SOC Survey [3] , led by Christopher Crowley, adds a view from inside the SOC: 85% of respondents say endpoint security alerts are their primary trigger for response. Network, identity, and cloud signals can easily join the investigation later. 42% of SOCs dump all incoming data into a SIEM, often without a retrieval or management plan. 42% use AI/ML tools “out of the box” with no customization, and AI/ML sat at the bottom of the survey’s satisfaction list. The SIEM finding is fragmentation hiding inside centralization. Everything lands in one store, yet an analyst who needs a specific session from three weeks ago may still have no practical way to pull it back out. Does Tool Consolidation Fix a Fragmented SOC Workflow? Only sometimes. Consolidation helps when it changes how evidence comes together. If it only moves the login screen, very little changes. A unified dashboard that still sends analysts into native consoles for detail is one more layer on top of the old ones. There’s a fair counterpoint here. Some separation is deliberate. A dedicated network or endpoint tool will usually show you more in its own area than a do-everything platform, and in regulated industries, keeping certain duties apart is a requirement. So, the number of tools may matter less than people assume. The real question is whether everyone in a case is looking at one timeline and one record. Security tool integration also has a cost. As Christopher Crowley, who led the SANS survey, put it, new tech eats budget, training and time, and it has to be worked into the workflow before it pays off. Buy an integration layer, leave case ownership as it was, and the delays usually stay. You just have one more product to patch and renew. Here’s a test worth running. Pick a closed incident from last quarter and count how many consoles an analyst had to open to scope it. If a new platform would not reduce that number, it will not reduce investigation time much either. Practical Steps for Reducing Mean Time to Respond Most of what helps is less dramatic than a platform swap. Measure each stage separately: Track time from alert to first touch, first touch to scoping decision, and decision to containment. A single mean time to respond figure hides where the delay actually is. Normalize identity early: Map users, hosts, and IPs to a common identifier so analysts are not translating between naming schemes mid-investigation. Correlate before triage: Group related alerts by entity and time window so one incident arrives as one case. This is where alert correlation and investigation pays off most. Give every decision an owner: Define who owns containment, scoping, and escalation for each incident type, as CIS Control 17 recommends. Keep enough history to look back: Short retention forces analysts to guess at scope. Session-level metadata kept for longer periods is often more practical than full packet capture. Put the evidence in the handoff note: Include the exact queries, timestamps, and ruled-out hypotheses so the next analyst does not repeat work. Tune before you automate: Automating a broken triage process produces wrong answers faster. Step three is the one most teams feel first. As Jim Skelly of Fidelis said: “ Security teams deal with millions of alerts every day. Even after policy-based filtering, SOC teams still have to investigate them. Having end-to-end visibility is important because it helps reduce that burden. ” Don’t Let Threats Go Unnoticed. See how Fidelis Elevate ® Helps You: Identify and neutralize threats faster Gain full visibility across your attack surface Automate security operations for efficiency Download Now How Fidelis Security Approaches Fragmented Investigations Fidelis Security brings network, endpoint, identity, deception, and cloud context into one investigation through Fidelis Elevate ® (Fidelis XDR), so analysts start with correlated evidence instead of assembling it themselves. Fragmentation point What the analyst ends up doing Why it adds time Alerts lack the “what happened before and after” Session-level forensic context Deep Session Inspection in Fidelis Network ® (Fidelis NDR) retains more than 300 metadata fields per session Analysts rebuild timelines by hand Correlated incident timeline Fidelis Elevate ® links activity tied to an IP address across subsequent alerts Endpoint and network evidence live apart Cross-domain correlation Fidelis Endpoint ® (Fidelis EDR) data correlated with network sessions in Fidelis XDR Compromised accounts are hard to trace Identity-to-network correlation Active Directory Intercept ties directory activity to network behavior Too many alerts to triage High-fidelity detection Fidelis Deception ® decoys, where any interaction has no legitimate explanation, so fewer alerts need checking Cloud evidence arrives late or in batches Continuous cloud telemetry Fidelis Halo ® (Fidelis CNAPP) keeps cloud evidence collected before the investigation starts On the timeline point, Jim Skelly of Fidelis explained: “ In Fidelis XDR, we take a timeline from when we first see activity associated with an IP address through every subsequent alert. That timeline gives analysts the forensic context they need to investigate incidents, take ownership of alerts, and escalate them when necessary. ” Go back to step 4 of the walk-through, where the analyst had a suspicious login and no quick way to see the network side. That is the gap Skelly described here: “ With Fidelis, we can correlate Active Directory activity with network behavior through our NDR product to identify compromised users, privilege escalation attempts, and understand what that user is doing across the network. ” Cloud telemetry has its own version of the problem. Gaurav Bahadur of Fidelis noted: “ Telemetry collected only a few times a day can leave significant visibility gaps. ” A correlated timeline still depends on people. If nobody agrees on who acts on it, the case sits in a queue just as it did before. Pull up the last incident your team closed and count the tabs. That number is a decent proxy for how fragmented your SOC workflow really is. Frequently Asked Questions How can a team tell how long its investigations really take? Timestamp three points per case: first opened, scope agreed, containment started. The gaps between them show where cases stall, which a single MTTR average can’t. Should tier 1 analysts have access to every security console? Usually not. A single correlated case view, with read-only access to the evidence behind it, tends to be quicker for them to work from and carries less risk. Can Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) fix a fragmented SOC workflow on its own? SOAR automates steps between tools, but it does not create missing context. If the underlying data is not correlated, playbooks move incomplete cases faster. How much network metadata history do investigators need? Enough to reach back past your likely attacker dwell time and satisfy your compliance rules. Otherwise, an incident spotted weeks later can’t be fully scoped. Where should a team start if it wants less fragmentation? Make sure a user, host, or IP carries the same identifier across your identity, endpoint, and network data. It is low risk, needs no new tool, and removes a translation step from almost every investigation. Citations: ^ CIS Control 17 ^ https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach ^ SANS 2025 SOC Survey

Two details from the same report connect directly to fragmentation:

  • Breaches involving data stored across multiple environments took 276 days to identify and contain, longer than the average.
  • Breaches resolved in under 200 days cost an average of $3.87 million, compared with $5.01 million for those that took longer.

The report also found that organizations using security AI and automation extensively shortened the breach lifecycle by 80 days and saved about $1.9 million per breach on average.

A word of caution here. These are breach lifecycle figures, and they measure something wider than SOC investigation time. A 241-day lifecycle includes long stretches when nobody knew a breach existed. The numbers show that speed and cost move together. They can’t tell you how many days any single workflow change will save.

The SANS 2025 SOC Survey[3], led by Christopher Crowley, adds a view from inside the SOC:

  • 85% of respondents say endpoint security alerts are their primary trigger for response. Network, identity, and cloud signals can easily join the investigation later.
  • 42% of SOCs dump all incoming data into a SIEM, often without a retrieval or management plan.
  • 42% use AI/ML tools “out of the box” with no customization, and AI/ML sat at the bottom of the survey’s satisfaction list.

The SIEM finding is fragmentation hiding inside centralization. Everything lands in one store, yet an analyst who needs a specific session from three weeks ago may still have no practical way to pull it back out.

Does Tool Consolidation Fix a Fragmented SOC Workflow?

Only sometimes.

Consolidation helps when it changes how evidence comes together. If it only moves the login screen, very little changes. A unified dashboard that still sends analysts into native consoles for detail is one more layer on top of the old ones.

There’s a fair counterpoint here. Some separation is deliberate. A dedicated network or endpoint tool will usually show you more in its own area than a do-everything platform, and in regulated industries, keeping certain duties apart is a requirement. So, the number of tools may matter less than people assume. The real question is whether everyone in a case is looking at one timeline and one record.

Security tool integration also has a cost. As Christopher Crowley, who led the SANS survey, put it, new tech eats budget, training and time, and it has to be worked into the workflow before it pays off. Buy an integration layer, leave case ownership as it was, and the delays usually stay. You just have one more product to patch and renew.

Here’s a test worth running. Pick a closed incident from last quarter and count how many consoles an analyst had to open to scope it. If a new platform would not reduce that number, it will not reduce investigation time much either.

Practical Steps for Reducing Mean Time to Respond

Most of what helps is less dramatic than a platform swap.

  • Measure each stage separately: Track time from alert to first touch, first touch to scoping decision, and decision to containment. A single mean time to respond figure hides where the delay actually is.
  • Normalize identity early: Map users, hosts, and IPs to a common identifier so analysts are not translating between naming schemes mid-investigation.
  • Correlate before triage: Group related alerts by entity and time window so one incident arrives as one case. This is where alert correlation and investigation pays off most.
  • Give every decision an owner: Define who owns containment, scoping, and escalation for each incident type, as CIS Control 17 recommends.
  • Keep enough history to look back: Short retention forces analysts to guess at scope. Session-level metadata kept for longer periods is often more practical than full packet capture.
  • Put the evidence in the handoff note: Include the exact queries, timestamps, and ruled-out hypotheses so the next analyst does not repeat work.
  • Tune before you automate: Automating a broken triage process produces wrong answers faster.

Step three is the one most teams feel first. As Jim Skelly of Fidelis said: “Security teams deal with millions of alerts every day. Even after policy-based filtering, SOC teams still have to investigate them. Having end-to-end visibility is important because it helps reduce that burden.”

On the timeline point, Jim Skelly of Fidelis explained: “In Fidelis XDR, we take a timeline from when we first see activity associated with an IP address through every subsequent alert. That timeline gives analysts the forensic context they need to investigate incidents, take ownership of alerts, and escalate them when necessary.”

Go back to step 4 of the walk-through, where the analyst had a suspicious login and no quick way to see the network side. That is the gap Skelly described here: “With Fidelis, we can correlate Active Directory activity with network behavior through our NDR product to identify compromised users, privilege escalation attempts, and understand what that user is doing across the network.”

Cloud telemetry has its own version of the problem. Gaurav Bahadur of Fidelis noted: “Telemetry collected only a few times a day can leave significant visibility gaps.”

A correlated timeline still depends on people. If nobody agrees on who acts on it, the case sits in a queue just as it did before.

Pull up the last incident your team closed and count the tabs. That number is a decent proxy for how fragmented your SOC workflow really is.

Frequently Asked Questions
How can a team tell how long its investigations really take?

Timestamp three points per case: first opened, scope agreed, containment started. The gaps between them show where cases stall, which a single MTTR average can’t.

Should tier 1 analysts have access to every security console?

Usually not. A single correlated case view, with read-only access to the evidence behind it, tends to be quicker for them to work from and carries less risk.

Can Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) fix a fragmented SOC workflow on its own?

SOAR automates steps between tools, but it does not create missing context. If the underlying data is not correlated, playbooks move incomplete cases faster.

How much network metadata history do investigators need?

Enough to reach back past your likely attacker dwell time and satisfy your compliance rules. Otherwise, an incident spotted weeks later can’t be fully scoped.

Where should a team start if it wants less fragmentation?

Make sure a user, host, or IP carries the same identifier across your identity, endpoint, and network data. It is low risk, needs no new tool, and removes a translation step from almost every investigation.

items.title: Cisco Talos Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI to Automate Cyberattacks
items.summary: AI-powered penetration testing tools are helping hackers automate reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on attacks with less hands-on work. Cisco Talos warns that these platforms can connect familiar security utilities with AI agents, allowing operators to pursue targets faster and run several tasks at once. The danger comes from how legitimate testing capabilities are being used against organizations without permission. ARTEX, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI illustrate different approaches to this automation. Instead of simply suggesting commands, these frameworks connect AI models with tools that perform security tasks. Their growing availability lowers technical barriers for attackers, while giving experienced operators ways to scale operations and shorten the time defenders have to respond. Cisco Talos researchers identified growing malicious use of these frameworks in a November 13 report, including ARTEX activity associated with credential theft and malware deployment. The distinction matters: these platforms are dual-use security tools, not malware families themselves. Earlier reporting on ARTEX AI attack automation explains how agents turn operator goals into connected technical actions. Hackers Use ARTEX, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI ARTEX appeared on GitHub in July 2026 under the developer name Autumn-27. An operator supplies a target and objective, and a planner agent divides the work into tasks. Worker agents execute those tasks using security tools, while a shared graph records discovered assets, findings, and progress. This structure lets subsequent actions build on earlier results with relatively little operator input. PentAGI provides a self-hosted, multi-agent testing environment with a web interface for monitoring activity and viewing attack-chain graphs. Talos found more than 700 reachable PentAGI instances online. HexStrike AI connects with Claude Code, VS Code, and other clients supporting Model Context Protocol, or MCP. These differences concern how operators connect, manage, and observe automated workflows, rather than proving equivalent malicious activity across all three platforms. ARTEX has the clearest campaign evidence in the report. Talos cites Microsoft findings that Storm-0940 used compromised ConnectWise application credentials to accelerate sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants. The previously documented Microsoft 365 tenant attacks show how trusted application access can extend a compromise into connected customer environments. Other reported activity involved password spraying, weak administrative credentials, missing API authentication, command injection, and authorization flaws. Agents also searched public repositories for exposed secrets. In one Microsoft-observed case, the transition from GitHub searches to Azure Key Vault data theft took five minutes. Reporting on GitHub secrets theft automation details how leaked credentials became a bridge into cloud resources. Detection and Containment Must Match Automated Attack Speeds Talos identified more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated infrastructure IP addresses and examined tools present during overlapping periods. These included PentAGI, VShell, AdaptixC2, Mimikatz, Cobalt Strike, and several scanners. However, shared infrastructure does not prove that ARTEX launched every tool or that one operator controlled everything. ARTEX also does not ship with a traditional command-and-control framework, although MCP allows operators to add compatible servers. That distinction matters when assessing alerts. A recognizable tool or user agent can provide an investigative lead, but defenders need supporting evidence. Talos recommends correlating authentication, endpoint, and cloud API logs for rapid requests, unfamiliar applications, unusual token use, and privilege changes. Its findings reinforce the concerns described in the FBI ARTEX security warning about attackers compressing intrusion timelines. Organizations should patch exposed systems, remove default passwords, enforce multifactor authentication, and apply rate limits against credential attacks. Public repositories need secret scanning, while exposed credentials require immediate revocation and rotation. Least-privilege application permissions can reduce downstream access. Talos also advises endpoint tamper protection and tested procedures for disabling suspicious applications, revoking tokens, and isolating affected systems quickly. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator type Source-listed value Context IPv4 92.255.57.95 ARTEX-associated address IPv4 38.38.174.152 ARTEX-associated address IPv4 62.171.139.26 ARTEX-associated address IPv4 155.2.192.70 ARTEX-associated address IPv4 38.12.90.84 ARTEX-associated address Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . items.title: Google Reveals How Hackers Are Using AI Agents to Automate Real-World Cyberattacks
items.summary: Hackers are no longer just asking AI chatbots for help. They now run AI agents that can scan, break in, and move through networks with very little human input. In its latest AI Threat Tracker, published on November 16, 2026, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant said AI misuse has reached a “critical inflection point” across cybercrime, spying, and influence campaigns. The findings come from Mandiant incident response cases, global tracking of threat groups, and Google’s own platform defenses. Google says attackers are using AI to shorten attack timelines, grow their operations, and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. LLM maturity timeline (Image Source: Google) Google AI Agent Cyberattacks Google says threat actors are actively using open-source, multi-agent hacking frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. GTIG saw CAIRN and PentAGI used in the wild and spotted testing of CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI. Tool Main purpose Reported use by threat actors Observation status ARTEX Multi-agent penetration testing that turns an operator’s goals into commands Automated network discovery, privilege escalation, lateral movement, and data theft tasks Used in real-world intrusions CAIRN Coordinates specialized agents through a shared workspace and an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act loop Navigated attack paths against targets, including organizations in the US aerospace sector Used in real-world intrusions PentAGI Automates penetration testing through agents that divide objectives into smaller tasks A customized version performed reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations across Asia between late August and early October 2026 Deployed in the wild CyberStrikeAI Connects AI models to more than 100 security tools, attack recipes, and custom scripts Tested for coordinating and automating attack workflows Threat actor experimentation observed HexStrike AI Uses Model Context Protocol to connect AI clients to more than 150 offensive security tools Tested for AI-driven reconnaissance, web testing, exploitation, and binary analysis Threat actor experimentation observed Agent Zero General-purpose agent framework supporting autonomous code execution and dynamic tool creation Explored as part of threat actor interest in autonomous attack systems Threat actor experimentation observed CAIRN was used in intrusions against US aerospace targets. A custom platform built on PentAGI scanned many organizations in Asia between late August and early October 2026. ARTEX remains the best-known example. Cyber Security News earlier reported how hackers use ARTEX AI agents to automate Active Directory attacks , with single bursts of activity lasting just 2 to 25 seconds. Wiz researchers also tracked an ARTEX-using actor, overlapping with Microsoft’s Storm-0940, that went after Okta, Entra, and Cognito identity systems at IT and software vendors. There is a weak spot. Google says these tools trade stealth for speed, leaving noisy traffic, known names, and clear code traces behind. Even so, they still reach their goals, and Google expects less human involvement and better stealth over time. Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks (Image Source: Google) For the first time, GTIG found attackers using AI to find and exploit flaws with no human in the loop. An exposed staging server hosted a framework called “exploit_agent” that compares web software code before and after patches, finds bugs, writes exploits, and runs them on its own. Russian comments in its setup files pointed to a pilot project. The operator focused on French media, entertainment, and education websites. Real cases back this up. After two PaperCut flaws (CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078) were exploited as zero-days in August 2026, GreyNoise reported an AI-assisted campaign that hit hundreds of organizations and reached domain admin within minutes. Zero-day exploits climbed from 8 per month in 2025 to 11 per month in 2026, then jumped to 22 in August. Money-driven groups keep stealing AI keys and cloud access, then reselling it through “LLM Mixers.” Google’s LLMJacking research found fake charges topping $100,000 in a single day, with some victims reaching $1 million. Our earlier report on LLM Hijacking attacks and million-dollar cloud bills explains how attackers test stolen keys with tiny requests to avoid alerts. A suspected North Korean cluster, MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE, used fake recruiter profiles with AI-made images and ClickFix lures to break into crypto firms. It then changed .claude/settings.json files so Claude Code would download the SOMBERMEME backdoor at startup. It also hid its tracks with GitHub tokens named after Microsoft Copilot. Influence groups now use AI as part of their normal work. One contractor used the Gemini API while building a platform designed to run over 100,000 social media accounts with cloud phone farms. Fake accounts were “aged” by AI that copied normal scrolling and viewing habits before posting political messages. Google SecOps has released behavior-based rules to detect ARTEX. Mandiant’s five-layer defense guide advises teams to lock down admin systems, use short-lived credentials, limit access, split networks, and watch for sudden spikes in API and identity activity. For AI services, teams should set budget alerts, scan code for leaked keys, and treat any unexpected AI service activation as a serious warning. As Google notes, the methods have not changed. AI simply lets attackers chain them together much faster, so defenders have less time to respond. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How Agentic AI Reshapes Security Operations and Economics
items.summary: Enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) and Managed Security Service Providers (MSSPs) have operated under a foundational assumption that scaling security requires hiring more people. When threat volumes increased, the hunt was on for more Tier-1 security analysts to help investigate and close out incoming threat alerts faster. Every time the enterprise infrastructure expanded, organizations purchased additional point products and assigned headcount to monitor them. That outdated SecOps model has officially reached its limit, both economically and practically. The truth is, it hasn’t been sustainable for SecOps to scale by throwing more people at the problem for some time. The introduction of AI has simply illuminated the problem. Modern enterprise SOCs and MSSPs must investigate far more alerts, respond more quickly, and expand defenses across cloud, endpoint, network, and identity attack surfaces, all while operating amid persistent, structural staffing shortages and mounting financial pressures. Something’s got to give. The math has been broken for far too long. To resolve the crisis, the industry must move beyond treating AI as an incremental assistant or a superficial alert summarizer and examine the economics of the situation. To have any chance against attackers, who are upping the ante and increasing their sophistication, SecOps must transition to a human-augmented, verdict-first operating model powered by agentic AI. Machine-Speed Attacks vs. Manual Triage The underlying driver of this shift is time. More specifically, Mean Time to Detect (MTTD), the average elapsed time between the first occurrence of a security threat or system fault, and the time at which an organization or monitoring tool identifies it. And as the old saying goes, time is money. Threat actors have already been leveraging AI, automation, and frontier LLMs to accelerate and increase the sophistication and scale of attacks. Recent industry reports indicate that the time required for bad actors to move from initial access to full data exfiltration has dropped to approximately 72 minutes. In widespread automation events, such as the Axiom incident, exploitation of vulnerabilities and credential exfiltration across massive host environments occurred within a handful of hours. Attackers, emboldened by these automation tools, are relying less on traditional malware to breach networks. Instead, the new crown jewels are stolen user credentials and compromised service accounts. At first glance, these identity-led attacks look like legitimate activity, making them exceptionally difficult for legacy correlation rules to flag without deeper contextual analysis. When facing an onslaught of machine-speed security intrusions, traditional, human-led triage creates a bottleneck. The average Tier-1 alert investigation takes a human analyst 30 to 45 minutes, with complex cases taking 2 to 4 hours. According to the Microsoft SOC 2026 Report , non-actionable false positives make up 46% of total threat alert volume. Chasing these false alerts is draining nearly half of an analyst’s daily throughput without delivering much defensive value. These findings align with the 2025 SANS Detection and Response Survey , in which 73% of SecOps teams cited false positives as their primary detection obstacle. When an adversary exfiltrates sensitive data in under an hour, an operational model that relies on sifting through a mountain of false positives in an ever-increasing ticket queue means defenders have lost before an analyst even opens the ticket. The Financial Consequences of Tool Sprawl Adding to the false-positive alert challenge is the operational drag of fragmented security stacks. Most SOCs and MSSPs operate a disconnected patchwork of SIEM, EDR, NDR, identity protection, cloud security, and threat intelligence tools. The average organization manages between 60 and 70 security tools across 10 to 15 different vendors, according to research cited by Deloitte WSJ and Gartner. Analysts spend a substantial portion of their working hours pivoting between disparate consoles, manually re-entering parameters, and stitching together missing context. This is even more time-consuming for MSSPs. Every single “swivel-chair moment” in the SOC burns valuable investigation and response time. For MSSPs in particular, this inefficiency severely erodes profitability. Tier-1 triage leads to severe analyst burnout, high turnover, and soaring operational expenses. This is especially troubling in an industry where qualified human security professionals are already at a premium. Attempting to solve machine-speed threats by throwing under-resourced humans at endless alert queues is no longer just inefficient—it is the wrong shape of solution entirely. Transitioning to a Verdict-First Architecture To break the efficiency bottleneck, security operations must shift from a “fire-first” workflow to a “verdict-first” architecture. What does this mean? In a traditional, fire-first model, static detection rules and audit logs trigger alerts and dump them into human queues for further investigation. In a verdict-first model, such as the Verdict Signal Check (VSC) framework, raw detections must earn their way up a confidence ladder through automated, structured validation by an autonomous AI agent before reaching a human. When a potential threat triggers this course of action, agentic AI agents can execute hundreds of investigative checks in real time. This includes: Threat Intel Enrichment: Automatically cross-referencing observables against active threat intelligence. Deep Telemetry Queries: Pulling endpoint behavior, process execution chains, and network flow data. Identity Context Checks: Assessing user behavior analytics (UEBA), impossible travel anomalies, privilege levels, and non-human account activity. Multi-Source Threat Correlation: Bringing together cross-domain telemetry with a consolidated incident narrative guided by MITRE ATT&CK framework mapping. Rather than delivering a raw alert with zero context, an agentic system generates a fully-reasoned verdict, backed by an auditable evidence chain. Not a black box calling all the shots, but an agent that shows its work so human analysts can verify it. The value of AI agents as threat investigators is especially impactful when measured in tangible time. In an independent operational study evaluating 138,475 real-world security alerts, automatic triage-trained AI agents matched the verdict of their human analyst counterparts with 99.7% accuracy. The agentic AI agents reduced triage response times from several hours down to approximately 1 minute and 15 seconds. Crucially, the AI agents automatically closed 64% of false positives and accurately escalated the remaining true threats requiring human judgment. Redefining SOC Economics with AI Agents The economic impact of agentic AI adoption in the SOC can be profound, especially for midmarket organizations with lean security teams. By deploying AI triage agents, SecOps can reduce analysts’ workload by approximately one workday per analyst each week. Overall, AI-powered auto triage agents demonstrate productivity gains exceeding 80% and false-positive reductions exceeding 90%. This efficiency transforms SOC financial dynamics. Consider these benefits: Scaling Detection and Response Without Increasing Headcount: Enterprises and MSSPs can handle significant increases in alert telemetry without scaling analyst headcount proportionally. Improving Service Profit Margins: MSSPs will be able to protect their service margins and deliver on SLA guarantees (such as lower MTTD and Mean Time to Contain) at a more predictable operational cost. Continuous Learning Yields Smarter Agents: Modern agentic systems are built on feedback loops that learn from analyst corrections and input. This increases the rate of correct verdicts on previously corrected alerts, helping to avoid repeating past triage mistakes. The Evolving Role of the Human SOC Analyst Contrary to what you may have heard, adopting AI in security operations doesn’t eliminate the human element.
