items.summary_html:
Enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) and Managed Security Service Providers (MSSPs) have operated under a foundational assumption that scaling security requires hiring more people. When threat volumes increased, the hunt was on for more Tier-1 security analysts to help investigate and close out incoming threat alerts faster. Every time the enterprise infrastructure expanded, organizations purchased additional point products and assigned headcount to monitor them.

That outdated SecOps model has officially reached its limit, both economically and practically. The truth is, it hasn’t been sustainable for SecOps to scale by throwing more people at the problem for some time. The introduction of AI has simply illuminated the problem. Modern enterprise SOCs and MSSPs must investigate far more alerts, respond more quickly, and expand defenses across cloud, endpoint, network, and identity attack surfaces, all while operating amid persistent, structural staffing shortages and mounting financial pressures.

Something’s got to give. The math has been broken for far too long. To resolve the crisis, the industry must move beyond treating AI as an incremental assistant or a superficial alert summarizer and examine the economics of the situation. To have any chance against attackers, who are upping the ante and increasing their sophistication, SecOps must transition to a human-augmented, verdict-first operating model powered by agentic AI.

Machine-Speed Attacks vs. Manual Triage

The underlying driver of this shift is time. More specifically, Mean Time to Detect (MTTD), the average elapsed time between the first occurrence of a security threat or system fault, and the time at which an organization or monitoring tool identifies it. And as the old saying goes, time is money.

Threat actors have already been leveraging AI, automation, and frontier LLMs to accelerate and increase the sophistication and scale of attacks. Recent industry reports indicate that the time required for bad actors to move from initial access to full data exfiltration has dropped to approximately 72 minutes. In widespread automation events, such as the Axiom incident, exploitation of vulnerabilities and credential exfiltration across massive host environments occurred within a handful of hours.

Attackers, emboldened by these automation tools, are relying less on traditional malware to  breach networks. Instead, the new crown jewels are stolen user credentials and compromised service accounts. At first glance, these identity-led attacks look like legitimate activity, making them exceptionally difficult for legacy correlation rules to flag without deeper contextual analysis.

When facing an onslaught of machine-speed security intrusions, traditional, human-led triage creates a bottleneck. The average Tier-1 alert investigation takes a human analyst 30 to 45 minutes, with complex cases taking 2 to 4 hours. According to the Microsoft SOC 2026 Report, non-actionable false positives make up 46% of total threat alert volume. Chasing these false alerts is draining nearly half of an analyst’s daily throughput without delivering much defensive value.

These findings align with the 2025 SANS Detection and Response Survey, in which 73% of SecOps teams cited false positives as their primary detection obstacle.

When an adversary exfiltrates sensitive data in under an hour, an operational model that relies on sifting through a mountain of false positives in an ever-increasing ticket queue means defenders have lost before an analyst even opens the ticket.

The Financial Consequences of Tool Sprawl

Adding to the false-positive alert challenge is the operational drag of fragmented security stacks. Most SOCs and MSSPs operate a disconnected patchwork of SIEM, EDR, NDR, identity protection, cloud security, and threat intelligence tools. The average organization manages between 60 and 70 security tools across 10 to 15 different vendors, according to research cited by Deloitte WSJ and Gartner. Analysts spend a substantial portion of their working hours pivoting between disparate consoles, manually re-entering parameters, and stitching together missing context. This is even more time-consuming for MSSPs.

Every single “swivel-chair moment” in the SOC burns valuable investigation and response time. For MSSPs in particular, this inefficiency severely erodes profitability. Tier-1 triage leads to severe analyst burnout, high turnover, and soaring operational expenses. This is especially troubling in an industry where qualified human security professionals are already at a premium.

Attempting to solve machine-speed threats by throwing under-resourced humans at endless alert queues is no longer just inefficient—it is the wrong shape of solution entirely.

Transitioning to a Verdict-First Architecture

To break the efficiency bottleneck, security operations must shift from a “fire-first” workflow to a “verdict-first” architecture.

What does this mean?

In a traditional, fire-first model, static detection rules and audit logs trigger alerts and dump them into human queues for further investigation.

In a verdict-first model, such as the Verdict Signal Check (VSC) framework, raw detections must earn their way up a confidence ladder through automated, structured validation by an autonomous AI agent before reaching a human.

When a potential threat triggers this course of action, agentic AI agents can execute hundreds of investigative checks in real time. This includes:

  • Threat Intel Enrichment: Automatically cross-referencing observables against active threat intelligence.
  • Deep Telemetry Queries: Pulling endpoint behavior, process execution chains, and network flow data.
  • Identity Context Checks: Assessing user behavior analytics (UEBA), impossible travel anomalies, privilege levels, and non-human account activity.
  • Multi-Source Threat Correlation: Bringing together cross-domain telemetry with a consolidated incident narrative guided by MITRE ATT&CK framework mapping.

Rather than delivering a raw alert with zero context, an agentic system generates a fully-reasoned verdict, backed by an auditable evidence chain. Not a black box calling all the shots, but an agent that shows its work so human analysts can verify it.

The value of AI agents as threat investigators is especially impactful when measured in tangible time. In an independent operational study evaluating 138,475 real-world security alerts, automatic triage-trained AI agents matched the verdict of their human analyst counterparts with 99.7% accuracy. The agentic AI agents reduced triage response times from several hours down to approximately 1 minute and 15 seconds. Crucially, the AI agents automatically closed 64% of false positives and accurately escalated the remaining true threats requiring human judgment.

Redefining SOC Economics with AI Agents

The economic impact of agentic AI adoption in the SOC can be profound, especially for midmarket organizations with lean security teams. By deploying AI triage agents, SecOps can reduce analysts’ workload by approximately one workday per analyst each week. Overall, AI-powered auto triage agents demonstrate productivity gains exceeding 80% and false-positive reductions exceeding 90%.

This efficiency transforms SOC financial dynamics.

Consider these benefits:

  1. Scaling Detection and Response Without Increasing Headcount: Enterprises and MSSPs can handle significant increases in alert telemetry without scaling analyst headcount proportionally.
  2. Improving Service Profit Margins: MSSPs will be able to protect their service margins and deliver on SLA guarantees (such as lower MTTD and Mean Time to Contain) at a more predictable operational cost.
  3. Continuous Learning Yields Smarter Agents: Modern agentic systems are built on feedback loops that learn from analyst corrections and input. This increases the rate of correct verdicts on previously corrected alerts, helping to avoid repeating past triage mistakes.
The Evolving Role of the Human SOC Analyst

Contrary to what you may have heard, adopting AI in security operations doesn’t eliminate the human element. Instead, it elevates it, making human analysts more productive. The analyst’s position shifts from performing every manual triage step to “human-on-the-loop.” Instead of chasing down alerts, SOC agents are supervising autonomous systems, handling complex edge cases, giving AI agents feedback, and steering strategic security posture.

Junior analysts, in turn, make the transition from tedious ticket sorting to supervising AI workflows and conducting faster, more accurate incident response. They can shift the focus from manual data correlation to proactive threat hunting, detection engineering, and the refinement of AI feedback mechanisms. In short, the gruntwork is delegated to AI agents, so humans can focus on what they do best.

The AI SOC isn’t about black-box decision-making. Instead, the foundation of the AI SOC is governed access, tenant isolation, transparent reasoning, and explicit human authorization for high-impact containment actions. By pairing machine-speed agentic AI analysis with directed human judgment, organizations can finally solve the operational math of the modern SOC. As a result, they can finally achieve scalable, cost-effective, and highly resilient defensive systems.

About the author

items.title: Mustang Panda-Linked Hackers Deploy LOTUSLITE V2 Through Malicious Zoho WorkDrive Downloads
items.summary: Hackers linked to Mustang Panda are distributing LOTUSLITE V2 through public Zoho WorkDrive downloads, using an Indo-Pacific assessment lure to draw victims into running malware. The campaign, focused on Thailand, combines a trusted PDFgear executable, malicious DLL loading, registry persistence, and encrypted command-and-control communications to establish access to Windows systems. The operation shows how attackers can reuse familiar delivery methods while changing the backdoor underneath. Earlier reporting on LOTUSLITE espionage targeting India documented a Microsoft-signed launcher, whereas this campaign uses PDFgear software as its execution cover. Both approaches place malicious code beside a legitimate application so that running the trusted program also activates the attacker’s payload. Researchers from Antares Research identified the malware as a modernized .NET successor to LOTUSLITE in their November 15 technical analysis. Authors Kyaw Pyiyt Htet and PHYO PAING HTUN assessed the lineage with high confidence, citing shared protocol design, execution methods, persistence techniques, and regional targeting. That assessment links the activity to Mustang Panda, also known as Earth Preta, rather than establishing attribution through geography alone. Mustang Panda-Linked Hackers Deploy LOTUSLITE V2 The infection chain starts with a public WorkDrive link that immediately downloads an assessment-themed ZIP archive when clicked. Inside are an executable named to resemble the promised assessment and a companion malicious library. Downloading the archive is the delivery step; execution follows when the victim runs its executable. The report does not establish how the link initially reached each target. The use of a business file-sharing platform gives the download a familiar setting. Separate reporting on Zoho WorkDrive malware delivery described unrelated PureRAT distribution through shared folders, showing why a legitimate hosting service cannot establish a file’s safety. Here, the evidence describes abuse of a public download link, not exploitation of a Zoho vulnerability. After launch, the assessment-themed executable stages two components in a Microsoft-themed directory beneath ProgramData. Attack Flow (Source – Antares Research) A trusted PDFgear executable then loads the malicious library from that location through DLL sideloading. The signed application provides the execution path, but its signature does not make the adjacent library trustworthy. This distinction matters when investigators review apparently legitimate software activity. The malware establishes persistence through conditional registry changes. When running as SYSTEM, it writes a system-wide Run entry; otherwise, it uses the current user’s Windows Load value. It also changes PDFgear’s file-opening association to point to an attacker-controlled launcher, forwarding the selected document path. These changes provide multiple routes for restarting execution during normal Windows use. Encrypted Communications and Detection Priorities LOTUSLITE V2 moves from the family’s earlier native C++ implementation to managed C#. Previous Mustang Panda cloud abuse involved WorkDrive-based command exchange and data theft, but the roles differ here: WorkDrive delivers the archive, while this implant contains two hardcoded command-server addresses. Keeping those functions separate helps defenders avoid treating all cloud-related activity as the same technique. The configuration stores those addresses in byte arrays decoded at runtime with a single-byte XOR key. Antares describes UDP communication and secure WebSocket options across several ports, alongside progressively longer connection retries. Its network evidence includes process-attributed outbound traffic, giving investigators a way to connect suspicious communications with the staged executable rather than relying on destination addresses alone. Execution (Source – Antares Research) The backdoor also introduces a versioned protocol marker and application-layer AES-256-GCM encryption. Unlike encryption supplied only by a transport connection, this additional layer protects the payload itself. The implementation calls Windows cryptographic functions directly through a compatibility wrapper, which researchers say supports older Windows endpoints without relying on .NET’s higher-level encryption wrapper. Defenders should correlate unexpected PDFgear execution, registry changes, unusual library loading, and outbound connections. Earlier Mustang Panda sideloading techniques show why execution behavior remains useful even when filenames change. Antares also warns that signatures matching older LOTUSLITE protocol markers will miss the updated identifier. Its conclusions remain subject to revision as further evidence emerges. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Context Download host files-accl[.]zohoexternal[.]com Public archive delivery C2 address 31[.]59[.]184[.]185 Observed network activity C2 address 103[.]175[.]50[.]32 Multiport communications Executable C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\DeviceSync\RegExt.exe Staged executable DLL C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\DeviceSync\CommonLib.dll Sideloaded library Launcher PDFLauncher.exe File-association persistence Mutex PDFgear_DeviceSync_Mutex Memory artifact Protocol marker 0x50524F31 ( PRO1 ) Updated packet signature XOR key 0x55 Configuration decoding Network ports UDP 53 ; WSS 443 , 80 , 22 , 21 , 8080 , 1080 Configured communication options SHA-256 d74fee10090cae17655d137e060398ce6fe52eb811ebc67a439ef37297e5014f Archive SHA-256 33cf56f15b9e069e3f21d23338ec96c2aaf6edd4f2baadcea2af39e1968515ea Assessment executable and staged executable SHA-256 4748571d98c6af34f4967a3886f73b4421239a1203f048140d3bfdaf8aa78937 Malicious DLL Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: Leaked Credentials Are an Enterprise Problem: GitGuardian Extends Its Good Samaritan Program to Security Teams
items.summary: New York, USA, November 16th, 2026, CyberNewswire AI attribution has linked more than 3,913 high-impact leaks to 1,532 companies since spring; security experts handle critical disclosures to enterprise security teams. GitGuardian , the secrets security platform, today announced the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program , an expansion of its longstanding responsible disclosure efforts aimed at strengthening security across the broader digital ecosystem. Combining AI-powered attribution with expert security analysis, the program identifies high-impact credential leaks that could give attackers a path into an organization’s systems or data. It traces these exposures to affected companies and delivers actionable disclosures to their security teams, showing how an attacker could exploit the credentials and what they could gain access to. For the first time, GitGuardian can extend these warnings to any company in the world, regardless of its size or whether it’s a GitGuardian customer. Since 2018, GitGuardian’s original Good Samaritan Program has detected more than 83 million exposed secrets on public GitHub, sending 11.9 million alerts to 5.9 million developers. But notifying a developer doesn’t necessarily lead to revocation. Approximately 90% of valid secrets remain unrevoked a week after the developer responsible for the leak has been alerted. To date, the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program has linked more than 3,913 high-impact leaks to 1,532 companies. GitGuardian followed up with them, typically reaching at least five people at each organization. The scale of the problem is growing. GitGuardian’s 2026 State of Secrets Sprawl report found that 28.65 million new secrets were exposed on public GitHub in 2025, a 34% year-over-year increase. The Enterprise Good Samaritan Program gets exposed credentials to the security teams that can revoke them. “For years, we’ve warned developers, but they’re not always the ones who can revoke it. Our expertise combined with AI now helps us identify at scale the organizations behind serious exposures at scale, and our researchers work to reach the people who can respond. Attackers now have the ability, with AI offensive harnesses like ARTEX, to use these credentials to target companies at scale. Those companies deserve to know, whether they’re our customers or not. And if a company has no clear way to receive a warning, the warning doesn’t help. Every company needs a door for these reports, and someone behind it.” — Eric Fourrier, CEO at GitGuardian Extending Responsible Disclosure To The Enterprise The Enterprise Good Samaritan Program combines continuous public monitoring, AI-assisted analysis, and human-led disclosure to identify serious credential exposures and help organizations respond. GitGuardian monitors public sources, including GitHub and Docker Hub, for exposed credentials. Its AI agents now screen more than 1 million public incidents each month and investigate over 100,000 in depth , helping identify the affected organizations and assess the potential impact of exposure, including credential validity, permissions, and the systems or data at risk. Human experts review high-impact findings before disclosure, providing the affected organization with the context needed to investigate and remediate the exposure. Rather than relying exclusively on notifications to individual developers, GitGuardian contacts multiple people within affected organizations, works to reach the relevant security teams, and escalates manually when automated outreach goes unanswered. The value of this escalation was demonstrated in May 2026, when GitGuardian researchers identified a public GitHub repository containing sensitive CISA-related data and valid cloud credentials. Nine automated alerts had failed to resolve the exposure. After GitGuardian researchers escalated through CERT/CC and established contacts, the repository was taken offline within 26 hours of human escalation. The need for timely disclosure is becoming more urgent as attackers automate credential discovery and exploitation. In November 2026, Microsoft documented attackers using agentic AI to search public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials. In one observed case, an AI agent went from searching for a leaked secret to extracting data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. The speed of these attacks makes unresolved credential exposures especially dangerous, and reinforces the need for organizations to have a reliable way to receive and act on external security disclosures. Making Organizations Easier To Warn With only 35% of contacted organizations responding to the program’s outreach, GitGuardian is calling on companies to establish clear, monitored channels for receiving security disclosures from external researchers, such as a security.txt file and a staffed security inbox. The Enterprise Good Samaritan Program operates under GitGuardian’s published disclosure principles, which emphasize timely notification, non-destructive verification, transparency, traceable research activity, and persistent follow-up. Organizations receive the full details of their exposures without needing to sign up or become customers. To learn more about the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program and GitGuardian’s responsible disclosure principles, visit GitGuardian’s Enterprise Good Samaritan Program Page . Organizations can also assess their exposure on public GitHub using GitGuardian’s GitHub Security Audit . About GitGuardian GitGuardian is the secrets security platform built to protect the credentials that let code, machines, and AI agents access critical systems. The platform helps organizations detect exposed credentials across code, endpoints, and public sources; remediate incidents at scale with identity context, risk prioritization, and guided workflows; and prevent new leaks with security controls embedded in developer and AI coding workflows. More than 600,000 developers worldwide trust GitGuardian. Enterprise customers include DigitalOcean, ING, BASF, Datadog, Euronext, and Bouygues Telecom. For more information, visit the GitGuardian website . Contact Holly Hagerman hollyh@connectmarketing.com

Claude Fable 5 vs 5.1 vs 5.2: What changes when you upgrade
items.summary: Fable 5.2 is a clear improvement on Fable 5 and Fable 5.1. Moving to it from either one gets you more working code, fewer findings and a stronger security profile. The trade is concurrency bugs, which keep growing, and cost, which rises with the extra reasoning. Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 came out a few months ago and we had not evaluated either of them. So rather than review Fable 5.2 against a single predecessor, we ran all three together. If your team is still on Fable 5 or Fable 5.1, the useful question is what changes when you move to Fable 5.2. All three ran the same tasks and were analyzed together, so we can answer that directly. How were the Fable models evaluated? Models: Claude Fable 5, Fable 5.1 and Fable 5.2, all with thinking at high effort Language: Java Benchmark: the same Java benchmark we use for every model, covering HumanEval, MBPP and ComplexCodeEval. Each run covers 4,444 tasks. Of those, 544 come with executable tests, and the pass rate is measured on those 544. All 4,444 are analyzed for code quality and security, which is where every density figure below comes from. Analyzer: SonarQube systematic code analysis, with all three runs analyzed on the same rule set. Complexity and code smell densities are per 1,000 lines of code (kLOC). Bug and vulnerability densities, and all category breakdowns, are per million lines (mLOC). Three terms worth defining first: Cyclomatic complexity: counts independent paths through a function. Cognitive complexity: a SonarQube metric that weights nested and deeply branched logic more heavily, reflecting how hard the code is for a human to read. Severity: the impact level a finding carries, inherited from the rule that raised it. It describes how much a finding affects the software qualities Sonar measures. Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 came out a few months ago and we had not evaluated either of them. So rather than review Fable 5.2 against a single predecessor, we ran all three together. All three ran the same tasks and were analyzed together, so we can answer that directly.

Concurrency is first. It is the largest bug category, it grew with every release, and it is now nearly half of Fable 5.2's bugs. These are among the harder findings to catch in review and to reproduce once they ship, and the rules that flag them are well covered by automated analysis.

Injection attack is second. It is a small category, but it doubled from Fable 5.1 and ends a little above Fable 5.

Null and data value bugs are third. They dipped in Fable 5.1 and then rose in Fable 5.2 to above where Fable 5 started, which makes them the second largest bug category after concurrency.

Security is the good news. Vulnerabilities fell at every release, blocker vulnerabilities are down to 4, and two categories went to zero.

Three takeaways:

  • Fable 5.2 is the strongest of the three on correctness and issue density. It passes 491 of the 544 test-backed tasks, 14 more than Fable 5 and Fable 5.1, and its overall issue density is 22.0% below Fable 5.
  • Security improved at every release. Vulnerabilities went from 269 to 222 to 167, and blocker vulnerabilities from 24 to 18 to 4.
  • Plan for concurrency and cost. Concurrency bugs grew with every release and are now nearly half of all bugs. Running the benchmark cost 37.5% more than with Fable 5, but less than a tenth more than with Fable 5.1, so budget for the extra reasoning before you switch.

If you are on Fable 5 or Fable 5.1, move to Fable 5.2: you get more working code and fewer findings for a modest cost increase. Just do not read a higher pass rate as a reason to verify less. The bugs that remain are concentrated in concurrency, one of the hardest categories to catch by eye, so keep independent verification on every change the model makes.

Full evaluation results for all three Fable models, along with every other model we have measured, are on the Sonar LLM Leaderboard.

According to Cybernews , criminals hijacked expired Bitly links and redirected them to unrelated Wikipedia pages, making legitimate posts appear to promote offensive or embarrassing content. Bitly is a URL-shortening service. URL shorteners turn long web addresses into compact links that are easier to share. When you click a shortened link, the service redirects your browser to the original destination. The trade-off is that the short link hides that destination , making it harder to tell at a glance whether you’re heading to a legitimate website or somewhere suspicious. Attackers apparently exploited what Bitly described as a flaw involving expired links to make old short links point somewhere new. Those links were still sitting in genuine posts from McDonald’s, Burger King, and others, so anyone clicking them was redirected to the attackers’ chosen pages instead of the original destinations. The attackers didn’t need to edit the posts or break into the brands’ social media accounts; they just changed the address where the links led. One example involved a McDonald’s post from June 7, 2011, which read: “Check out what our McDonald’s team in Sweden did.” Its shortened link had been redirected to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11 attacks. So, the link in that tweet now takes you to an error page: You’ve got the wrong address In these cases, the redirects went to unrelated Wikipedia pages. The concern is that the same kind of redirection could instead send people to phishing pages, fake promotions, or malicious downloads. Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it. Check now How to check a shortened link before opening it Hovering over a link on a computer is still a useful first check: It can reveal a mismatch between the visible text and the underlying address. But if all you see is a shortened URL, you still haven’t established the final destination. That’s where checking the link and its redirects becomes useful. You can copy a suspicious link without opening it: Right-click it and choose the option to copy the link, then paste it into Malwarebytes’ free Scam Link Check . It scans the site and its redirects, then provides a result and suggested next steps. No download, payment, or login is required. Treat unexpected destinations as a reason to stop. Don’t continue simply because the original post came from a recognizable account. The Bitly incidents show why the source of a post and the current destination of its links are separate questions. Don’t mistake HTTPS for a safety verdict. It means your connection to the website is encrypted, not that the website is legitimate . Phishing sites can use HTTPS too. Use browser protection as an additional layer. items.title: Fake Prime Gaming x FC 27 reward site harvests EA passwords and 2FA codes
items.summary: .kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column488555_cd7867-a4 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article A fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward site leads to a copied EA sign-in form The site collects passwords and 2FA codes, putting gamers’ EA accounts at risk If you entered your login details, change your EA password and review account security settings Football fans looking for free player packs in EA SPORTS FC 27 could end up handing over their gaming account instead. FC 27 is the latest installment in EA’s soccer video game series. Its Ultimate Team mode lets players build squads using virtual player cards, which they can get by opening packs. Following the game’s September 25 launch, we identified a fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward page targeting players’ login details. Prime Gaming offers games and in-game rewards as part of an Amazon Prime membership. The fake page borrows that branding, tells visitors their reward is waiting, and asks them to “connect” their EA account—the account they use to access EA games and services. The series attracts millions of players. EA reported that FC 24 reached more than 11.3 million players worldwide in its first week in 2023, including through EA Play. On this fake site, there is no reward. The “EA sign-in” that follows is a copy hosted on the scammers’ own domain. It asks for your email address, your password, and the security code from your two-factor authentication (2FA), and sends each one to a server the criminals control. The page’s code is designed to use the server’s replies to decide whether to show a password error or ask for a 2FA code. This site is not affiliated with EA, Amazon, or Prime Gaming. If you entered your details on a page like this, go to the “How to stay safe” section below. A reward that’s waiting for you The landing page is dark purple and styled like a game promo. It says “Your Prime Gaming reward is waiting. Connect your EA account to continue.” Under the button, a smaller line reads “You’ll continue to EA’s official authorization page.” You don’t. Clicking the button shows “Connecting…” and “Redirecting to EA authorization…”. The code waits a fixed 1.4 seconds and then moves you to /in , which is still on the same domain. A copied EA sign-in page The sign-in page closely imitates EA’s own. It has a dark layout, a “Phone or Email” field, “Keep me signed in,” “Sign in with a Passkey,” and a row of Google, Facebook, Apple, and Steam buttons. The social sign-in buttons do nothing when clicked. Instead, the page steers visitors toward entering their email address and password. How the theft works, step by step Each step sends what you type to a separate server, fedserv.thenewsip[.]site. Email. You enter your email address and move on to the password page. Password . You enter your password, which is sent to the server. The page uses the server’s reply to decide whether to show an EA-style “Your credentials are incorrect” error or continue, including whether to request a 2FA code. This is consistent with an attempt to check the details against EA, but the captured page code alone does not confirm how the server handles them. The code. If the account has 2FA, a “Verify your identity” page asks you to click “Send Code” and then enter the six-digit code. The code goes straight to the server. The exit. The page redirects you to EA’s real Ultimate Team web app at ea.com. Accounts without 2FA skip step three. Arriving at the real site does not mean the preceding sign-in was legitimate. Capturing a valid 2FA code could let the attackers complete a sign-in before it expires. This doesn’t disable 2FA, but it could allow them to get past that check for a particular login. Tracking where victims come from The page records where each visitor came from and sends that “traffic source” to the server along with the submitted details. It recognizes Facebook, Messenger, Meta’s Audience Network, Instagram, and TikTok, through tracking parameters in the link and through Facebook and TikTok ad-click IDs ( fbclid , ttclid ). Everything else is labeled “direct” or “unknown.” The kit also has built-in support for Umami web analytics. Whether it’s on depends on a separate settings file that wasn’t part of what we captured. In its default mode, the server’s replies decide whether a visitor’s later steps (password, sending the code, success) show up in the statistics, and the page where victims type their security code isn’t counted in page-view tracking. The settings can also switch to a mode that counts every page. Together, these features give the operators a way to track traffic attributed to social platforms. They show that the page was built to handle those sources, but do not establish that ads actually ran on them. Dressed up as an “internal tool” The HTML asks search engines not to index, archive, or show previews of the page, with a comment that reads “Private team tool — do not index or archive.” The “Privacy Policy” and “Terms of Service” pages describe an “authentication portal” for “internal use by authorized personnel.” The kit has two switches. One turns off the Prime Gaming landing page, so the same code would show a plain fake EA sign-in instead. The other chooses between sending victims to EA’s real site and showing the “enrolled for weekly FC 27 rewards” page. In the version we analyzed, both the Prime Gaming lure and the redirect to EA were on. Why your EA account is worth stealing An EA account is more than a login. It can hold an FC Ultimate Team club with coins and tradable players, access to purchased games, and saved payment methods. Losing access could put years of purchases and progress at risk. Attackers could also use a compromised account to impersonate you and trick your gaming contacts into sharing information or clicking scam links. Safer. Cleaner. Ad-free browsing. INSTALL BROWSER GUARD How to stay safe Start at EA’s website. Type ea.com into your browser and navigate from there. Before entering your EA password or security code, check that the sign-in page is on ea.com or a genuine subdomain, such as accounts.ea.com . Check the address bar. A page that looks exactly like EA’s sign-in is not EA if the address says something like fc27-prime[.]shop. Keep security codes private. Only enter an EA verification code on EA’s genuine sign-in page for a login you initiated. Be wary of free packs, coins, and rewards in ads and posts. A sponsored post isn’t proof that an offer is real. Use a password manager. It generally won’t offer to autofill your EA password on an unrelated domain, which can help flag a fake page Already entered your details? Go directly to ea.com and change your password immediately, even if you didn’t submit a 2FA code. Review your security settings and trusted devices, remove unfamiliar devices, and check for changes to your email address, linked accounts, and purchases. Keep 2FA enabled. Change any reused passwords elsewhere, especially on your email account. If you see unfamiliar linked accounts, are locked out, or have missing content, follow EA’s account-recovery guidance and contact EA Help. How Malwarebytes helps Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks phishing and scam sites before the page can load. If you’re unsure about a website, link, or reward offer, you can ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard to check it first. items.title: Microsoft Releases Out-of-band Update to Address Windows Licensing and Activation Errors
items.summary: Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update on November 13, 2026, to fix licensing and activation errors affecting a limited number of enterprise devices. The issue appeared after the November 2026 Windows security update and mainly affects organizations that use scripts or automated tools to manage Windows licenses. Affected operations may fail with error 0x80041008, shown as “Invalid parameter,” when using the Software Licensing Management Tool, commonly called SLMGR. Microsoft says devices that were already activated remain activated. Existing Key Management Service configurations are also unaffected when no additional slmgr.vbs commands are required. The problem affects certain licensing tasks carried out through slmgr.vbs, including configuring Key Management Service activation, installing product keys, and managing Windows licensing. Microsoft’s release notes identify the affected operations but do not explain the underlying code fault. Microsoft Windows Licensing Error Microsoft’s SLMGR documentation describes the tool as a built-in Visual Basic script for managing activation from the command line. Administrators can use /ipk to install a product key, /ato to request activation, and /dlv to display detailed license information. These functions explain why the bug matters to teams using automated licensing workflows. KMS lets organizations activate Windows devices through a host on their local network. The reported fault concerns licensing management operations rather than a general loss of activation across previously activated systems. This limits the immediate impact, although affected scripts may still interrupt routine administration. Microsoft has issued separate packages for the affected Windows releases. Windows Server 2025 receives KB5136489, while Windows Server 2022 receives KB5136487. Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019 receive KB5136490. Windows 11 version 23H2 receives KB5136483. Windows 10 version 22H2 devices covered by Extended Security Updates, along with Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021, receive KB5136493. These optional, non-security updates are cumulative and include improvements from the November security release. Microsoft’s out-of-band update guidance explains that such releases address problems that cannot wait for the next scheduled update. The release timing alone does not mean a new security threat exists. Microsoft has previously used this approach for Windows reset and recovery failures and Remote Desktop credential prompt failures . Those cases involved different faults but show how targeted fixes can restore functions disrupted by earlier updates. For the listed Windows Server and Windows 10 releases, the packages are available only through the Microsoft Update Catalog. Windows 11 version 23H2 users can also open Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates. Before deployment, administrators should match the package to the affected Windows version, check prerequisites and restart requirements, and test it on representative devices. Microsoft advises installing optional non-security OOB updates on systems experiencing the issue. Unaffected organizations can generally wait for a later cumulative update that includes the fix. Affected operations may fail with error 0x80041008, shown as “Invalid parameter,” when using the Software Licensing Management Tool, commonly called SLMGR.

Microsoft says devices that were already activated remain activated. Existing Key Management Service configurations are also unaffected when no additional slmgr.vbs commands are required.

The problem affects certain licensing tasks carried out through slmgr.vbs, including configuring Key Management Service activation, installing product keys, and managing Windows licensing. Microsoft’s release notes identify the affected operations but do not explain the underlying code fault.

Microsoft Windows Licensing Error

Microsoft’s SLMGR documentation describes the tool as a built-in Visual Basic script for managing activation from the command line. Administrators can use /ipk to install a product key, /ato to request activation, and /dlv to display detailed license information. These functions explain why the bug matters to teams using automated licensing workflows.

KMS lets organizations activate Windows devices through a host on their local network. The reported fault concerns licensing management operations rather than a general loss of activation across previously activated systems. This limits the immediate impact, although affected scripts may still interrupt routine administration.

Microsoft has issued separate packages for the affected Windows releases. Windows Server 2025 receives KB5136489, while Windows Server 2022 receives KB5136487. Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019 receive KB5136490.

Windows 11 version 23H2 receives KB5136483. Windows 10 version 22H2 devices covered by Extended Security Updates, along with Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021, receive KB5136493.

These optional, non-security updates are cumulative and include improvements from the November security release. Microsoft’s out-of-band update guidance explains that such releases address problems that cannot wait for the next scheduled update. The release timing alone does not mean a new security threat exists.

Microsoft has previously used this approach for Windows reset and recovery failures and Remote Desktop credential prompt failures. Those cases involved different faults but show how targeted fixes can restore functions disrupted by earlier updates.

For the listed Windows Server and Windows 10 releases, the packages are available only through the Microsoft Update Catalog. Windows 11 version 23H2 users can also open Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates.

Before deployment, administrators should match the package to the affected Windows version, check prerequisites and restart requirements, and test it on representative devices. Microsoft advises installing optional non-security OOB updates on systems experiencing the issue. Unaffected organizations can generally wait for a later cumulative update that includes the fix.

  • Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours
  • The attacks target organizations, potentially putting customers’ personal information at risk

Cybercriminals have found another AI tool to do more of the hacking for them.

The FBI issued a FLASH advisory on November 13 warning that attackers are abusing ARTEX, a tool originally developed for authorized security testing, to automate intrusions against organizations worldwide. In some observed attacks, criminals went from selecting a target to gaining privileged access in under three hours, leaving defenders little time to respond.

ARTEX is an open-source penetration-testing framework. Penetration testing means trying to break into systems with the owner’s permission to find weaknesses before criminals do.

An operator gives ARTEX a target and an objective. Its a planning agent divides the work into tasks, while other AI agents use security tools to carry them out and share their findings. Rather than having its own AI model, ARTEX connects to external large language models (LLMs). Once a task begins, it requires relatively little human input.

The FBI says attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against sectors including finance, government, healthcare, and technology. Separately, Microsoft reported that a China-state-aligned group used ARTEX to accelerate attacks after compromising ConnectWise application credentials.

While these attacks can generate plenty of suspicious activity, their speed leaves defenders little time to respond. An alert is only useful if defenders can investigate and act before the damage is done.

ARTEX helps attackers connect individual weaknesses into a bigger intrusion. An overlooked employee portal or exposed cloud credential can become a route to sensitive records, additional accounts, or connected organizations. For home users, that could mean personal information stolen from a company is later used for fraud or targeted scams.

How to stay safe

ARTEX changes how quickly attackers can work. It does not make basic security controls obsolete, but it makes leaving familiar weaknesses unfixed more dangerous. Most of the FBI’s recommendations are aimed at organizations. Businesses and IT teams should:

  • Protect credentials and limit permissions: Scan for exposed passwords and API keys, rotate compromised secrets, and give applications only the access they need.
  • Monitor and log: Watch for rapid bursts of requests, unusual data access, and unexpected credential or privilege changes. Prepare procedures to revoke access and isolate affected systems quickly.

  • Run an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution on your devices.

items.title: Fake “Binance” and “KuCoin” machines planted on ScreenConnect servers in apparent trap for IT technicians
items.summary: Huntress researchers have found that an unknown operator has planted more than 2,000 fake guest sessions on self-hosted ScreenConnect remote-access servers. The sessions are dressed up to look like computers belonging to cryptocurrency exchanges. Since 3 November, the campaign has hit at least 118 servers belonging to 109 organisations protected by Huntress. Most of those organisations are managed service providers (MSPs) and businesses that run their own ScreenConnect instances to support customers and staff. The fake machines carry names such as “LAPTOP-BINANCE” and “KUCOIN-SRV”. Their thumbnails resemble trading desktops, and they always appear online. That makes them look like a high-value customer waiting for support. Built to look convincing According to Huntress, a scripted emulator creates the sessions and impersonates a genuine Windows ScreenConnect client. The operator was able to register the sessions because guest installers on the affected servers were publicly downloadable. Those installers gave away the relay address needed to connect. The researchers counted more than 1,000 distinct fake machine names. The operator revisits each server roughly every 151 seconds to create or reconnect sessions, so they always look live. More than 100 servers were revisited every day over a ten-day period. Around 97.8% of the crypto-named connections came from a single IP address hosted by IONOS. Huntress says this points to one deliberate, sustained operation rather than background noise. Huntress also rejected a theory circulating publicly that the sessions were a by-product of malware analysis in the Joe Sandbox service. The researchers say the behaviour matched an emulator, not a sandbox. A lure for the helpers Huntress’s leading hypothesis is that the sessions are bait for technicians. A technician who joins one of the fake machines using an unpatched ScreenConnect client could be exposed to CVE-2026-84869. That critical vulnerability lets a malicious guest run a file on the technician’s client. Huntress has not seen the flaw exploited in this campaign. However, some technicians have already taken the bait. In a few cases, technicians opened the fake sessions, mostly for less than 30 seconds. In one case, a technician typed text into a session twice, which Huntress is treating as a possible credential exposure. So far, there are no confirmed compromises or losses. Huntress saw no files pushed, commands run, or data sent from the fake sessions. The MSP that first reported the activity had a clean server. What organisations should do Huntress recommends that organisations running self-hosted ScreenConnect: Patch technician clients. Upgrade all technician ScreenConnect clients to version 26.6.5 or later, along with any affected Access agents. Preserve evidence, then clean up. Back up the App_Data\Session.db file and its WAL file before finding and deleting the fake sessions. Check for exposure. Find out whether any technician joined a fake session. If one did so with an unpatched client, inspect their workstation. Set a simple rule. Technicians should not join sessions they cannot tie to a known customer. Crypto-themed names, blank company fields or mismatched client versions are reasons to pause. Lock down installers. Restrict installer and web access where supported, keep Access installer links private, and rebuild any installers that have leaked. Monitor for warning signs. Watch for new guest sessions with an empty guest public key, guest version 25.3.4.9288, or many guests connecting from one external IP. Block known bad IPs, although the operator may move. The full research, including indicators of compromise, is available on the Huntress blog .

items.title: How to prepare your digital accounts for after your death
items.summary: A little preparation can make your digital life easier for loved ones to manage after your death. Here’s how to record your wishes, protect your privacy, and give the right people a way to act. Start with a digital inventory Your next of kin cannot manage accounts they do not know exist. Create an inventory of the important parts of your digital life, including: Primary and recovery email addresses Phones, computers, tablets, and the mobile carrier associated with them Cloud storage, photo services, and backups Social media, messaging, and professional networking accounts Your password manager and its emergency-access arrangements Online banking, payment, shopping, subscription, and utility accounts Domains, websites, digital businesses, and developer accounts Cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets, and the location of securely stored recovery materials For each service, include the account email or username and a profile link or account reference where relevant. For each account, record what you want to happen: preserve it, download important data, memorialize it, transfer an asset where permitted, or close it. Identify any photos, documents, or other files you want loved ones to keep, and note where they are stored. For websites or digital businesses, record who should take over administration and which domains, hosting plans, or other services need renewing. Keep the inventory separate from sensitive credentials. Do not put your master password, recovery codes, or cryptocurrency seed phrases into an ordinary document and email it around. Store the inventory securely and make sure your trusted person knows how to find and access it. Check it periodically, especially after changing phones, password managers , email addresses, or financial providers. Choose who will handle your digital affairs Choose a trusted person, or several people, to handle your digital affairs. This might be an executor, partner, adult child, or another trusted contact. Someone who can handle financial administration is not necessarily the person you want reading private messages or looking through photographs and journals. Those responsibilities do not have to go to the same person. Record your preferences as part of your estate planning. Laws and platform policies vary, and a provider may require proof of authority, a death certificate, or a court order. In US states that have adopted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (RUFADAA), an executor’s access to digital assets is subject to specific rules. Access to the contents of emails and other private communications generally requires your consent, so discuss recording that permission with your estate-planning lawyer. If you run a business, own intellectual property, maintain a large online archive, or hold cryptocurrency, consider speaking with an estate-planning lawyer in your jurisdiction. Set up official legacy tools Where a provider offers a legacy-contact or inactive-account feature, use it to record your choices. Do not assume that giving someone your password will provide an appropriate or reliable way to manage your account later. Apple: Add a Legacy Contact Apple lets you designate one or more Legacy Contacts . After your death, a Legacy Contact can request access to certain Apple Account data using the access key created when you added them and a death certificate. On an iPhone or iPad, go to: Settings > your name > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact > A dd Legacy Contact Give your chosen person the access key and explain where to find it. A Legacy Contact can access eligible data, such as photos, messages, and files. They cannot access passwords, passkeys, or payment information stored in iCloud Keychain, or purchased movies, music, books, and subscriptions. Google: Set up Inactive Account Manager Google’s Inactive Account Manager lets you choose what should happen if your account becomes inactive. You can nominate trusted contacts, choose which data they may receive, and decide whether the account should later be deleted. Visit Google’s Inactive Account Manager to set it up. It is triggered by a period of inactivity, rather than confirmation of your death, so choose the waiting period carefully. Think beyond Gmail. Your Google Account may also hold photographs, documents, calendars, Android backups, and YouTube content. Be specific about what you want to share. Google says it will not provide survivors with passwords or other login details, so plan for data transfer through the official tool rather than expecting someone to take over your account. Facebook: Choose memorialization or deletion Facebook lets you select a legacy contact for your main profile or choose permanent deletion after death. A legacy contact has limited capabilities after memorialization. These can include posting a pinned notice, changing profile and cover photographs, requesting removal, and if you’ve enabled it, downloading a copy of material you shared. Review the options in Facebook’s settings and explain your choice to the person you appoint. Memorialization is not the same as granting full access to your account. Instagram: Record whether you want preservation or removal Instagram allows people to report an account for memorialization , while verified immediate family members can request removal. Decide whether you want your posts to remain as a memorial or would prefer the account to be removed. Make that preference known to your family. Microsoft: Set up OneDrive Digital legacy Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital legacy feature lets you give a trusted contact read-only access to your files and photos. In OneDrive on the web, go to Settings > Digital legacy , invite your contact, and follow the instructions to generate and securely share an access code. Your contact will need a Microsoft account. This covers OneDrive files and photos. Access to Outlook email or other Microsoft account information may require a separate legal process. Other services: Check their individual policies Not every platform offers legacy contacts or memorialization. LinkedIn provides a process for an authorized person to request closure of a deceased member’s account, subject to documentation requirements. Others can report a member as deceased for memorialization. X allows a verified immediate family member or estate representative to request deactivation, but says it cannot provide access to the deceased person’s account. Check the current policies for every service that matters to you. The requirements may depend on where you live. Plan for secure access The goal is to prepare a route for authorized access, not leave a pile of credentials for anyone to find. A written password list can be lost, copied, photographed, or discovered by the wrong person. Shared credentials can also conflict with a provider’s rules. Instead: Use a reputable password manager for unique, strong passwords. Explore its emergency-access or trusted-contact feature, if available. Keep recovery information and device access instructions in a protected estate-planning location—not an unencrypted note, shared inbox, or group chat. Account for passkeys and multi-factor authentication . Your plan should cover authenticator apps, trusted devices, recovery methods, and security keys. Keep securely stored recovery instructions for critical assets, especially cryptocurrency wallets. Limit access to what each person needs. Someone cancelling subscriptions may not need your private photographs or messages. Record where sensitive recovery materials are stored and who is authorized to retrieve them, without exposing those materials in the inventory itself. Leave a short guide for the first week Alongside your formal plan, leave a short practical guide that answers these questions: Who should be contacted first? Where is the digital inventory? Which email address is the main recovery hub? Which phone number and mobile carrier are associated with important accounts? Which profiles should be memorialized, downloaded, or deleted? Which subscriptions and recurring payments need attention? Which devices should be preserved before anyone resets, sells, or wipes them? Which accounts contain work, business, or other people’s data and require special care? Which files should be saved before accounts are closed or devices are wiped? Do not make “log in as me” your default instruction. Use official processes and obtain qualified legal advice where necessary, particularly when accounts contain financial assets, business information, or other people’s private data. Warn your family about impersonation scams Include a reminder that anyone contacting your family about your accounts should be verified independently. Leave these precautions with your instructions: Do not trust an unsolicited caller, email, text, or direct message offering to unlock, recover, memorialize, or close an account. Do not pay an upfront fee to a stranger offering “recovery” help. Navigate to the company’s official support site independently. Do not send death certificates, identity documents, account credentials, recovery codes, or financial information until the recipient and process have been verified. Preserve suspicious messages and report scams through the appropriate official channel. Warn family and friends about fake funeral livestream links , which can lead to requests for card details and recurring subscription charges. Confirm any livestream link directly with the funeral organizer. Work through your plan over time You do not need to finish everything in one afternoon. Begin with your primary email, phone, password manager, cloud storage, social profiles, and financial or cryptocurrency accounts. Name a trusted person, record your wishes, and set up the available legacy tools. Then work through the rest of your inventory over time. To learn more about preparing your data for after your death, listen to this Lock and Code podcast episode with Jed Brubaker, founder of the Digital Legacy Clinic at the University of Colorado Boulder. We discuss the practical work of preserving digital memories, the tools major platforms offer, and the one step that matters more than any account setting. Something feel off? Check it before you click. Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly. Instagram: Record whether you want preservation or removal

Instagram allows people to report an account for memorialization, while verified immediate family members can request removal.

Decide whether you want your posts to remain as a memorial or would prefer the account to be removed. Make that preference known to your family.

Microsoft: Set up OneDrive Digital legacy

Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital legacy feature lets you give a trusted contact read-only access to your files and photos. In OneDrive on the web, go to Settings > Digital legacy, invite your contact, and follow the instructions to generate and securely share an access code. Your contact will need a Microsoft account.

This covers OneDrive files and photos. Access to Outlook email or other Microsoft account information may require a separate legal process.

Other services: Check their individual policies

Not every platform offers legacy contacts or memorialization.

  • LinkedIn provides a process for an authorized person to request closure of a deceased member’s account, subject to documentation requirements. Others can report a member as deceased for memorialization.
  • X allows a verified immediate family member or estate representative to request deactivation, but says it cannot provide access to the deceased person’s account.

Check the current policies for every service that matters to you. The requirements may depend on where you live.

Plan for secure access

The goal is to prepare a route for authorized access, not leave a pile of credentials for anyone to find.

A written password list can be lost, copied, photographed, or discovered by the wrong person. Shared credentials can also conflict with a provider’s rules. Instead:

  • Use a reputable password manager for unique, strong passwords.
  • Explore its emergency-access or trusted-contact feature, if available.
  • Keep recovery information and device access instructions in a protected estate-planning location—not an unencrypted note, shared inbox, or group chat.
  • Account for passkeys and multi-factor authentication. Your plan should cover authenticator apps, trusted devices, recovery methods, and security keys.
  • Keep securely stored recovery instructions for critical assets, especially cryptocurrency wallets.
  • Limit access to what each person needs. Someone cancelling subscriptions may not need your private photographs or messages.

Record where sensitive recovery materials are stored and who is authorized to retrieve them, without exposing those materials in the inventory itself.

Leave a short guide for the first week

Alongside your formal plan, leave a short practical guide that answers these questions:

  • Who should be contacted first?
  • Where is the digital inventory?
  • Which email address is the main recovery hub?
  • Which phone number and mobile carrier are associated with important accounts?
  • Which profiles should be memorialized, downloaded, or deleted?
  • Which subscriptions and recurring payments need attention?
  • Which devices should be preserved before anyone resets, sells, or wipes them?
  • Which accounts contain work, business, or other people’s data and require special care?
  • Which files should be saved before accounts are closed or devices are wiped?

Do not make “log in as me” your default instruction. Use official processes and obtain qualified legal advice where necessary, particularly when accounts contain financial assets, business information, or other people’s private data.

Warn your family about impersonation scams

Include a reminder that anyone contacting your family about your accounts should be verified independently.

Leave these precautions with your instructions:

  • Do not trust an unsolicited caller, email, text, or direct message offering to unlock, recover, memorialize, or close an account.
  • Do not pay an upfront fee to a stranger offering “recovery” help.
  • Navigate to the company’s official support site independently.
  • Do not send death certificates, identity documents, account credentials, recovery codes, or financial information until the recipient and process have been verified.
  • Preserve suspicious messages and report scams through the appropriate official channel.

Warn family and friends about fake funeral livestream links, which can lead to requests for card details and recurring subscription charges. Confirm any livestream link directly with the funeral organizer.

Work through your plan over time

You do not need to finish everything in one afternoon. Begin with your primary email, phone, password manager, cloud storage, social profiles, and financial or cryptocurrency accounts.

Name a trusted person, record your wishes, and set up the available legacy tools. Then work through the rest of your inventory over time.

items.title: How to prepare your data for your death (Lock and Code S07E23)
items.summary: Your family will one day want your photos. They may not be able to get them. For a considerable portion of our shared history, whenever people have died, they have left behind physical remains. There are the photo albums, and jewelry, and clothes, even cars. And as surviving loved ones were forced to puzzle out who keeps what, much of the work—at the very least—was tangible. Death today is different. It’s digital. Photo “albums” are increasingly stored on smartphones and handwritten letters have become a series of texts (never mind the loss of cursive), while social media posts, streaming playlists, and shared online documents have developed a sometimes-equal feeling of sentimentality. But digital remains can be thorny to preserve. For starters, they’re often managed by companies, not by people. Further, there’s a whole lot more digital remains than most people can organize. In fact, according to Jed Brubaker, founder of the Digital Legacy Clinic at the University of Colorado Boulder, the average American internet user has 190 online accounts to their name. And preserving what’s in those accounts, Brubaker said, is deeply important not only to loved ones, but to the preservation and continuation of the human species. “What’s at stake is nothing short of our personal, family, and cultural heritages. All of the things that we use, whether it’s us as individuals to reflect on who we are and our parents, whether it’s that aunt we all have who’s the family genealogist, or whether it’s cultural historians, they have relied on materials that are now increasingly digital. And when everything’s wrapped up into these digital vaults, we are at real risk of that being lost.” This enormous task, which has very personal demands, is actually within reach. Earlier this year, Lock and Code looked at what happens to a person’s data after they die , including what rights they have to, say, not be used for training by an AI chatbot. But knowing what happens after your death is hardly useful information if you don’t know how to prepare before. Today, on the Lock and Code podcast with host David Ruiz, we speak with Brubaker about what can be done beforehand: the actual work of preserving digital remains, what the biggest platforms have built for death, and the one step that matters more than any account setting. “The most important thing I would encourage them to do is actually not a technical thing. It’s an interpersonal thing, and it’s to tell your loved ones what you want. And you know what? If you don’t know what you want, or if you don’t care, tell them that too.” Tune in today to listen to the full conversation. items.title: Usable Security at Luxury Hotels
items.summary: Interesting case study from luxury hotels. Attackers used a fake booking request to gain access to a reservations inbox, where they copied genuine refund requests and got fraudulent ones approved. This is a good illustration why “just don’t click on links” is bad advice. It can’t work when answering strangers’ emails is the job. Even worse, in this case the guest-first culture punishes hesitation. More interesting, the case study shows that splitting security between owner, operator, and brand leaves nobody accountable. And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer.

items.title: Protecting Microsoft's SAP workload with Microsoft Sentinel for SAP: the RISE with SAP chapter
items.summary: Inside Track | Microsoft Digital When infrastructure operations shift, security visibility must evolve with the operating model Four years ago, we told the story of how Microsoft became Customer Zero for using Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM for its own SAP estate, pairing a then-new product “Sentinel Solution for SAP” with our existing SOAR platform and proving out cross-correlation between SAP and the rest of the enterprise. The ambition was stated plainly at the time: an internally managed and configured SIEM that could baseline user behaviors and detect anomalies across SAP, spanning the OS and network layer, the database layer, and the application and business logic layers. Then we moved to RISE with SAP on Azure. With that move, responsibility for instrumenting one of those layers transitioned to SAP under the RISE operating model. The visibility challenge shared responsibility creates In RISE with SAP, SAP operates the underlying infrastructure, operating system, and database as part of the managed service. This changes how customers obtain security telemetry from those layers and raises an important shared-responsibility question: how can the customer SOC maintain end-to-end visibility while SAP operates the platform? The layers remain relevant to security monitoring, so visibility must extend across both SAP-managed and customer-managed parts of the landscape. What changed: SAP LogServ meets Sentinel for SAP SAP LogServ is SAP's centralized log service for RISE-managed landscapes, carrying the security-relevant telemetry from the layers SAP now operates. Microsoft Sentinel for SAP ingests it directly, authenticated with managed identity for Azure. There is no stored secret, no rotation calendar and no bespoke connector for a future engineer to inherit and maintain. The integration is a configuration, not a project . “RISE with SAP introduces a shared operating model in which SAP manages the infrastructure while customers remain responsible for maintaining end-to-end security oversight. The integration of SAP LogServ with Microsoft Sentinel for SAP, secured through managed identity for Azure, brings telemetry from SAP-managed layers together with application-layer signals and the wider enterprise context. Our SOC can continue using familiar detections and workflows without a separate integration or credential-management process. At Microsoft, we believe in being Customer Zero, so we are putting this approach to work in our own RISE with SAP on Azure environment.” — Narasa Reddy Pekety, Principal Platform Lead, Microsoft Commerce Financial Platforms (CFP) For our SOC, the practical effect is that almost nothing about the working day changed. Events from SAP-managed layers land in the same tables queried by existing analytics rules based on Microsoft’s Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM), so detections tuned before the move can continue operating after it. Analysts remain in one console rather than managing a separate SAP queue and specialist on-call rotation. Cross-correlation – the ability to examine the points where SAP meets Dynamics 365 and the rest of our IT estate – remains especially important because it preserves the context that could otherwise be lost when telemetry is distributed across operating boundaries. “What I appreciate most is that we did not have to create a parallel operating model for SAP. We can reuse the analytics, investigation workflows, and response processes our SOC already knows, while adding the signals we were missing.” — Satya Veera Phaneendra Bonda, Platform Engineer, Microsoft Digital Who runs what, and where the signal comes from. An opinionated excerpt: Layer Operated by Signal path into our ISOC in Microsoft Defender Application and business logic Microsoft Microsoft Sentinel for SAP, as before the move Database SAP, Global Cloud Operations SAP LogServ Operating system and infrastructure SAP, Global Cloud Operations SAP LogServ Identity, endpoint and the wider cloud estate Microsoft Existing Microsoft Defender connectors, correlated with the above Co-engineering, in the open The part that matters most here is not the connector. It is a standing engineering relationship. The SAP LogServ team and the Microsoft Sentinel for SAP team work as one co-engineering group, shipping new security content on a continuous cadence: detections, analytics rules, watchlists and normalization for log sources as SAP exposes them. “By co-engineering SAP LogServ with Microsoft Sentinel for SAP, we turn SAP-managed telemetry into security insights customers can use immediately – and continue improving together as threats and landscapes evolve.” — Lalit Patil, EVP & CTO Global Cloud Operations, SAP That cadence is the direct continuation of the commitment made in the original solution, that the SAP and Sentinel teams would keep expanding threat-detection capabilities and the risk scenarios the product addresses as it evolves. “We built this as a co-engineering relationship rather than a connector handover, and that is what makes the estate legible to our perception agents. A security AI agent is only as good as the signal and the semantics it is handed. An agent reasoning over an unlabeled log stream is guessing; an agent reasoning over normalized, curated, continuously refreshed detection content is making an informed decision about what to escalate, what to correlate and what to close. Every piece of content the two teams ship raises the floor for every AI agent downstream of it.” — Martin Pankraz, Product Manager, SAP Security, Microsoft That work also attacks a problem we named in the first edition and never stopped working on: separating permissible activity from genuine threats, and improving alert fidelity rather than drowning analysts in false positives. Content that arrives already tuned to the layer it describes is the most direct lever we have on that ratio. Find the latest guidance always on the running engineering blog series on the SAP community . The foundation we need for the Agentic SOC This work also lays the groundwork for what comes next. Project Perception , Microsoft Security’s model for multi-agent defense, relies on blue team agents that detect, triage and respond to incidents, and those agents are only as effective as the signals they can reason over. SAP LogServ and Microsoft Sentinel for SAP provide exactly that: normalized, curated telemetry from the SAP-managed layers and the application layer, correlated with the wider enterprise estate in Sentinel. With that foundation in place, blue team agents can handle incidents involving SAP with the same context as any other part of our environment, rather than treating SAP as a black box. What comes next We intend to do what we did in 2022. We will share the challenges and the remedies as the work proceeds, so that customers can accelerate their own implementations with what we learn rather than rediscovering it. RISE with SAP does not have to mean less security visibility, but it does mean visibility has to be designed in rather than assumed , and designed in early enough that the SOC never works a period without it. We are running it ourselves first, as always. Final words We encourage all fellow RISE with SAP customers to verify their own cloud security posture, integrated SIEM practices, and choose to integrate with SAP LogServ as foundational service. Till next time. Related reading The first edition of this story: “Protecting Microsoft's SAP workload with Microsoft Sentinel,” Inside Track, February 4, 2022 — www.microsoft.com/insidetrack/blog/protecting-microsofts-sap-workload-with-microsoft-sentinel/ Microsoft Sentinel solutions for SAP | Microsoft Learn SAP LogServ integration with Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP overview | Microsoft Learn Microsoft Ignite 2026 Sentinel Connector announcments | TechCommunity

Inside Track | Microsoft Digital

When infrastructure operations shift, security visibility must evolve with the operating model

Four years ago, we told the story of how Microsoft became Customer Zero for using Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM for its own SAP estate, pairing a then-new product “Sentinel Solution for SAP” with our existing SOAR platform and proving out cross-correlation between SAP and the rest of the enterprise. The ambition was stated plainly at the time: an internally managed and configured SIEM that could baseline user behaviors and detect anomalies across SAP, spanning the OS and network layer, the database layer, and the application and business logic layers.

Then we moved to RISE with SAP on Azure. With that move, responsibility for instrumenting one of those layers transitioned to SAP under the RISE operating model.

The visibility challenge shared responsibility creates

In RISE with SAP, SAP operates the underlying infrastructure, operating system, and database as part of the managed service. This changes how customers obtain security telemetry from those layers and raises an important shared-responsibility question: how can the customer SOC maintain end-to-end visibility while SAP operates the platform? The layers remain relevant to security monitoring, so visibility must extend across both SAP-managed and customer-managed parts of the landscape.

What changed: SAP LogServ meets Sentinel for SAP

SAP LogServ is SAP's centralized log service for RISE-managed landscapes, carrying the security-relevant telemetry from the layers SAP now operates. Microsoft Sentinel for SAP ingests it directly, authenticated with managed identity for Azure. There is no stored secret, no rotation calendar and no bespoke connector for a future engineer to inherit and maintain. The integration is a configuration, not a project.

 

 

“RISE with SAP introduces a shared operating model in which SAP manages the infrastructure while customers remain responsible for maintaining end-to-end security oversight. The integration of SAP LogServ with Microsoft Sentinel for SAP, secured through managed identity for Azure, brings telemetry from SAP-managed layers together with application-layer signals and the wider enterprise context. Our SOC can continue using familiar detections and workflows without a separate integration or credential-management process. At Microsoft, we believe in being Customer Zero, so we are putting this approach to work in our own RISE with SAP on Azure environment.”

— Narasa Reddy Pekety, Principal Platform Lead, Microsoft Commerce Financial Platforms (CFP)

For our SOC, the practical effect is that almost nothing about the working day changed. Events from SAP-managed layers land in the same tables queried by existing analytics rules based on Microsoft’s Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM), so detections tuned before the move can continue operating after it. Analysts remain in one console rather than managing a separate SAP queue and specialist on-call rotation. Cross-correlation – the ability to examine the points where SAP meets Dynamics 365 and the rest of our IT estate – remains especially important because it preserves the context that could otherwise be lost when telemetry is distributed across operating boundaries. 

“What I appreciate most is that we did not have to create a parallel operating model for SAP. We can reuse the analytics, investigation workflows, and response processes our SOC already knows, while adding the signals we were missing.”

— Satya Veera Phaneendra Bonda, Platform Engineer, Microsoft Digital

Who runs what, and where the signal comes from. An opinionated excerpt:
