Co-engineering, in the open

The part that matters most here is not the connector. It is a standing engineering relationship. The SAP LogServ team and the Microsoft Sentinel for SAP team work as one co-engineering group, shipping new security content on a continuous cadence: detections, analytics rules, watchlists and normalization for log sources as SAP exposes them.

“By co-engineering SAP LogServ with Microsoft Sentinel for SAP, we turn SAP-managed telemetry into security insights customers can use immediately – and continue improving together as threats and landscapes evolve.”

— Lalit Patil, EVP & CTO Global Cloud Operations, SAP

That cadence is the direct continuation of the commitment made in the original solution, that the SAP and Sentinel teams would keep expanding threat-detection capabilities and the risk scenarios the product addresses as it evolves. 

“We built this as a co-engineering relationship rather than a connector handover, and that is what makes the estate legible to our perception agents. A security AI agent is only as good as the signal and the semantics it is handed. An agent reasoning over an unlabeled log stream is guessing; an agent reasoning over normalized, curated, continuously refreshed detection content is making an informed decision about what to escalate, what to correlate and what to close. Every piece of content the two teams ship raises the floor for every AI agent downstream of it.” 

— Martin Pankraz, Product Manager, SAP Security, Microsoft 

That work also attacks a problem we named in the first edition and never stopped working on: separating permissible activity from genuine threats, and improving alert fidelity rather than drowning analysts in false positives. Content that arrives already tuned to the layer it describes is the most direct lever we have on that ratio. 

Find the latest guidance always on the running engineering blog series on the SAP community.

The foundation we need for the Agentic SOC

This work also lays the groundwork for what comes next. Project Perception, Microsoft Security’s model for multi-agent defense, relies on blue team agents that detect, triage and respond to incidents, and those agents are only as effective as the signals they can reason over. SAP LogServ and Microsoft Sentinel for SAP provide exactly that: normalized, curated telemetry from the SAP-managed layers and the application layer, correlated with the wider enterprise estate in Sentinel. With that foundation in place, blue team agents can handle incidents involving SAP with the same context as any other part of our environment, rather than treating SAP as a black box.

What comes next

We intend to do what we did in 2022. We will share the challenges and the remedies as the work proceeds, so that customers can accelerate their own implementations with what we learn rather than rediscovering it. RISE with SAP does not have to mean less security visibility, but it does mean visibility has to be designed in rather than assumed, and designed in early enough that the SOC never works a period without it.

We are running it ourselves first, as always.

Final words

We encourage all fellow RISE with SAP customers to verify their own cloud security posture, integrated SIEM practices, and choose to integrate with SAP LogServ as foundational service. Till next time.

Certitude gets access to Anthropic’s Mythos AI model for offensive security testing
items.summary: The cybersecurity specialist Certitude Consulting is among the first companies in Europe to receive Red Team Access as part of Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program. Companies in German-speaking countries can now have their software analysed for security vulnerabilities using an advanced AI model for security research. The cybersecurity firm Certitude Consulting is among the first companies in Europe to receive “Red Team Access” as part of Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program. This grants Certitude access to Claude Mythos, an AI model whose capabilities in identifying and analysing software vulnerabilities have attracted international attention. For companies in the DACH region, this opens up a new opportunity to have the security of their software and IT systems tested using current AI technology: Certitude can use Mythos’s capabilities as part of professional security assessments, authorised penetration tests and targeted security research projects. “We are currently witnessing a fundamental shift in cybersecurity. AI is changing not only the capabilities of potential attackers but also the tools we can use to defend ourselves. With Mythos, we can examine software in ways that were barely imaginable just a few months ago,” explains Marc Nimmerrichter, Managing Partner at Certitude Consulting, adding: “Our goal is to use this technology responsibly and, as part of our audits and consulting projects, make it accessible to companies in the DACH region within a secure environment.” Claude Mythos: capabilities and access With Claude Mythos, the US-based AI company Anthropic has developed a model with particularly strong capabilities in complex software and security analyses. Mythos can independently analyse extensive codebases, identify previously unknown vulnerabilities and investigate complex interrelationships in software and IT systems. The model’s capabilities are not only relevant for defence. The same technologies could also be used by attackers to detect and exploit vulnerabilities. For this reason, Anthropic initially made a conscious decision not to release Mythos to the general public. Access was initially limited to a very small circle of selected organisations as part of Project Glasswing. In April 2026, access was restricted to approximately 200 organisations, including selected technology companies and operators of critical infrastructure. Anthropic is thus pursuing a controlled approach: the new AI capabilities are initially intended to be available to those who use them to make software and digital infrastructure more secure. What does Red Team Access mean? With the Cyber Verification Program, Anthropic has created a special access programme for verified cybersecurity experts and companies. Defense Access is the first tier of the programme; it allows the use of advanced models for defensive purposes and is aimed at corporate security teams. Red Team Access is much more strictly limited to organisations whose primary focus is offensive security and security research. This tier requires verification of the organisation and its field of activity by Anthropic, including through publications in this sector. It allows authorised security testing, including: Advanced penetration tests and red team assessments Identification and analysis of previously unknown vulnerabilities Simulation of realistic attack scenarios Investigation of complex software and system architectures Development and validation of proofs of concept and exploits in an authorised testing environment This specialised access authorisation takes into account that professional security researchers sometimes require the same technical skills for their work as potential attackers. Benefits for companies in German-speaking countries For companies, Certitude’s access to Mythos means they can have their own software, applications and IT systems analysed with the support of an advanced AI model for security research. Mythos can analyse large volumes of source code, detect potential vulnerabilities and assist security researchers in investigating complex bugs. The use of such models opens up new possibilities, particularly in areas where traditional automated testing methods reach their limits. The combination of artificial intelligence and human expertise is crucial here. The AI must be guided by security researchers, and the results must be technically validated by experienced experts and evaluated in terms of their actual impact. “In addition, a technical control and monitoring framework must be developed and operated that embeds the AI in a controlled environment, enabling but also limiting its actions,” explains Marc Nimmerrichter. Experience in international security research Certitude already brings extensive experience in independent security research. Organisations such as Microsoft, Google and the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) have already publicly acknowledged the findings of Certitude’s security research specialists. A recent example is the discovery of two serious vulnerabilities in the Google Chrome browser and in Arm GPU drivers by Certitude security researcher Florian Schweitzer. The vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-9034 and CVE-2026-93374) affect the GPU software stack and, under certain conditions, can enable a so-called sandbox escape. The vulnerabilities were responsibly reported to the affected vendors, who have addressed them. Google and Arm publicly credit the Certitude researcher as the discoverer of the respective security vulnerabilities. This research highlights what matters most in modern cybersecurity: not only examining known attack patterns, but also identifying previously overlooked vulnerabilities in complex software and hardware architectures. With access to Mythos, Certitude can expand this research to include a new technological dimension. Consequences for software security The development of powerful AI models presents a new challenge for companies. As AI becomes increasingly capable of identifying security vulnerabilities that were previously difficult to detect, defence strategies must also evolve accordingly. Certitude aims to provide companies in the DACH region with access to these new opportunities through a combination of advanced AI technology, years of security research experience and in-depth technical expertise. About Certitude Consulting Certitude Consulting is a Vienna-based consulting firm specialising in cybersecurity that helps organisations identify digital risks early on and manage them effectively. By closely integrating research, regulation and practical experience, Certitude develops solutions that are not only standards-compliant but, above all, practical and suitable for everyday use.

Claude Mythos: capabilities and access

With Claude Mythos, the US-based AI company Anthropic has developed a model with particularly strong capabilities in complex software and security analyses. Mythos can independently analyse extensive codebases, identify previously unknown vulnerabilities and investigate complex interrelationships in software and IT systems.

The model’s capabilities are not only relevant for defence. The same technologies could also be used by attackers to detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

For this reason, Anthropic initially made a conscious decision not to release Mythos to the general public. Access was initially limited to a very small circle of selected organisations as part of Project Glasswing. In April 2026, access was restricted to approximately 200 organisations, including selected technology companies and operators of critical infrastructure.

Anthropic is thus pursuing a controlled approach: the new AI capabilities are initially intended to be available to those who use them to make software and digital infrastructure more secure.

What does Red Team Access mean?

With the Cyber Verification Program, Anthropic has created a special access programme for verified cybersecurity experts and companies.

Defense Access is the first tier of the programme; it allows the use of advanced models for defensive purposes and is aimed at corporate security teams.

Red Team Access is much more strictly limited to organisations whose primary focus is offensive security and security research. This tier requires verification of the organisation and its field of activity by Anthropic, including through publications in this sector. It allows authorised security testing, including:

  • Advanced penetration tests and red team assessments
  • Identification and analysis of previously unknown vulnerabilities
  • Simulation of realistic attack scenarios
  • Investigation of complex software and system architectures
  • Development and validation of proofs of concept and exploits in an authorised testing environment

This specialised access authorisation takes into account that professional security researchers sometimes require the same technical skills for their work as potential attackers.

Benefits for companies in German-speaking countries

For companies, Certitude’s access to Mythos means they can have their own software, applications and IT systems analysed with the support of an advanced AI model for security research.

Mythos can analyse large volumes of source code, detect potential vulnerabilities and assist security researchers in investigating complex bugs. The use of such models opens up new possibilities, particularly in areas where traditional automated testing methods reach their limits.

The combination of artificial intelligence and human expertise is crucial here. The AI must be guided by security researchers, and the results must be technically validated by experienced experts and evaluated in terms of their actual impact.

“In addition, a technical control and monitoring framework must be developed and operated that embeds the AI in a controlled environment, enabling but also limiting its actions,”

explains Marc Nimmerrichter.

Experience in international security research

Certitude already brings extensive experience in independent security research. Organisations such as Microsoft, Google and the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) have already publicly acknowledged the findings of Certitude’s security research specialists.

A recent example is the discovery of two serious vulnerabilities in the Google Chrome browser and in Arm GPU drivers by Certitude security researcher Florian Schweitzer. The vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-9034 and CVE-2026-93374) affect the GPU software stack and, under certain conditions, can enable a so-called sandbox escape.

The vulnerabilities were responsibly reported to the affected vendors, who have addressed them. Google and Arm publicly credit the Certitude researcher as the discoverer of the respective security vulnerabilities.

This research highlights what matters most in modern cybersecurity: not only examining known attack patterns, but also identifying previously overlooked vulnerabilities in complex software and hardware architectures.

With access to Mythos, Certitude can expand this research to include a new technological dimension.

Consequences for software security

The development of powerful AI models presents a new challenge for companies. As AI becomes increasingly capable of identifying security vulnerabilities that were previously difficult to detect, defence strategies must also evolve accordingly.

Certitude aims to provide companies in the DACH region with access to these new opportunities through a combination of advanced AI technology, years of security research experience and in-depth technical expertise.

About Certitude Consulting

Certitude Consulting is a Vienna-based consulting firm specialising in cybersecurity that helps organisations identify digital risks early on and manage them effectively. By closely integrating research, regulation and practical experience, Certitude develops solutions that are not only standards-compliant but, above all, practical and suitable for everyday use.

items.summary: Key Takeaways Identity technical debt is the accumulated security, governance, and operational burden created by unmanaged identities, excessive permissions, outdated access, and fragmented controls. It’s caused by identity sprawl, privilege creep, dormant and orphaned accounts, excessive permissions, unmanaged non-human identities (NHIs), and persistent policy exceptions. It increases breach blast radius, Security Operations Center (SOC) investigation time, audit fatigue, operational disruption, delivery friction, and tool complexity. It should be measured using a five-part framework that covers inventory and ownership, dormancy, privilege, credentials, and remediation, rather than a single score. It can be reduced through four maturity stages and a six-step roadmap: Discover, Classify, Prioritize, Remediate, Prevent, and Measure. Qualys ETM Identity correlates identity sprawl, privilege exposure, and NHIs with Enterprise TruRisk , so this debt can be discovered, prioritized, and reduced through verified, closed-loop remediation. The Hidden Cost of Identity Technical Debt Most identity decisions are made under pressure: a contractor needs access today, a migration needs a service account now, an acquired business needs users provisioned on day one. Each solves an immediate need and quietly leaves risk behind. That’s identity technical debt: the accumulated security, governance, and operational burden created by unmanaged identities, excessive permissions, outdated access, weak authentication, and fragmented identity controls. What Is Identity Technical Debt? Identity technical debt is the backlog of unresolved identity risks, control gaps, exceptions, and lifecycle failures. It includes dormant and overprivileged accounts, as well as hidden relationships among users, machines, applications, credentials, and permissions. Most debt comes from thousands of small decisions that were never revisited. Identity Technical Debt vs. Identity Risk, Identity Sprawl, and Identity Hygiene These terms are related but distinct: Term What It Describes Identity technical debt The accumulated backlog and future cost when sprawl and risk go unaddressed Identity risk The likelihood and impact of an identity being compromised right now Identity sprawl Uncontrolled growth of identities and identity silos across systems and clouds Identity hygiene The day-to-day practices that prevent debt from accumulating Sprawl drives growth, risk reflects current exposure, hygiene prevents accumulation, and technical debt is the resulting backlog. Left unmanaged, that backlog widens the identity attack surface over time. How Identity Technical Debt Accumulates Identity debt grows through thousands of small access and lifecycle decisions. 1. Identity Sprawl Across Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Systems Users, applications, cloud accounts, service principals, workloads, bots, and AI agents multiply across disconnected systems, making ownership and access visibility difficult to maintain. 2. Privilege Creep from Role Changes and Temporary Access Role changes, projects, and emergency access often leave old permissions behind, turning temporary access into a persistent identity attack surface. 3. Dormant, Orphaned, and Shadow Accounts Former employees, unused accounts, disconnected apps, and duplicates often remain active. Dormant accounts are unused, orphaned accounts lack owners, and shadow identities were never sanctioned. 4. Excessive Permissions and Hidden Effective Access Direct privileges, nested groups, inherited roles, and trust relationships can create toxic combinations, while nominal roles may understate an identity’s effective reach. 5. Non-Human Identity Risk and Unmanaged Credentials Service accounts, API keys, tokens, secrets, and AI agents often lack clear ownership. Long-lived credentials make cleanup risky. Entro Labs found NHIs grew 44% year-over-year and now outnumber human identities 144 to 1. 6. Weak Identity Policies and Persistent Exceptions Inconsistent MFA, non-expiring passwords, legacy authentication, and permanent break-glass access create persistent debt when temporary exceptions lack expiry dates. The Hidden Costs of Identity Technical Debt Identity debt often surfaces later as wider breach impact, slower investigations, and persistent audit backlogs. 1. Larger Blast Radius When an Identity is Compromised Excessive permissions and weak trust relationships can expand the blast radius of a compromised identity. 2. Higher SOC Investigation and Incident-Response Costs Analysts spend more time determining who owns an account, what access is legitimate, and what’s reachable from it. 3. Audit Fatigue and Access-Review Backlogs Low-context certifications and recurring exceptions turn reviews into an administrative backlog instead of risk reduction. 4. Operational Disruption and Service Outages Expired certificates and unrotated secrets can interrupt applications and authentication with little warning. 5. Slower Cloud, SaaS, DevOps, and AI Delivery Unclear ownership and ungoverned machine identities force teams to choose between speed and control. 6. Growing Tool and Governance Complexity Disconnected Identity and Access Management (IAM), Privileged Access Management (PAM), Identity Governance and Administration (IGA), and directory systems create duplicated records and inconsistent risk scores. How to Measure Identity Technical Debt Measure identity technical debt across coverage, exposure, ownership, recurrence, and remediation rather than through a single score. 1. Identity Inventory and Ownership Metrics Track known and unknown identities, human-to-non-human ratios, unowned identities, duplicates, shadow accounts, disconnected applications, and authoritative-source coverage. 2. Dormancy and Lifecycle Metrics Track inactive identities, terminated users with active access, stale service accounts, and overdue deprovisioning. Apply dormancy thresholds based on identity type and risk. 3. Privilege and Permissions Metrics Track privileged identities, excessive permissions, standing admin access, toxic combinations, nested groups, and direct or indirect paths to critical assets. Measure effective access, not just assigned roles. 4. Credentials and Authentication Metrics Track Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) coverage, legacy authentication, password and secret age, non-expiring credentials, exposed secrets, and certificate or key expiry. Pay particular attention to long-lived credentials used by NHIs. For non-human identity risk, track service-account ownership, token and API-key age, secret rotation, excessive permissions, and credentials that remain active after their associated workload is retired. 5. Remediation and Recurrence Metrics Track ownership and remediation times, verified versus reopened findings, expired exceptions, attack paths closed, and risk reduction over time. Recurrence tracking shows whether resolved risks return. Identity Technical Debt Maturity Model Maturity is measured by fewer recurring exposures and faster, verified remediation across four stages. 1. Reactive Cleanup Identity work is incident-driven, with spreadsheet-based inventories, one-off cleanup, and inconsistent ownership. Debt is addressed after problems emerge rather than proactively. 2. Unified Inventory Organizations establish an authoritative identity inventory, assign ownership, implement baseline hygiene policies, and conduct scheduled access reviews. Debt growth slows, but prioritization remains largely rule-based. 3. Risk-Based Prioritization Organizations continuously assess identity posture, use attack-path context, and apply explainable risk scoring. Teams prioritize exploitable identity risks based on exposure rather than treating all findings equally. 4. Closed-Loop Identity Risk Reduction Remediation is automated where appropriate, technically verified, and monitored for recurrence. Organizations track risk reduction over time to ensure resolved debt does not return. How to Reduce Identity Technical Debt The roadmap follows six stages: Discover, Classify, Prioritize, Remediate, Prevent, and Measure. Build an authoritative identity inventory across human, machine, service, and shadow identities, with assigned owners. Automate safe lifecycle and remediation workflows, verify closure, monitor recurrence, and report risk reduction. Identity Technical Debt Ownership and Operating Model No single team owns identity technical debt end-to-end. IAM, IGA, PAM, application, SOC, compliance, HR, and business owners each control part of the lifecycle. Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM) provides the continuous risk-management layer that connects these teams, brings identity exposure into a unified view, prioritizes debt by risk, and tracks whether remediation actually reduces exposure. The challenge is continuously turning this fragmented identity data into a prioritized risk view, driving remediation, and proving that exposure is actually decreasing. This is where ISPM becomes central to reducing identity technical debt. Qualys ETM Identity provides this ISPM layer by correlating identity exposure with Enterprise TruRisk , connecting identity risk to the broader attack-surface risk framework. With Qualys ETM Identity, teams can: Build a unified identity inventory across Active Directory (AD), Entra ID, and Okta, covering human, machine, service, and shadow identities and their relationships. Correlate identity risk with Enterprise TruRisk by combining Qualys Cloud Agent and native connector data and applying Identity TruRisk scoring based on risk factors. Key Takeaways
  • Identity technical debt is the accumulated security, governance, and operational burden created by unmanaged identities, excessive permissions, outdated access, and fragmented controls.
  • It’s caused by identity sprawl, privilege creep, dormant and orphaned accounts, excessive permissions, unmanaged non-human identities (NHIs), and persistent policy exceptions.
  • It increases breach blast radius, Security Operations Center (SOC) investigation time, audit fatigue, operational disruption, delivery friction, and tool complexity.
  • It should be measured using a five-part framework that covers inventory and ownership, dormancy, privilege, credentials, and remediation, rather than a single score.
  • It can be reduced through four maturity stages and a six-step roadmap: Discover, Classify, Prioritize, Remediate, Prevent, and Measure.
  • Qualys ETM Identity correlates identity sprawl, privilege exposure, and NHIs with Enterprise TruRisk, so this debt can be discovered, prioritized, and reduced through verified, closed-loop remediation.
The Hidden Cost of Identity Technical Debt

Most identity decisions are made under pressure: a contractor needs access today, a migration needs a service account now, an acquired business needs users provisioned on day one. Each solves an immediate need and quietly leaves risk behind. That’s identity technical debt: the accumulated security, governance, and operational burden created by unmanaged identities, excessive permissions, outdated access, weak authentication, and fragmented identity controls.

What Is Identity Technical Debt?

Identity technical debt is the backlog of unresolved identity risks, control gaps, exceptions, and lifecycle failures. It includes dormant and overprivileged accounts, as well as hidden relationships among users, machines, applications, credentials, and permissions. Most debt comes from thousands of small decisions that were never revisited.

Identity Technical Debt vs. Identity Risk, Identity Sprawl, and Identity Hygiene

These terms are related but distinct: 

Term What It Describes Identity technical debt The accumulated backlog and future cost when sprawl and risk go unaddressed Identity risk The likelihood and impact of an identity being compromised right now Identity sprawl Uncontrolled growth of identities and identity silos across systems and clouds Identity hygiene The day-to-day practices that prevent debt from accumulating 

Sprawl drives growth, risk reflects current exposure, hygiene prevents accumulation, and technical debt is the resulting backlog. Left unmanaged, that backlog widens the identity attack surface over time. 

How Identity Technical Debt Accumulates 

Identity debt grows through thousands of small access and lifecycle decisions. 

1. Identity Sprawl Across Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Systems 

Users, applications, cloud accounts, service principals, workloads, bots, and AI agents multiply across disconnected systems, making ownership and access visibility difficult to maintain. 

2. Privilege Creep from Role Changes and Temporary Access 

Role changes, projects, and emergency access often leave old permissions behind, turning temporary access into a persistent identity attack surface. 

3. Dormant, Orphaned, and Shadow Accounts 

Former employees, unused accounts, disconnected apps, and duplicates often remain active. Dormant accounts are unused, orphaned accounts lack owners, and shadow identities were never sanctioned. 

4. Excessive Permissions and Hidden Effective Access 

Direct privileges, nested groups, inherited roles, and trust relationships can create toxic combinations, while nominal roles may understate an identity’s effective reach. 

5. Non-Human Identity Risk and Unmanaged Credentials 

Service accounts, API keys, tokens, secrets, and AI agents often lack clear ownership. Long-lived credentials make cleanup risky. Entro Labs found NHIs grew 44% year-over-year and now outnumber human identities 144 to 1. 

6. Weak Identity Policies and Persistent Exceptions 

Inconsistent MFA, non-expiring passwords, legacy authentication, and permanent break-glass access create persistent debt when temporary exceptions lack expiry dates. 

The Hidden Costs of Identity Technical Debt 

Identity debt often surfaces later as wider breach impact, slower investigations, and persistent audit backlogs. 

1. Larger Blast Radius When an Identity is Compromised 

Excessive permissions and weak trust relationships can expand the blast radius of a compromised identity. 

2. Higher SOC Investigation and Incident-Response Costs 

Analysts spend more time determining who owns an account, what access is legitimate, and what’s reachable from it. 

3. Audit Fatigue and Access-Review Backlogs 

Low-context certifications and recurring exceptions turn reviews into an administrative backlog instead of risk reduction. 

4. Operational Disruption and Service Outages 

Expired certificates and unrotated secrets can interrupt applications and authentication with little warning. 

5. Slower Cloud, SaaS, DevOps, and AI Delivery 

Unclear ownership and ungoverned machine identities force teams to choose between speed and control. 

6. Growing Tool and Governance Complexity 

Disconnected Identity and Access Management (IAM), Privileged Access Management (PAM), Identity Governance and Administration (IGA), and directory systems create duplicated records and inconsistent risk scores. 

How to Measure Identity Technical Debt 

Measure identity technical debt across coverage, exposure, ownership, recurrence, and remediation rather than through a single score.  

1. Identity Inventory and Ownership Metrics 

Track known and unknown identities, human-to-non-human ratios, unowned identities, duplicates, shadow accounts, disconnected applications, and authoritative-source coverage. 

2. Dormancy and Lifecycle Metrics 

Track inactive identities, terminated users with active access, stale service accounts, and overdue deprovisioning. Apply dormancy thresholds based on identity type and risk. 

3. Privilege and Permissions Metrics 

Track privileged identities, excessive permissions, standing admin access, toxic combinations, nested groups, and direct or indirect paths to critical assets. Measure effective access, not just assigned roles. 

4. Credentials and Authentication Metrics 

Track Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) coverage, legacy authentication, password and secret age, non-expiring credentials, exposed secrets, and certificate or key expiry. Pay particular attention to long-lived credentials used by NHIs. For non-human identity risk, track service-account ownership, token and API-key age, secret rotation, excessive permissions, and credentials that remain active after their associated workload is retired. 

5. Remediation and Recurrence Metrics 

Track ownership and remediation times, verified versus reopened findings, expired exceptions, attack paths closed, and risk reduction over time. Recurrence tracking shows whether resolved risks return. 

Identity Technical Debt Maturity Model 

Maturity is measured by fewer recurring exposures and faster, verified remediation across four stages. 

1. Reactive Cleanup 

Identity work is incident-driven, with spreadsheet-based inventories, one-off cleanup, and inconsistent ownership. Debt is addressed after problems emerge rather than proactively. 

2. Unified Inventory 

Organizations establish an authoritative identity inventory, assign ownership, implement baseline hygiene policies, and conduct scheduled access reviews. Debt growth slows, but prioritization remains largely rule-based. 

3. Risk-Based Prioritization 

Organizations continuously assess identity posture, use attack-path context, and apply explainable risk scoring. Teams prioritize exploitable identity risks based on exposure rather than treating all findings equally. 

4. Closed-Loop Identity Risk Reduction 

Remediation is automated where appropriate, technically verified, and monitored for recurrence. Organizations track risk reduction over time to ensure resolved debt does not return. 

How to Reduce Identity Technical Debt 

The roadmap follows six stages: Discover, Classify, Prioritize, Remediate, Prevent, and Measure. 

  1. Build an authoritative identity inventory across human, machine, service, and shadow identities, with assigned owners. 
  1. Segment debt by identity type and business impact, since dormancy and remediation rules differ by identity type. 
  1. Remove dormant, orphaned, and unnecessary access after validating dependencies. 
  1. Secure privileged and non-human identities by rotating secrets, reducing standing privilege, and defining ownership. 
  1. Close high-risk attack paths and trust gaps that reach high-value assets. 
  1. Automate safe lifecycle and remediation workflows, verify closure, monitor recurrence, and report risk reduction.

Each of these contributes to identity technical debt, not a synonym for it: debt is the cumulative backlog that results when none of them are consistently addressed.

No single team owns identity technical debt end-to-end. IAM, IGA, PAM, application, SOC, compliance, HR, and business owners each control part of the lifecycle. Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM) provides the continuous risk-management layer that connects these teams, brings identity exposure into a unified view, prioritizes debt by risk, and tracks whether remediation actually reduces exposure. A shared Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed (RACI) matrix defines who discovers debt, validates access, approves exceptions, remediates exposure, and verifies risk reduction.

items.title: Weekly Update 530: Email Dependencies & Apps
items.summary: Email is just one of those utilities like power or water where you always expect it to just, well, to just be there. You sign up with a provider and use as much of it as you need, when you need it, and the idea of it being unavailable for any extended period of time is foreign. Microsoft's outage a few days ago was one of those exceptional circumstances, and whilst it absolutely rocked the whole internet, it's far from a reason not to decry using email for most of the things we currently apply it to. But it is a good time to look at where redundancy makes sense; maybe start with redundant channels for alerts about things that could hurt people !

items.title: Flash Alert: Weaponizing the November 2026 Microsoft Outage
items.summary: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team Cofense Intelligence has identified an active phishing campaign exploiting confusion surrounding the Microsoft November 2026 outage to deliver a credential phishing attack. The email, supposedly from Microsoft and personalized using the recipient’s organization, claims that emails are unavailable due to disruptions to Exchange Online. The recipient is instructed to click the button to “Restore Messages”. Clicking on the button, however, redirects the user to a Microsoft 365-spoofing credential phishing page. Threat actors move quickly on big news. The first sample was seen one day into the outage. By combining the recent outage news with their phishing attacks and likely with generative AI, the threat actors have quickly created an ongoing and likely effective campaign. After this outage, people expect email problems, so a message about stuck emails matches what they already expect, and they may check emails less carefully. Email Content Figure 1: Held message notification used in credential phishing. (ATR 426633) This campaign email sends a fake held message notification with a button leading to a credential phishing site. The email, as shown in Figure 1, is styled like a legitimate Microsoft notification. The email appears to come from the organization’s “Outage Notification” based on the email recipient’s company. Recipients are informed that “messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours unless released”, because threat actors use urgency to get victims to act. Clicking on the button in the email to “RESTORE MESSAGES” will redirect the email recipient to a Microsoft 365 credential phishing site instead. Microsoft-Spoofing Sign-In Page Figure 2: Microsoft credential phishing page used in campaign. (ATR 426633) In prior campaigns, threat actors were already good at creating realistic login pages. As seen in Figure 2, the Microsoft credential phishing page used in this campaign is a good mimicry of the real Microsoft login page. When a victim first submits credentials, the phishing page will say that the credentials are incorrect. If they try a second time, the page will redirect to Microsoft to obfuscate the fact that they were on a phishing page. Although this type of phishing lure has been used before, threat actors are combining it with breaking news regarding the outage to create a dangerous attack. Cofense Intelligence provides early warning of emerging phishing campaigns through Flash Alerts like this one, giving security teams advance notice of new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) before they reach more inboxes. In this case, the campaign bypassed Abnormal Security, Mimecast, and Microsoft ATP. Despite the bypass of email security controls, employees trained using Cofense’s Security Awareness Training (SAT) were able to identify the phishing campaign emails like those found in ATR 426633. items.title: ARTEX Moves at Machine Speed: What Risk Owners Need to Change
items.summary: Key Takeaways ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework released in July 2026, doesn’t exploit new kinds of vulnerabilities. It automates the discovery, chaining, and retrying of existing weaknesses, often across many targets at once. In observed campaigns, attackers using ARTEX went from first targeting an organization to privileged access in under three hours, while the median time for customers to fix critical vulnerabilities is 7 days. In most AI attack tools of this kind, the limits are set by prompts or by user-adjustable settings, so organizations should identify and approve these tools and question any pentest provider that runs them. To keep pace, vulnerability programs need to detect exposures at disclosure, rank them by confirmed exploitability, and make automatic patching the default, with hours-long deadlines for internet-facing systems. ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework, didn’t change what gets exploited. It changed how long you have, and how many of your weak points get tried at once. Frameworks like ARTEX don’t need a new class of vulnerability. They automate the work of finding, chaining, and retrying existing weaknesses, often across many targets in parallel. Observed campaigns show that some intrusions reach privileged access within hours. That strengthens the case for faster remediation and mitigation, and for ensuring that a single unpatched system, exposed credential, or excessive permission doesn’t become a much larger intrusion. ARTEX was released as an open-source penetration-testing framework in July 2026. You give it a target and a goal. It scans, picks a way in, uses what it finds there to reach the next system, and keeps going until it reaches the goal or runs out of routes. It was published in July as a research and testing tool. By October, it was turning up in incident reports. For vulnerability and risk management teams, the implication is direct: every hour an exposure remains open gives attackers more time to find and exploit a path through your environment. When they can pursue several paths at once, the question is how quickly you can close the exposures that put critical systems within reach. What ARTEX is We read its source code. The simplest description is a project manager for a break-in. A planning agent takes the goal and keeps an ordered to-do list. The example in ARTEX’s own documentation is the familiar one: find an injection point, take the credentials, move sideways, raise privileges. Worker agents carry out the steps, several at a time, with the same ordinary tools a human tester would use. Each one writes down what it learned, and the planner reads those notes and decides what to try next. A person can watch and redirect it from a web console, and it runs on whichever language model you connect to it. None of that is new to a penetration tester. Scanners have found weaknesses quickly for 20 years. The slow, skilled part of an intrusion was joining those weaknesses into a route, keeping track of what worked, and carrying a stolen credential from one machine to the next, and that is the part ARTEX does. ARTEX did not ship without an authorization-scope mechanism. It shipped with one removed, and the comment saying so is still in the source. The gates that replaced it are seeded as ordinary settings, and a user can disable or delete them. Anatomy of an AI attacker. Seven capabilities taken from the source code of ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Hermes, and Cairn, four tools already seen in real attacks. Every layer rests on one weakness you have not fixed yet. What The Reports Say The public evidence comes mainly from Microsoft and CrowdStrike, and it is more measured than the headlines. Microsoft watched one group use ARTEX to attempt sign-ins at more than 2,250 tenants. Most attempts failed, but in several cases the group went from targeting an organization to gaining privileged access in under three hours. CrowdStrike saw another group turn it on more than 200 organizations in 11 days and confirmed follow-on activity at nine, with a human operator steering at the decision points. The agents ran on a cheap, open-weight model, not a premium one. In a separate case, Microsoft timed an agent at 5 minutes from searching GitHub for leaked secrets to pulling data from a cloud key vault. That is the evidence. ARTEX Has Relatives ARTEX has the name, but your team is as likely to meet one of its relatives. We also read the code and documentation for five of them. Tool What it is Used in attacks What keeps it in bounds ARTEX and its forks Runs a full penetration test on its own. The original is closed; the copies are not. Yes By default, lets an action through when its own safety check fails. Cairn Many agents working from one shared board of findings. Yes No controls of its own. In local mode, agents run with your permissions and no sandbox. Hermes General-purpose agent that learns by writing its own skills. Yes Approval for the skills it writes is off by default. CyberStrikeAI Security testing platform with built-in command-and-control, now owned by ThreatBook. Yes Mixed. Unanswered approvals are denied, but tool filtering is a pattern blocklist. Strix Application security agent that aims to prove each finding with a working exploit. Yes Scope is largely set by instructions to the model. PentestGPT Academic project that now runs as an agent. None we found Relies on the isolation you deploy it in. RedAgents / Artex Pro ThreatBook’s commercial bundle, including a paid ARTEX. Not applicable We have not seen the code. The pattern repeats. In most of these tools, the limits are written in prompts, or in settings that someone can change. One platform in the table turns on exactly one rule out of the box: its tool filter blocks government domains, and nothing else. When that rule fires, the message to the agent tells it to pick an authorized non-government target instead. In another case, it goes further. While the agent is writing its reply, a second copy of the conversation runs in the background, writing new skills for it. The approval gate for those writes is off unless you switch it on, and once written, a skill becomes part of its instructions in every session that follows. The tool you approve and the tool that runs next month are not guaranteed to be the same tool. Two Additions to The Asset Inventory The first is everything you forgot. These agents work many targets at once and have no reason to skip the dull ones, so the unowned server gets the same attention as your front door. Gaps in the inventory were tolerable when an attacker had to choose where to spend a week. Now the inventory has to be complete and current, which is what Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) is built for. The second is the tools themselves. Sooner or later someone in your organization, or at one of your suppliers, will run one of these with good intentions. Each install holds the findings and credentials from every test it has run. One popular mirror’s source was clean, but its installer pulled a Docker image with a backdoor in the login page . The image had been pulled 7,946 times before researchers disclosed it. Treat them like any other software: find them, then approve or remove them. Before your team or your pentest provider runs one Ask five questions, and ask your provider the same ones When a safety check errors out or times out, does the tool stop or carry on? By default, ARTEX carries on. Is scope enforced by the software, or requested in a prompt? What counts as a finding, and what evidence comes with it? Can you show that the build you are running matches source code someone has reviewed? Is every action logged in a way you can tie back to your own test? Seven Da ys Against Three Hours Most vulnerability programs rest on an assumption that rarely gets written down, which is that attackers are short on time. It is why a critical vulnerability on an internet-facing server can be given 30 days, why a privilege escalation bug that needs local access waits behind the remote ones, and why risk exceptions get signed when exploitation looks complicated. ARTEX makes attacker time cheap, and the assumption goes with it. An attacker who can get from first contact to privileged access in under three hours is not going to wait for your change window. Defenders are getting faster too. We are seeing customers fix critical vulnerabilities in a median of 7 days, down from 9 last year, even as volumes rise. More to fix and less time taken to fix it tells you teams are treating this as urgent, and a count alone would never show that. We also see 12% to 16% of our customers fix vulnerabilities before the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. They are acting on their threat-risk signals rather than waiting for the government to tell them. Our Threat Research Unit’s five-year analysis covered more than 1.5 billion critical vulnerability instances, and approximately 173 million of them were remediated before the vulnerability entered that catalog. Seven days is real progress, and it is still 168 hours against an attacker who needs three. The speed is not even across the environment, either. It shows up where the fix arrives on its own and deployment can be done automatically, and the network edge is still where it lags. The edge is also where a tool like ARTEX starts. So the patch window measured in weeks is finished, and policy should say so. If a fix can be deployed automatically, it goes on the same day, and people approve the exceptions instead of the rule. An internet-facing system that cannot be patched within hours gets a mitigation or comes off the internet until it can. Every risk exception signed because exploitation was hard, needed prior access, or seemed unlikely gets reopened, because in risk-register terms the impact column is where it was and the likelihood column has moved. Break The Chain at Machine Speed In ARTEX’s source, the pause between one step landing and the next step being assigned is a constant set to 800 milliseconds. That is the cadence your change window is racing. The design that makes ARTEX fast also gives you something to aim at. It works in order, and each step depends on what the previous one produced, so removing one link stops everything behind it on that route. Its planner is instructed to put depth ahead of coverage, which means it pushes a promising route all the way through instead of testing everything lightly. To a tool built that way, two medium findings on the same route are worth more than a critical on a server that leads nowhere, and a queue sorted by severity alone will keep fixing the wrong one first. The defense is to reach the link before the agent does. A program that scans on a schedule and patches on a calendar is working by the week against an attacker working by the hour, so three things have to happen without waiting for a person. The first is finding the exposure, and that has gone from weeks to minutes. Qualys InstaScan detects newly disclosed vulnerabilities on customer systems a median of 14 minutes after disclosure, with 96% detection coverage across supported vendors. Where we can compare head to head, it finds the exposure about a day before a scheduled scan would, and for a quarter of them, close to a week earlier. As AI shortens the time from disclosure to exploit, every hour of early warning counts. The second is knowing which exposures are real. Across approximately 9 million exploit validations through Qualys TruConfirm , just 11% confirmed exploitability. That turns a queue of 9 million into a queue of about 1 million, and it puts proof where a severity score used to be. Validate again after the fix, because an installed patch does not prove the route is closed. The third is fixing them without a person in the loop. Over the last 12 months, our customers deployed more than 180 million patches with Qualys Patch Management . Since frontier AI models like Mythos arrived in mid-2026, our customers have been patching 47% more each month, and the share of patches running fully automated has doubled, from about 30% last September to about 60% this September. The usual objection to automatic patching is that it breaks things. Fewer than 1 in 8,000 patches deployed through Qualys needed a rollback, and that reliability is what lets customers move at machine speed. It also frees people for the network edge, where the fix still needs hands. Not every link is a missing patch. The second step in ARTEX’s own example is credentials, and a reused admin password, an over-privileged service account, or an access key left in a public code repository will carry an attacker further than most Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). Put those in the program too, with owners and deadlines. What We Would Do This Week: List every internet-facing system with an open critical vulnerability or a known, exploited vulnerability, then fix it, apply mitigations, or take it offline. Search your environment for these tools, including the tomicdd/artex and congdonglinux/artex container images. Rotate any secret that was ever committed to a public repository. Deleting it from the repository is not enough. This Quarter: Move from scheduled scans to detection at disclosure wherever it is supported. Make automatic patching the default, and set the deadline for internet-facing systems in hours. Rank what is left by confirmed exploitability. Reopen the risk acceptances that were justified by attacker effort. Put credentials and exposed secrets into the vulnerability program, with owners and deadlines. Set a policy on who may run AI pentest tools, including suppliers. If you report one number upward, make it how long weaknesses on internet-facing systems stay open, because that is the number these tools are racing against. Attackers now measure time in hours.   • In most AI attack tools of this kind, the limits are set by prompts or by user-adjustable settings, so organizations should identify and approve these tools and question any pentest provider that runs them.
  • To keep pace, vulnerability programs need to detect exposures at disclosure, rank them by confirmed exploitability, and make automatic patching the default, with hours-long deadlines for internet-facing systems.

ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework, didn’t change what gets exploited. It changed how long you have, and how many of your weak points get tried at once. Frameworks like ARTEX don’t need a new class of vulnerability. They automate the work of finding, chaining, and retrying existing weaknesses, often across many targets in parallel. Observed campaigns show that some intrusions reach privileged access within hours. That strengthens the case for faster remediation and mitigation, and for ensuring that a single unpatched system, exposed credential, or excessive permission doesn’t become a much larger intrusion.

ARTEX was released as an open-source penetration-testing framework in July 2026. You give it a target and a goal. It scans, picks a way in, uses what it finds there to reach the next system, and keeps going until it reaches the goal or runs out of routes. It was published in July as a research and testing tool. By October, it was turning up in incident reports.

For vulnerability and risk management teams, the implication is direct: every hour an exposure remains open gives attackers more time to find and exploit a path through your environment. When they can pursue several paths at once, the question is how quickly you can close the exposures that put critical systems within reach.

What ARTEX is

We read its source code. The simplest description is a project manager for a break-in. A planning agent takes the goal and keeps an ordered to-do list. The example in ARTEX’s own documentation is the familiar one: find an injection point, take the credentials, move sideways, raise privileges. Worker agents carry out the steps, several at a time, with the same ordinary tools a human tester would use. Each one writes down what it learned, and the planner reads those notes and decides what to try next. A person can watch and redirect it from a web console, and it runs on whichever language model you connect to it.

None of that is new to a penetration tester. Scanners have found weaknesses quickly for 20 years. The slow, skilled part of an intrusion was joining those weaknesses into a route, keeping track of what worked, and carrying a stolen credential from one machine to the next, and that is the part ARTEX does. ARTEX did not ship without an authorization-scope mechanism. It shipped with one removed, and the comment saying so is still in the source. The gates that replaced it are seeded as ordinary settings, and a user can disable or delete them.

Anatomy of an AI attacker. Seven capabilities taken from the source code of ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Hermes, and Cairn, four tools already seen in real attacks. Every layer rests on one weakness you have not fixed yet. What The Reports Say

The public evidence comes mainly from Microsoft and CrowdStrike, and it is more measured than the headlines. Microsoft watched one group use ARTEX to attempt sign-ins at more than 2,250 tenants. Most attempts failed, but in several cases the group went from targeting an organization to gaining privileged access in under three hours. CrowdStrike saw another group turn it on more than 200 organizations in 11 days and confirmed follow-on activity at nine, with a human operator steering at the decision points. The agents ran on a cheap, open-weight model, not a premium one. In a separate case, Microsoft timed an agent at 5 minutes from searching GitHub for leaked secrets to pulling data from a cloud key vault.

That is the evidence.

ARTEX Has Relatives

ARTEX has the name, but your team is as likely to meet one of its relatives. We also read the code and documentation for five of them.

ToolWhat it isUsed in attacksWhat keeps it in boundsARTEX and its forksRuns a full penetration test on its own. The original is closed; the copies are not.YesBy default, lets an action through when its own safety check fails.CairnMany agents working from one shared board of findings.YesNo controls of its own. In local mode, agents run with your permissions and no sandbox.HermesGeneral-purpose agent that learns by writing its own skills.YesApproval for the skills it writes is off by default.CyberStrikeAISecurity testing platform with built-in command-and-control, now owned by ThreatBook.YesMixed. Unanswered approvals are denied, but tool filtering is a pattern blocklist.StrixApplication security agent that aims to prove each finding with a working exploit.YesScope is largely set by instructions to the model.PentestGPTAcademic project that now runs as an agent.None we foundRelies on the isolation you deploy it in.RedAgents / Artex ProThreatBook’s commercial bundle, including a paid ARTEX.Not applicableWe have not seen the code.

The pattern repeats. In most of these tools, the limits are written in prompts, or in settings that someone can change. One platform in the table turns on exactly one rule out of the box: its tool filter blocks government domains, and nothing else. When that rule fires, the message to the agent tells it to pick an authorized non-government target instead.

In another case, it goes further. While the agent is writing its reply, a second copy of the conversation runs in the background, writing new skills for it. The approval gate for those writes is off unless you switch it on, and once written, a skill becomes part of its instructions in every session that follows. The tool you approve and the tool that runs next month are not guaranteed to be the same tool.

Two Additions to The Asset Inventory

The first is everything you forgot. These agents work many targets at once and have no reason to skip the dull ones, so the unowned server gets the same attention as your front door. Gaps in the inventory were tolerable when an attacker had to choose where to spend a week. Now the inventory has to be complete and current, which is what Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) is built for.

The second is the tools themselves. Sooner or later someone in your organization, or at one of your suppliers, will run one of these with good intentions. Each install holds the findings and credentials from every test it has run. One popular mirror’s source was clean, but its installer pulled a Docker image with a backdoor in the login page. The image had been pulled 7,946 times before researchers disclosed it. Treat them like any other software: find them, then approve or remove them.

Before your team or your pentest provider runs one Ask five questions, and ask your provider the same ones
  1. When a safety check errors out or times out, does the tool stop or carry on? By default, ARTEX carries on.
  2. Is scope enforced by the software, or requested in a prompt?
  3. What counts as a finding, and what evidence comes with it?
  4. Can you show that the build you are running matches source code someone has reviewed?
  5. Is every action logged in a way you can tie back to your own test?
Seven Days Against Three Hours

Most vulnerability programs rest on an assumption that rarely gets written down, which is that attackers are short on time. It is why a critical vulnerability on an internet-facing server can be given 30 days, why a privilege escalation bug that needs local access waits behind the remote ones, and why risk exceptions get signed when exploitation looks complicated. ARTEX makes attacker time cheap, and the assumption goes with it. An attacker who can get from first contact to privileged access in under three hours is not going to wait for your change window.

Defenders are getting faster too. We are seeing customers fix critical vulnerabilities in a median of 7 days, down from 9 last year, even as volumes rise. More to fix and less time taken to fix it tells you teams are treating this as urgent, and a count alone would never show that. We also see 12% to 16% of our customers fix vulnerabilities before the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. They are acting on their threat-risk signals rather than waiting for the government to tell them. Our Threat Research Unit’s five-year analysis covered more than 1.5 billion critical vulnerability instances, and approximately 173 million of them were remediated before the vulnerability entered that catalog.

Seven days is real progress, and it is still 168 hours against an attacker who needs three. The speed is not even across the environment, either. It shows up where the fix arrives on its own and deployment can be done automatically, and the network edge is still where it lags. The edge is also where a tool like ARTEX starts.

So the patch window measured in weeks is finished, and policy should say so. If a fix can be deployed automatically, it goes on the same day, and people approve the exceptions instead of the rule. An internet-facing system that cannot be patched within hours gets a mitigation or comes off the internet until it can. Every risk exception signed because exploitation was hard, needed prior access, or seemed unlikely gets reopened, because in risk-register terms the impact column is where it was and the likelihood column has moved.

Break The Chain at Machine Speed

In ARTEX’s source, the pause between one step landing and the next step being assigned is a constant set to 800 milliseconds. That is the cadence your change window is racing. The design that makes ARTEX fast also gives you something to aim at. It works in order, and each step depends on what the previous one produced, so removing one link stops everything behind it on that route. Its planner is instructed to put depth ahead of coverage, which means it pushes a promising route all the way through instead of testing everything lightly. To a tool built that way, two medium findings on the same route are worth more than a critical on a server that leads nowhere, and a queue sorted by severity alone will keep fixing the wrong one first.

The defense is to reach the link before the agent does. A program that scans on a schedule and patches on a calendar is working by the week against an attacker working by the hour, so three things have to happen without waiting for a person.

The first is finding the exposure, and that has gone from weeks to minutes. Qualys InstaScan detects newly disclosed vulnerabilities on customer systems a median of 14 minutes after disclosure, with 96% detection coverage across supported vendors. Where we can compare head to head, it finds the exposure about a day before a scheduled scan would, and for a quarter of them, close to a week earlier. As AI shortens the time from disclosure to exploit, every hour of early warning counts.

The second is knowing which exposures are real. Across approximately 9 million exploit validations through Qualys TruConfirm, just 11% confirmed exploitability. That turns a queue of 9 million into a queue of about 1 million, and it puts proof where a severity score used to be. Validate again after the fix, because an installed patch does not prove the route is closed.

The third is fixing them without a person in the loop. Over the last 12 months, our customers deployed more than 180 million patches with Qualys Patch Management. Since frontier AI models like Mythos arrived in mid-2026, our customers have been patching 47% more each month, and the share of patches running fully automated has doubled, from about 30% last September to about 60% this September. The usual objection to automatic patching is that it breaks things. Fewer than 1 in 8,000 patches deployed through Qualys needed a rollback, and that reliability is what lets customers move at machine speed. It also frees people for the network edge, where the fix still needs hands.

Not every link is a missing patch. The second step in ARTEX’s own example is credentials, and a reused admin password, an over-privileged service account, or an access key left in a public code repository will carry an attacker further than most Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). Put those in the program too, with owners and deadlines.

What We Would Do This Week:
  • List every internet-facing system with an open critical vulnerability or a known, exploited vulnerability, then fix it, apply mitigations, or take it offline.
  • Search your environment for these tools, including the tomicdd/artex and congdonglinux/artex container images.
  • Rotate any secret that was ever committed to a public repository. Deleting it from the repository is not enough.
This Quarter:
  • Move from scheduled scans to detection at disclosure wherever it is supported.
  • Make automatic patching the default, and set the deadline for internet-facing systems in hours.
  • Rank what is left by confirmed exploitability.
  • Reopen the risk acceptances that were justified by attacker effort.
  • Put credentials and exposed secrets into the vulnerability program, with owners and deadlines.
  • Set a policy on who may run AI pentest tools, including suppliers.

If you report one number upward, make it how long weaknesses on internet-facing systems stay open, because that is the number these tools are racing against.

Attackers now measure time in hours. See how Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM) helps you find, prioritize, and close exposures at machine speed.

items.title: NoisyTCP: 11-Year-Old Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Crash Servers Remotely
items.summary: NoisyTCP is an 11-year-old Linux kernel bug . It lets a remote attacker crash a server without logging in. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-99288. Hyunwoo Kim (@v4bel) reported and patched it, and he released the NoisyTCP advisory on GitHub after the Linux distribution embargo ended. The flaw sits in the kernel’s TCP code, which handles almost all network traffic on Linux. Kim says it can be triggered against plain TCP listeners. A server doesn’t need unusual settings, firewall rules, or special sockets. It only has to call listen() and receive packets from the attacker. That puts Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers in their default setups at risk, as well as proxies. The attacker needs a server with two or more receive queues, or one with Receive Packet Steering (RPS) turned on. Both are common on modern hardware. The attacker sends IPv4 fragments and normal TCP packets that land on different CPUs. This creates a race condition, where two parts of the kernel touch the same memory at the same moment. NoisyTCP Linux Kernel Flaw In the first trigger path, one CPU finds an existing half-open connection record. Another CPU frees that record and quickly reuses the same memory for a new SYN cookie request with the same connection details. The first CPU grabs the new object and passes its checks. But the new object has no listener attached. The kernel then reads a NULL listener and panics. The result is a remote denial of service. Kim warns that a crash from a containerized web server takes down the whole host, not only the app. A second path could cause a remote use-after-free, but it needs several races to succeed in a row and is much harder to pull off. Timing matters here. On virtual machines such as QEMU/KVM, the tests took about 5 seconds to 2 minutes. On a quiet bare-metal server with 8 receive queues, the tuned proof-of-concept needed about 14 hours. Cloud and virtualized servers are therefore the most exposed. This is not a remote code execution bug, at least for now. Kim says he has only built a limited, lab-specific exploit for VM servers and is still researching a general one. A reliable crash is still serious for any internet-facing service. The bug was introduced in commit 079096f103fa on October 3, 2015. The fix, commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, landed on November 3, 2026. That means nearly every Linux distribution has carried the flaw for about 11 years. Administrators should install updated kernels from their vendors as soon as they are available and reboot. If patching must wait, Kim suggests two stopgaps. The first is to turn off SYN cookies with sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0. This setting applies per network namespace, so each container with its own namespace needs it too. It also weakens protection against SYN floods, a common way to knock servers offline. The second is to cut the network interface down to one receive queue and disable RPS and RFS, which stops the race. Linux networking code has had a rough few weeks. Cyber Security News recently covered attackers scanning for the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-98432 , a critical TCP/IPv4 bug with a 9.8 score. It also reported on a Linux kernel TCP flaw that sat hidden for seven years . Race conditions like these are hard to spot in code review, and they often stay hidden for years. Teams that run public Linux servers should check kernel versions now, test vendor patches, and watch for unexplained reboots. For background on the SYN cookie feature involved, see this LWN.net explainer. Give your SOC the alert context on the latest threats to stop incidents quickly -> Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs

items.title: AWS Restores Services in US-EAST-1 After Hours-Long Outage Disrupts Cloud Operations
items.summary: Amazon Web Services restored operations in its US-EAST-1 region on November 15 after an outage disrupted account signups, authentication, and network connections. Problems began at 3:05 a.m. PST, and the last network issue was resolved at 6:21 a.m. PST, leaving some customers affected for more than three hours. The disruption affected customers using IAM Identity Center to access the AWS Console and services including Kiro and Amazon Connect. AWS also reported failed sign-up requests. Its initial service notice confirmed that engineers were investigating connectivity issues alongside problems with account access and new registrations. Service Update: Multiple Services US-EAST-1 Region We are investigating reports of Connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region. IAM Identity center sign-in requests and AWS SignUps are also impacted at this time. Track status: https://t.co/pKjXtyzPPm #AWS #AWSSupport — AWS Support (@AWSSupport) November 15, 2026 Authentication Restored Before Network Recovery AWS engineers were automatically engaged at 3:10 a.m. PST, five minutes after the incident began. Teams investigated the cause while working to restore service. Authentication issues were fully resolved by 5:20 a.m. PST, when most affected AWS services also returned to normal operation, according to the company’s update. However, network recovery took longer for a subset of customers using Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, within a single cell. Those customers continued to experience connectivity problems until 6:21 a.m. PST. The separate recovery times show why successful authentication alone did not mean every affected service connection had recovered. In its final recovery statement, AWS listed the main disruption window as 3:05 a.m. to 6:10 a.m. PST while separately confirming the final NLB fix at 6:21 a.m. PST. The company advised customers to retry failed requests and said all AWS services were operating normally. Multiple Services US-EAST-1 Region Issue Resolved Between 3:05 AM and 6:10 AM PST we experienced signup errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region. Customers using IAM Identity Center for authentication into the AWS Console, or for… — AWS Support (@AWSSupport) November 15, 2026 Previous Cloud Outages The incident follows earlier problems in the same region. Cyber Security News previously covered AWS US-EAST-1 delays affecting EC2 deployments , which also disrupted related container services in October 2025. That event provides historical context, but available evidence does not establish a shared cause with the latest outage. The disruption also came after a major Microsoft 365 outage affected Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender XDR. Microsoft reported unavailable servers, failed health checks, and capacity problems during recovery. The separate incidents highlight how failures in shared cloud systems can interrupt access to several business and security services at once. AWS’s recovery statement did not disclose a detailed root cause or identify a cyberattack. Its findings described authentication and connectivity failures. Until further technical details emerge, the incident should be treated as a service availability event rather than evidence of malicious activity or a confirmed security breach. items.title: Tor Releases Emergency Security Update as Ongoing DDoS Attack Overwhelms Network Relays
items.summary: The Tor Project has released Tor 0.4.9.17 in an urgent response to an ongoing distributed denial-of-service attack that is overwhelming network relays. Announced on November 13, 2026, the stable release includes several security fixes, including one that addresses IPv6 handling in relay denial-of-service defenses. Tor says the attack has affected most relay operators and urges them to upgrade immediately. The attack involves a massive flood of client circuits, according to a release announcement from Tor Network Team developer David Goulet. These circuits are the connections handled across Tor’s relay network. By flooding relays with circuit activity, the attackers are placing heavy demand on the systems that carry user traffic. Tor has not published traffic volumes or identified those responsible in the announcement. IPv6 Fix Strengthens Relay Defenses The most important disclosed change concerns how relay DoS defenses handle IPv6. However, Tor’s public announcement does not explain the underlying code error, provide a CVE number, or describe the exact conditions needed to trigger it. The confirmed finding is narrower: the developers consider this fix especially important to relay protection during the current attack. That distinction matters because a security update does not automatically mean the wider attack has ended. Tor says its developers are still testing additional defenses and expect more releases soon. Version 0.4.9.17 should therefore be understood as an immediate response to an active problem, rather than a confirmed end to the disruption across the network. Tor has previously added other defenses against denial-of-service activity. Cyber Security News covered its proof-of-work protection for onion services , which makes clients complete a small computing task before their requests receive service. That earlier feature addresses onion-service access and should not be confused with the IPv6-related relay fix announced in this release. Relay Operators Urged to Update In the official security announcement , Goulet gave operators a direct instruction: “If you run a relay, please upgrade as soon as possible.” The project states that no further action is required after upgrading. It does not ask operators to apply extra configuration changes or manually adjust IPv6 settings as part of this release. The urgency reflects Tor’s reliance on volunteer-run infrastructure. Its relay operations guidance explains that volunteers provide the bandwidth supporting bridges, guards, middle relays, and exit relays. When many operators face the same circuit flood, the problem reaches beyond one server and becomes a shared network availability issue. This release targets Tor’s core relay software, not a newly announced Tor Browser build. Readers should distinguish it from browser updates, such as the previously reported Tor Browser security releases , which also address Firefox-based browser components. The immediate upgrade instruction in this announcement is specifically directed at relay operators. Tor also thanked operators sharing information through the tor-relays mailing list. Their continued reports are helping developers respond while the attack remains active. For now, the confirmed response is to install 0.4.9.17 promptly and follow further official release announcements as additional defenses become available.
