items.summary_html:
A car owner says an AI coding agent helped him read, copy, and then run code inside the engine computer of a 1994 Jeep Cherokee. The work took about a week. He used a $3 Arduino Nano, and the Jeep passed California’s smog test at the end. Muhammad Zulali shared the full story in a YouTube video on November 10, 2026.

The Jeep had no modern OBD2 port, so common scan tools could not talk to it. It failed the smog test at 25 mph because of high NOx, a gas that rises when an engine runs lean. Zulali first swapped the oxygen sensor, but the result got worse at 15 mph. Each test cost about $100, so he asked Claude Code to find a better way.

Claude found that the engine computer speaks an old, slow Chrysler protocol called SCI. The signal wire is flipped compared with a normal serial port, so a small translator was needed. A $3 Arduino Nano on a breadboard did the job, and the full parts list came to about $15.

Claude Cracks 32-Year-Old Jeep ECU

Tom’s Hardware reported that the link ran at about 7,800 baud. Only three wires from the six-hole diagnostic plug were used. One hole carries 12 volts with the key on, and touching it can fry the board.

The first reading came at 1:30 a.m. and showed only coolant temperature and battery voltage. Later data looked odd, with a fuel trim that seemed to add 22 percent extra fuel. Zulali tested fuel pressure and found a very low 10 PSI.

Claude then switched the fuel pump on by itself for about 10 seconds. He called this the moment the tool went from read-only to controlling the car.

The AI also made a mistake, and the cause was a public tool. Claude later found that the ChryslerScanner parameter table was wrong for his Jeep. The computer was removing fuel, not adding it. The scanner’s author, László Dániel, is credited in the project for the parameter tables.

Next, Claude copied the engine computer’s whole program to a laptop. The code showed a California-only fuel table that cuts fuel at the same load used in the smog test. This likely explained the high NOx. Reflashing the chip was the obvious fix, but the computer was built in December 1993, about four months too early to be reflashable.

That is where OpenAI’s Codex stepped in. It found a way to send a tiny program over the same three wires and have the computer run it. The first version was wiped out within seconds, so Codex moved the code into EEPROM, a memory that survives a dead battery. Zulali said Claude did most of the diagnosis and Codex did the memory work, while he handled wiring and driving.

The project is open source under the GPLv3 license. The xj-scanner repository on GitHub had 252 stars and 30 forks at the time of writing. It was tested on one car, a 1994 Cherokee XJ with a 4.0L engine, and the author warns that use is at your own risk.

For security readers, the lesson is about how fast AI agents can learn forgotten systems. Researchers once showed that car computers could be pushed to turn off brakes through physical access. Agents now cut the skill and time needed for that kind of work.

Our earlier report on Claude Code finding a hidden model backdoor shows the same pattern. Agents also carry their own risk, as seen when hackers hijacked Codex and Claude Code with files in Downloads. Anthropic’s Claude Code security guide advises users to review commands before approval.

Zulali admits he is not a mechanic and that some of his engine claims may be wrong. The owner reported the result himself, so it has not been independently tested.

items.title: AI chatbots vs. AI agents: what’s the difference?
items.summary: By now, most people are familiar with AI through chatbots. You send a message to a chatbot asking it for questions or advice. For instance, “can you explain the ending of ‘The Brothers Karamazov’ to me? And then recommend a breezier read for my beach trip.” The bot answers your questions, and that’s the broad extent of what it can do. With an AI agent, however, you can say, “I’m hosting this month’s book club meeting. Send out a calendar invite to everyone with the updated address. Also, place a grocery pickup order with the ingredients I’d need to make this hors d’oeuvres recipe.” In short: through agents, AI can now do a whole lot more than answer questions. Naturally, the differences between chatbots and agents go much deeper, and a lot of people lack solid answers on what those differences are. In a 2026 poll , 66% of consumers were comfortable generally using AI in their personal and professional lives, but only 31% said they were likely to trust AI to independently make decisions for them. This signals a growing trust gap. People are comfortable using AI, but don’t feel confident letting it make decisions for them. The source of this disconnect is clear; the survey also found that only 12% of respondents felt very confident that they knew what agentic AI is. Users need information to build confidence and trust in agentic AI. Even so, four in ten AI users had tried an AI agent in 2026, and consumers are seeing a growing number of personal AI agents becoming available on the market. There’s no better time to gain a better understanding of the differences between AI chatbots and AI agents, and how you can use each in the most safe and effective ways possible. Key differences between AI chat and agents For those who are curious or apprehensive about using AI agents, or who are just hoping to understand how they work, read on for an overview of the uses, needs, and respective risks of both AI chatbots and AI agents. Uses: responding versus acting There are different kinds of AI chatbots, like the ones purpose-built to handle tasks like customer service, but broadly speaking, consumer chatbots are useful for reactive tasks . The chatbot can respond to your requests and questions, but without a specific prompt or ask from you, it won’t proactively do anything beyond that set task or beyond the scope of its existing knowledge-base. AI Agents, however, operate very differently, and can do a lot more proactive tasks . Most agents will use a chatbot interface, but that’s just the beginning. With an agent, you ask it a question or assign it a task, and the agent itself will plan out the best course of action. Most importantly, the agent can then execute on that plan. For instance, AI coding agents, and “ vibe coding ,” can famously let people build and code through an agent. Whether you’re a developer or not, you can ask the agent to create an app that performs a specific task, and the agent will fill in the blanks in order to build and design that app without needing any particular oversight or guidance beyond your initial ask. In terms of day-to-day tasks, an AI chatbot can help you write an email asking when your friends are available next week for game night. The difference is that an AI agent can draft the email, and then send it out to your guest list. When your friends respond, the agent can find an appropriate time for everyone, create a calendar event, and send out the calendar invites. On the night of the get-together, it can even place an order for pizza and snacks. Examples like this come with natural follow-up questions. For instance: “that sounds great, but wouldn’t the agent need to access my email, calendar, and Uber Eats account to do that?” The short answer is “yes.” The more an AI can do on your behalf, the more access it may need to your accounts and information. Access: predictable connections versus changing needs An AI chatbot has a defined set of permissions. It has access to certain knowledge-repositories, and can then access your conversation and any other relevant information that you directly share with it, like a document or integration. More importantly, chatbots typically have fairly consistent access requirements across their various use-cases. If a chatbot needs more information to answer a question or request, it might ask you to share that information with it, but it won’t take action beyond that to seek the information out. An agent, however, may need access to several systems to complete a task, and those access needs will vary from task to task. Planning a vacation could involve your calendar, email, travel websites, or airline accounts. Building an app could require access to code repositories, development tools, cloud services, and API keys. Personal assistants and coding agents become useful when they can finish the work in the real account or app where the work belongs. That means they eventually reach a sign-in or protected resource. To interface with those systems, the agent will need you to give it access to that system. And the key question isn’t whether an agent is connected, but how it connects, and for how long? Context: short-term conversations versus dynamic retention Imagine: you’re several paragraphs into a conversation with an AI chatbot when you ask it to “draft an email to Melissa.” The chatbot asks you to clarify who Melissa is, even though you’d shared information about her at the beginning of the chat. At an essential level, this happens because LLMs and AI tools work within context windows. That refers to the amount of information (measured in tokens ) that the AI tool is capable of “thinking” about at any given time. Note: context is different from the memory or history stored by a platform. Many AI chatbot platforms store your past conversations and history indefinitely for you to retrieve later. While specific context windows vary across platforms, it’s an essential truth that AI chatbots have much smaller context windows than AI agents do. When you start a new chat session, the chatbot can’t “remember” or consider anything from your previous chats. In a long enough conversation, it will even “forget” information that you shared earlier in the conversation. With AI agents, context works very differently. As Salesforce puts it , “...agents rely on persistent memory…Unlike one-off interactions, agents need to remember user preferences and ongoing tasks to accurately help customers.” Agents can store context for longer periods and use it far more dynamically. They can “remember” information you previously shared for separate tasks, and may even draw on information from the other services you’ve given them access to. Risk: leaked information vs unintended action To summarize: AI agents typically need far more access to your information and accounts than AI chatbots do. AI agents store and use your information in far longer context windows, in more varied ways, and for longer periods of time. AI agents are capable of taking proactive and complex action across different systems, without requiring an explicit command or oversight from the user. All of these factors contribute to one of the most drastic distinctions between AI chatbots and AI agents: the level of risk they pose to your information. AI chatbots are not without risk. Certainly you shouldn’t share any sensitive information like credentials within a chat window, to reduce the risk of that information being leaked from your chat history. AI agent risk, however, is far less simple to handle. Unlike chatbots, agents require access to your accounts and sensitive information in order to help you effectively. But agents are also able to use that information and access in ways you didn’t intend. That’s why you need a clear moment requiring human approval to control when and how an agent can safely access your accounts. How to use AI agents safely When an agent first reaches a sign-in page that it can’t access, it asks you for the credential to sign in. At this point, you can either: Manually enter your sign-in information every time the agent needs it, which somewhat defeats the purpose of a tool that relies on convenience and automation. Paste your password into a prompt, which means allowing the agent to have access to your credential and account, potentially beyond the task at hand. Neither of those options is acceptable. With the 1Password for Agents platform, 1Password integrates with AI agents like Muse, from Meta, SpaceXSI Grok Bot, Instinct, and Town. When you ask an agent to complete a task, it has to follow a certain process: The agent reaches a sign-in page and requests a specific login. 1Password shows you what the agent is asking for and which saved login could help. You approve or deny the request. If you approve, 1Password fills the password or one-time code directly into the destination. The agent keeps working without seeing the password or the rest of your vault. Your credentials and secrets stay secure and out of the agent’s context, while letting your agent continue to get things done. Want to learn more? For instance, “can you explain the ending of ‘The Brothers Karamazov’ to me? And then recommend a breezier read for my beach trip.” The bot answers your questions, and that’s the broad extent of what it can do.

With an AI agent, however, you can say, “I’m hosting this month’s book club meeting. Send out a calendar invite to everyone with the updated address. Also, place a grocery pickup order with the ingredients I’d need to make this hors d’oeuvres recipe.”

In short: through agents, AI can now do a whole lot more than answer questions.

Naturally, the differences between chatbots and agents go much deeper, and a lot of people lack solid answers on what those differences are. In a 2026 poll, 66% of consumers were comfortable generally using AI in their personal and professional lives, but only 31% said they were likely to trust AI to independently make decisions for them.

Users need information to build confidence and trust in agentic AI.

Even so, four in ten AI users had tried an AI agent in 2026, and consumers are seeing a growing number of personal AI agents becoming available on the market. There’s no better time to gain a better understanding of the differences between AI chatbots and AI agents, and how you can use each in the most safe and effective ways possible.

Key differences between AI chat and agents

For those who are curious or apprehensive about using AI agents, or who are just hoping to understand how they work, read on for an overview of the uses, needs, and respective risks of both AI chatbots and AI agents.

Uses: responding versus acting

There are different kinds of AI chatbots, like the ones purpose-built to handle tasks like customer service, but broadly speaking, consumer chatbots are useful for reactive tasks. The chatbot can respond to your requests and questions, but without a specific prompt or ask from you, it won’t proactively do anything beyond that set task or beyond the scope of its existing knowledge-base.

AI Agents, however, operate very differently, and can do a lot more proactive tasks. Most agents will use a chatbot interface, but that’s just the beginning. With an agent, you ask it a question or assign it a task, and the agent itself will plan out the best course of action. Most importantly, the agent can then execute on that plan.

For instance, AI coding agents, and “vibe coding,” can famously let people build and code through an agent. Whether you’re a developer or not, you can ask the agent to create an app that performs a specific task, and the agent will fill in the blanks in order to build and design that app without needing any particular oversight or guidance beyond your initial ask.

In terms of day-to-day tasks, an AI chatbot can help you write an email asking when your friends are available next week for game night.

The difference is that an AI agent can draft the email, and then send it out to your guest list. When your friends respond, the agent can find an appropriate time for everyone, create a calendar event, and send out the calendar invites. On the night of the get-together, it can even place an order for pizza and snacks.

Examples like this come with natural follow-up questions. For instance: “that sounds great, but wouldn’t the agent need to access my email, calendar, and Uber Eats account to do that?”

The short answer is “yes.” The more an AI can do on your behalf, the more access it may need to your accounts and information.

Access: predictable connections versus changing needs

An AI chatbot has a defined set of permissions. It has access to certain knowledge-repositories, and can then access your conversation and any other relevant information that you directly share with it, like a document or integration.

More importantly, chatbots typically have fairly consistent access requirements across their various use-cases. If a chatbot needs more information to answer a question or request, it might ask you to share that information with it, but it won’t take action beyond that to seek the information out.

An agent, however, may need access to several systems to complete a task, and those access needs will vary from task to task. Planning a vacation could involve your calendar, email, travel websites, or airline accounts. Building an app could require access to code repositories, development tools, cloud services, and API keys.

Personal assistants and coding agents become useful when they can finish the work in the real account or app where the work belongs. That means they eventually reach a sign-in or protected resource. To interface with those systems, the agent will need you to give it access to that system.

And the key question isn’t whether an agent is connected, but how it connects, and for how long?

Context: short-term conversations versus dynamic retention

Imagine: you’re several paragraphs into a conversation with an AI chatbot when you ask it to “draft an email to Melissa.” The chatbot asks you to clarify who Melissa is, even though you’d shared information about her at the beginning of the chat.

At an essential level, this happens because LLMs and AI tools work within context windows. That refers to the amount of information (measured in tokens) that the AI tool is capable of “thinking” about at any given time.

Note: context is different from the memory or history stored by a platform. Many AI chatbot platforms store your past conversations and history indefinitely for you to retrieve later.

While specific context windows vary across platforms, it’s an essential truth that AI chatbots have much smaller context windows than AI agents do. When you start a new chat session, the chatbot can’t “remember” or consider anything from your previous chats. In a long enough conversation, it will even “forget” information that you shared earlier in the conversation.

With AI agents, context works very differently. As Salesforce puts it, “...agents rely on persistent memory…Unlike one-off interactions, agents need to remember user preferences and ongoing tasks to accurately help customers.”

Agents can store context for longer periods and use it far more dynamically. They can “remember” information you previously shared for separate tasks, and may even draw on information from the other services you’ve given them access to.

Risk: leaked information vs unintended action

To summarize:

  • AI agents typically need far more access to your information and accounts than AI chatbots do.

  • AI agents store and use your information in far longer context windows, in more varied ways, and for longer periods of time.

  • AI agents are capable of taking proactive and complex action across different systems, without requiring an explicit command or oversight from the user.

All of these factors contribute to one of the most drastic distinctions between AI chatbots and AI agents: the level of risk they pose to your information.

AI chatbots are not without risk. Certainly you shouldn’t share any sensitive information like credentials within a chat window, to reduce the risk of that information being leaked from your chat history.

AI agent risk, however, is far less simple to handle. Unlike chatbots, agents require access to your accounts and sensitive information in order to help you effectively. But agents are also able to use that information and access in ways you didn’t intend. That’s why you need a clear moment requiring human approval to control when and how an agent can safely access your accounts.

How to use AI agents safely

When an agent first reaches a sign-in page that it can’t access, it asks you for the credential to sign in. At this point, you can either:

  1. Manually enter your sign-in information every time the agent needs it, which somewhat defeats the purpose of a tool that relies on convenience and automation.

  2. Paste your password into a prompt, which means allowing the agent to have access to your credential and account, potentially beyond the task at hand.

Neither of those options is acceptable.

  5. The agent keeps working without seeing the password or the rest of your vault.

items.title: Chrome DevTools Keyboard Shortcuts Cheat Sheet
items.summary: DevTools has hundreds of shortcuts, and you need about twenty. This cheat sheet keeps the ones that save time every day, grouped by what you are doing, with the keys for Windows and Linux and for Mac side by side. Most of these only work while DevTools has focus : click inside it first. They work the same in Edge and every other Chromium browser. Open DevTools ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Open or close DevTools F12 or Ctrl + Shift + I ⌘ + Option + I Open DevTools on the Console Ctrl + Shift + J ⌘ + Option + J Inspect an element on the page Ctrl + Shift + C ⌘ + Shift + C Open the Command Menu Ctrl + Shift + P ⌘ + Shift + P Open a file of the page Ctrl + P ⌘ + P Search across all files Ctrl + Shift + F ⌘ + Option + F Open DevTools Settings F1 or ? F1 or ? Learn the Command Menu first. It is the one shortcut that replaces the others: type "screenshot", "dark", "disable JavaScript", "sensors", "coverage" or "blocking" and run the command, without knowing which panel or menu hides it. Delete the > and it becomes the file finder ( Ctrl + P ). Move around DevTools ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Next / previous panel Ctrl + ] / Ctrl + [ ⌘ + ] / ⌘ + [ Switch dock position (bottom, side, ...) Ctrl + Shift + D ⌘ + Shift + D Show or hide the drawer (Console, ...) Esc Esc Toggle device mode Ctrl + Shift + M ⌘ + Shift + M Zoom DevTools in / out / reset Ctrl + + / Ctrl + - / Ctrl + 0 ⌘ + + / ⌘ + - / ⌘ + 0 The drawer is underrated: press Esc in the Elements or Network panel and a Console opens underneath, so you can run code against what you are looking at. Debug JavaScript (Sources panel) ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Pause or resume F8 or Ctrl + \ F8 or ⌘ + \ Step over the next call F10 or Ctrl + ' F10 or ⌘ + ' Step into the next call F11 or Ctrl + ; F11 or ⌘ + ; Step out of the current function Shift + F11 or Ctrl + Shift + ; Shift + F11 or ⌘ + Shift + ; Toggle a breakpoint on the current line Ctrl + B ⌘ + B Deactivate all breakpoints Ctrl + F8 ⌘ + F8 Go to line Ctrl + G Ctrl + G Go to a function in the file Ctrl + Shift + O ⌘ + Shift + O On a Mac, the function keys may need Fn , which is why the letter versions exist. Deactivate, don't delete. Ctrl + F8 switches every breakpoint off at once and keeps them where they are, for when you want the page to run normally for a minute. Elements panel ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Hide the selected element H H Edit the element as HTML F2 Fn + F2 Delete the selected element Delete Delete Undo a change Ctrl + Z ⌘ + Z Expand or collapse a node → / ← → / ← Search the DOM (text, selector, XPath) Ctrl + F ⌘ + F H toggles visibility: hidden on the element, so the layout keeps its space. It is the fastest way to see what is underneath a modal, a banner or a sticky header. Console ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Clear the console Ctrl + L ⌘ + K New line without running Shift + Enter Shift + Enter Previous / next command ↑ / ↓ ↑ / ↓ Accept an autocomplete Tab or → Tab or → The Console also answers to a few shortcuts in code: $0 is the element selected in the Elements panel, $_ the last result, and copy(value) puts any value on your clipboard. Network panel ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Start or stop recording Ctrl + E ⌘ + E Reload, recording from the start Ctrl + R ⌘ + R Hard reload, ignoring the cache Ctrl + Shift + R ⌘ + Shift + R With DevTools open, right-click (or long-press) the browser's reload button for Empty cache and hard reload , which also clears what the page cached. Our guide to the Network tab covers the panel itself: filters, timing, Copy as cURL, blocking and overrides. Browser shortcuts developers use all day ​ Action Windows / Linux Mac Jump to the address bar Ctrl + L ⌘ + L Reopen the last closed tab Ctrl + Shift + T ⌘ + Shift + T Next / previous tab Ctrl + Tab / Ctrl + Shift + Tab ⌘ + Option + → / ⌘ + Option + ← View the page source Ctrl + U ⌘ + Option + U Open a new incognito window Ctrl + Shift + N ⌘ + Shift + N Open the history page Ctrl + H ⌘ + Y An incognito window is the quickest clean profile: no cookies, no cache, and no extensions unless you allowed them there. Shortcuts for what DevTools does not do ​ DevTools inspects what the page sends and receives. Changing it, so you can see how the page copes with a different answer, is where an extension takes over. tweak mocks and modifies responses, rewrites headers, redirects and blocks requests, and it has its own shortcuts: Action Windows / Linux Mac Start or stop tweak on the tab Ctrl + Shift + , ⌘ + Shift + , Open tweak Ctrl + Shift + . ⌘ + Shift + . Open or close the Developer Toolbox Ctrl + Shift + Y ⌘ + Shift + Y Search your rules (in tweak) Ctrl + K ⌘ + K The full list, and how to change them, is in the shortcuts docs . Make your own ​ DevTools : Settings ( F1 ) > Shortcuts lists every shortcut, lets you change one, and can switch the whole keymap to Visual Studio Code's. Extensions : chrome://extensions/shortcuts sets or changes the shortcuts of every extension you have installed. FAQ ​ What is the keyboard shortcut to open Chrome DevTools? F12 or Ctrl + Shift + I on Windows and Linux, Cmd + Option + I on a Mac. Ctrl + Shift + J (Cmd + Option + J) opens it on the Console, and Ctrl + Shift + C (Cmd + Shift + C) opens it in inspect element mode. What is the most useful DevTools shortcut to learn first? The Command Menu: Ctrl + Shift + P, or Cmd + Shift + P on a Mac. Type what you want (screenshot, dark mode, disable JavaScript, sensors, blocking) and run it, without knowing which panel or menu it lives in. How do I see every DevTools shortcut? Open DevTools Settings with F1 (or ? while DevTools has focus) and pick Shortcuts. It lists every shortcut, and you can switch the keymap to Visual Studio Code's. Why does a DevTools shortcut not work? Most of them only work while DevTools has focus. Click inside DevTools first. On a Mac, some function keys need Fn, and the operating system or another extension may take a combination before Chrome sees it. Summary ​ Learn three first: open DevTools ( F12 ), inspect an element ( Ctrl + Shift + C ) and the Command Menu ( Ctrl + Shift + P ). Add the debugger's step keys when you next set a breakpoint, and Esc for the drawer. The rest you can look up here, or in DevTools Settings > Shortcuts. If you liked this article, consider sharing ( tweeting ) it to your followers. Did you like this article? Yes No Need something else? Request a feature Thanks for your feedback!

FAQ​
What is the keyboard shortcut to open Chrome DevTools?

F12 or Ctrl + Shift + I on Windows and Linux, Cmd + Option + I on a Mac. Ctrl + Shift + J (Cmd + Option + J) opens it on the Console, and Ctrl + Shift + C (Cmd + Shift + C) opens it in inspect element mode.

What is the most useful DevTools shortcut to learn first?

The Command Menu: Ctrl + Shift + P, or Cmd + Shift + P on a Mac. Type what you want (screenshot, dark mode, disable JavaScript, sensors, blocking) and run it, without knowing which panel or menu it lives in.

How do I see every DevTools shortcut?

Open DevTools Settings with F1 (or ? while DevTools has focus) and pick Shortcuts. It lists every shortcut, and you can switch the keymap to Visual Studio Code's.

Why does a DevTools shortcut not work?

Most of them only work while DevTools has focus. Click inside DevTools first. On a Mac, some function keys need Fn, and the operating system or another extension may take a combination before Chrome sees it.

Summary​

Learn three first: open DevTools (F12), inspect an element (Ctrl + Shift + C) and the Command Menu (Ctrl + Shift + P). Add the debugger's step keys when you next set a breakpoint, and Esc for the drawer. The rest you can look up here, or in DevTools Settings > Shortcuts.
